items.title: 32 lanes, 8.6 chains
items.text:
mibz2 · Research blog

This post asks how much parallel work the CPU actually does inside mibz2's inverse-BWT decoder, and whether hardware capacity is lost to the way Rust compiles the loop.

The interesting part is that the suspected problem may not be too little parallelism at all. The figures could instead mean that the CPU already hides memory latency well, but spends too many instructions on each decoded byte.

items.title: 32 lanes, 8.6 chains: where the inverse BWT walk spends its cycles
items.text:
The decoder's 32-lane walk runs 8.6 times faster than one chain. That figure may not mean what it seems: the walk may already hide memory latency, and spend too many instructions on each byte.

31 October 2026 · 7 min read · Open question

items.title: 1. Why does the BWT decoder have 32 lanes?
items.text:
The inverse BWT repeatedly looks up the next position in a table. Simplifying the actual code:

let q = t[row];
row = q >> 8;
output.push(q as u8);

The next lookup depends on the result of the previous one: ri+1 = Ψ(ri).

The CPU cannot know where to look next until the current lookup completes. This is called pointer chasing, and along one chain it is inherently serial.

mibz2's answer is to divide the inverse-BWT traversal into 512 segments and walk up to 32 independent segments at once. Each lane has its own row position, destination and segment state.

Independent traversal chains

in flight togetherLane 0lookup 1lookup 2lookup 3lookup 4lookup 5Lane 1lookup 1lookup 2lookup 3lookup 4lookup 5Lane 2lookup 1lookup 2lookup 3lookup 4lookup 5⋮⋮ 28 more lanes ⋮Lane 31lookup 1lookup 2lookup 3lookup 4lookup 5timeAlong a lane, each lookup waits for the previous one. Across lanes, nothing waits. Four of the 32 lanes. Within a lane, each lookup waits for the one before it; across lanes, the CPU can overlap the lookups.

The source calls this walk room_segments::<32, PF_L1>. The PF_L1 part enables a prefetch hint for the next T-vector entry. The "room" algorithm batches output writes to avoid a buffer-capacity check on every byte, but it still performs one dependent lookup for every decoded byte.

items.title: 2. Where does "8.6 effective chains" come from?
items.text:
Two measured figures:

Measurement Cost One dependent chain 38.55 cycles/byte The 32-lane room walk 4.49 cycles/byte

Their ratio is 38.55 ÷ 4.49 = 8.59.

So the walk achieves about 8.6 times the byte rate of the serial chain, provided the two measurements are comparable. It does not mean that only 8.6 of the 32 lanes are working.

That distinction decides whether the next optimisation should look for more parallelism, or for less work per byte.

items.title: 3. Why 32 lanes might yield only an 8.6× speed-up
items.text:
Imagine a processor that takes 39 cycles to complete a dependent table lookup. If one lookup starts every 4.49 cycles, the average number in progress is about 39 ÷ 4.49 ≈ 8.7.

That is Little's law: concurrency equals request rate multiplied by latency. Computer architecture distinguishes this achieved memory-level parallelism from the number of independent chains a program makes available.

But consider what that means for mibz2. A full round of the walk, one step for each of the 32 lanes, takes 32 × 4.49 ≈ 144 cycles.

One round of the room walk, against one lookup's latency

One round: the walker steps each of its 32 lanes once, one step every 4.49 cycleslane 0lane 0 again32 × 4.49 ≈ 144 cyclesEach step starts a lookup that takes about 38.55 cycles to come backat any moment ≈ 38.55 ÷ 4.49 ≈ 8.6 lookups in progresslane 0’s lookup is back long before its next turn: all 32 lanes keep moving without 32 loads in flight Illustrative, from the two measured figures above. About 8.6 lookups overlap at any moment, yet every lane's lookup returns long before that lane's next turn.

If a lookup takes roughly 39 cycles, the CPU has ample time to finish a lane's lookup before it comes back to that lane in the next round. So all 32 lanes can be making progress without 32 loads ever being in flight at once.

That would place the bottleneck somewhere else.

There is another caveat. The room walk explicitly prefetches future entries, so its actual demand-load latency may be much lower than the 38.55 cycles of the single chain. The two figures also need the same CPU, revision and cache conditions. So 8.6 is best read as an illustrative latency-hiding factor, not a measured count of outstanding memory requests.

items.title: 4. What to look for in the machine code
items.text:
Here is one iteration of the hot loop, simplified:

for lane in lanes.iter_mut() {
    let q = t[lane.row];                   // dependent load
    if q & START != 0 { /* handoff */ }    // branch
    lane.row = q >> 8;                     // next link
    prefetch(t, lane.row);                 // future memory request
    *base[lane_index].add(off) = q as u8;  // output store
}

Several explanations compete:

Suspected limit What it means Register pressure Too few architectural registers to hold all 32 lanes' row and output state, so the generated loop keeps reloading and storing bookkeeping Instruction-window pressure Too many instructions separate successive independent T-vector loads, which limits what the CPU can have in flight Execution throughput Address generation, branches, prefetches and stores use enough execution resources to set a floor in cycles per byte Memory-system saturation The core already overlaps enough lookups, and exposing more chains won't help

A Zen 3 core, for example, has a 256-entry reorder window and a finite number of load and miss-tracking resources: substantial, but not unlimited.

Reading the disassembly, not just the Rust, shows which dependencies LLVM actually creates. One promising possibility is that the CPU spends too much time maintaining lane.row, lane.seg, lane.p and lane.end relative to the useful BWT lookup.

The segment-start branch, by contrast, is rarely taken: about 512 boundaries per 900,000 bytes, or 0.057% of steps. Even a 20-cycle misprediction at every boundary costs only about 0.011 cycles per byte, so boundary mispredictions alone can't explain an opportunity of more than 1 cycle per byte. The throughput of the per-byte branch and bookkeeping could still matter.

items.title: 5. What does "four groups of eight" mean?
items.text:
This is scalar batching, not necessarily SIMD. The idea is to arrange the 32 logical lanes as four groups of eight, so that each group's working state is easier for the compiler to keep in registers.

But there's a trap.

Batching the 32 lanes as four groups of eight

Interleaved groupseach step touches every groupgroup 0group 1group 2group 332 chains exposedbookkeeping per group, overlap keptOne group at a timeseveral rounds of group 0, then group 1, …group 0group 1group 2group 38 chains exposedlatency floor ≥ 38.55 ÷ 8 = 4.82 c/B (today: 4.49) Green lanes have a lookup the CPU can overlap. Batching helps only if every group still has lookups in flight within the processor's instruction window.

If an implementation runs several rounds of group 0 before touching groups 1 to 3, it may expose only eight independent chains to the CPU at once. Under the idealised 38.55-cycle latency, eight chains have a latency floor of 38.55 ÷ 8 = 4.82 cycles per byte, already slower than today's 4.49.

That doesn't prove batching fails: real latency changes with prefetching and caching. But it shows how saving register operations can lose to reduced overlap.

The better transformation reduces lane bookkeeping while still exposing independent loads from all four groups within the processor's instruction window.

items.title: 6. What would count as a breakthrough?
items.text:
The question is which of two fundamentally different paths applies.

Two diagnoses, two different optimisations

Path AInsufficient overlapGenerated code serialises loads thatthe algorithm keeps independent.Fix: remove those dependencies,without spilling lane state.Path B · current hypothesisToo much work per byteOverlap is already sufficient; theinstruction stream sets the pace.Fix: fewer reloads, address and outputsteps per byte, all 32 chains kept. Path B is an inference from the lane-count curve flattening near 24 lanes and from the 32-lane walk already tolerating one chain's latency. It is not yet a verified machine-code finding.

Path A, insufficient overlap: show that the generated code serialises independent loads unnecessarily, then remove those dependencies without giving up register locality or adding costly memory traffic.

Path B, too much work per byte: show that overlap is already sufficient and that the core is limited by its instruction stream, then reduce row-state reloads, address calculations or output bookkeeping while keeping all 32 chains.

The current hypothesis leans towards Path B, given that the measured lane-count curve flattens near 24 lanes, and that the 32-lane scheme already tolerates one chain's latency. That is an inference, not a verified finding.

So the question to settle is:

Are the 32 chains insufficiently exposed, or are they already exposed well enough, while the processor wastes cycles advancing each one?

The two answers call for completely different optimisations, which is why a careful, disassembly-level investigation is worth doing.

A way to save roughly 1.2 cycles per walked byte, on the later decoder baseline of 10.78 cycles per byte, would be worth about 11% of total decoder time, before any gain from the MTF stage. That is why this direction has much greater breakthrough potential than further polishing the MTF selector.

items.title: Block dispatch in mibz2
items.text:
mibz2 · Research blog

mibz2 has two very different kinds of parallelism:

  1. Across blocks: different CPU cores decompress different bzip2 blocks at the same time.
  2. Within a block: each worker follows 32 independent chains through the inverse BWT's table, to hide memory latency. The previous post is about that one.

This post is about the first kind: how work is handed to the workers, and an apparent delay in that handoff that may or may not be a real bottleneck. Finding out which takes a short tour of mutexes, futexes and the Linux scheduler.

items.title: Block dispatch in mibz2: mutexes, futexes and the scheduler
items.text:
How mibz2's parallel decoder hands blocks to its workers, why some take up to a millisecond to be picked up, and how to tell lock contention from scheduling delay.

1 November 2026 · 12 min read · Investigation in progress

items.title: 1. The journey of a bzip2 block
items.text:
The journey of a bzip2 block through mibz2

Compressed streamA long sequence of bzip2 blocks, read in chunks by the feeder thread (mibz2-read)Scanner · mibz2-scanFinds each block in order, reads its header and Huffman-decodes its symbolsShared job channel · Mutex<Receiver<Job>>Worker 0 · mibz2-0one block at a timeWorker 1 · mibz2-1one block at a timeWorker 2 · mibz2-2one block at a timeWorker 3 · mibz2-3one block at a timeMove-to-front, the inverse BWT, RLE1 and the block's CRCready · a map keyed by block positionEach worker publishes its finished block here, in whatever order it finishesReader · the caller's own threadTakes the blocks in stream order and hands back their bytes Seven threads in all at four workers: the feeder, the scanner, four workers and the caller's thread as the reader. At most a fixed number of blocks (the window, slots) is between the scanner and the reader at any time.

A bzip2 block goes through several stages. In mibz2 they are split between two kinds of thread:

Stage Thread Why there Find the block, read its header, Huffman-decode its symbols the scanner A block's end is only known once its symbols are read, so this part is sequential Move-to-front and its run expansion a worker Independent per block Inverse BWT: build the table, walk it a worker The expensive part, and independent per block RLE1 and the block's CRC a worker Independent per block

This split matters for everything below: a faster inverse BWT can't help if the scanner, or the handoff of jobs to workers, becomes the limit.

All seven threads (the feeder, the scanner, four workers and the reader) share the CPUs the operating system gives them. In the measurements below that is four physical cores, so there are moments when more threads could run than there are cores to run them.

items.title: 2. Two waits in three lines of Rust
items.text:
Here is how a worker gets its next job, from src/parallel.rs:

let job = {
    let rx = jobs.lock().unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner());
    rx.recv()
};

jobs is a Mutex<Receiver<Job>>: one standard-library channel receiver, shared by all the workers behind a mutex. Two different waits can happen here:

  1. Waiting for the mutex. Another worker holds it, so this one can't reach recv().
  2. Waiting for a job. This worker holds the mutex, but the channel is empty, so recv() parks the thread until the scanner sends something.

The second wait happens while the mutex is held: the guard rx lives until the end of the block. That makes possible a situation that is easy to miss in the code:

Four workers, one shared receiver

Worker AAsleep inside recv(): no job yetHolds the receiver mutexWorker BWaiting for the receiver mutexCannot reach recv() at allWorker CDecoding a blockWorker DDecoding another blockThe scanner enqueues two jobsA must wake, return from recv() and drop the lock before B can even start waiting for one The possible receiver convoy. A true multi-consumer queue would let A and B wait for jobs independently. Whether this sequence happens often enough to matter is what the diagnostic measures.

None of this is incorrect. Every job is still taken exactly once, in order. The question is only whether it is slow.

items.title: What a futex is
items.text:
When worker B "waits for the mutex", what actually happens? On Linux, Rust's standard Mutex is a single atomic word, with a futex ("fast userspace mutex") behind it.

How a futex-backed mutex waits

Worker B wants the receiver mutexRust's std Mutex on Linux: one atomic word, and a futex behind itThe lock is freeOne atomic compare-and-swap, entirely in userspace.No system call, no kernel involvement.Fast pathThe lock is heldSpin briefly, then futex(FUTEX_WAIT): the kerneltakes the thread off the CPU until it is woken.Contended pathUnlock: futex(FUTEX_WAKE)The kernel makes one waiter runnable.Runnable is not running: it still needs a CPU. Only the contended path reaches the kernel, which is why kernel traces see futex calls for contention and never for an uncontended lock. The trace marks in mibz2's own code cover both.

A futex is the kernel's way of letting a thread sleep on an address until another thread says "wake up". Most lock operations never need it. The channel's recv() sleeps the same way: it parks the thread on a futex of its own.

items.title: 3. Woken is not running
items.text:
This is the distinction the whole investigation turns on. A thread can be in three states:

State Using a CPU? What it means Running Yes Executing instructions, possibly stalled on memory Runnable No, not yet Ready to execute; waiting for the scheduler to give it a CPU Asleep No Waiting for an event: a futex wake, a job, a lock

A worker's wake-up, in three states

Runnable, not runningReady to execute; waiting for the scheduler to give it a CPUAsleepParked in recv() or on the mutexRunningTakes the lock, receivesJob arrivesWorker wokenWorker runningJob claimed Conceptual timing, not measured values. A futex moves a thread from asleep to runnable; only the scheduler moves it from runnable to running.

So when a job takes a long time to be claimed, there are at least three different explanations, each calling for a different response:

Explanation What would help Mutex ownership: the worker is asleep because another worker owns the receiver A true multi-consumer queue, so idle workers wait independently Scheduling: the worker is runnable, but every CPU is busy with another thread Nothing in the queue, and perhaps nothing at all if those threads are doing useful work Backlog: every worker is busy decoding, so the job simply waits its turn Nothing in the queue: decoding faster

A simple application-level trace can't tell these apart. All three show up as "the job was enqueued at t₀ and claimed at t₁".

items.title: 4. What the traces have shown so far
items.text:
The decoder can record its own timeline: a mark at each step of each thread, with a nanosecond timestamp. On an i9-10900K, decoding a 207 MB slice of Wikidata at four workers, some jobs took nearly a millisecond to be claimed. That looked suspicious, until the delays were sorted by how busy the workers were when the job arrived:

Most slow claims are queueing

Workers decoding when the job arrivedMedian time from enqueue to claim0 of 49% of jobs49.5 µs1 of 417% of jobs48.4 µs2 of 430% of jobs61.6 µs3 of 441% of jobs977 µs4 of 43% of jobs1,221 µs The i9-10900K's ten four-worker traces of the Wikidata corpus. With three or four workers busy, the next job usually waits behind decoding already under way: ordinary queueing, not evidence of lock contention by itself.

Most of the slow claims are backlog. But a smaller set is more interesting: jobs that arrived with three workers decoding, no older job waiting, and one worker free. For those, the free worker's last recorded step tells us where it was:

The free worker's last mark when the job arrived Cases Median time to claim JobRecv: holding the mutex, inside recv() 198 42 µs JobLock: about to take the mutex 149 454 µs

When the free worker is already inside recv(), it claims the job in a median of 42 µs. When it is still trying to take the mutex, it takes ten times as long, and another worker claimed the job first in 89 of the 149 cases.

That gap could be mutex contention. But the kernel's own accounting of each thread's run-queue wait, read between decodes, points elsewhere: in the 120 gaps between decodes that contain such a JobLock case, 78% of the elapsed time was runnable but not running. The workers were awake and eligible to run, but weren't on a CPU. Across all the gaps between decodes, the figure is 34%.

That still doesn't make the delay waste. With seven threads on four cores, a runnable worker may simply be waiting while the scanner or another worker does useful work. The question is what the other CPUs were doing at that moment.

items.title: 5. The reader has its own wait
items.text:
When a worker finishes a block it doesn't write to the output. It publishes the block into a shared ready map keyed by its position, and the reader takes blocks strictly in order.

Blocks finish out of order

#0Still decoding#1Ready#2Ready#3ReadyThe reader cannot hand back block 1 before block 0, though blocks 1–3 are finished.Four slots are held until #0 is done; with a window of eight, the scanner can admit only four more. Finished blocks wait in ready for their turn. The bounded window keeps that wait from turning into unbounded memory.

The scanner is held back by a bounded admission window: at most slots blocks may be between the scanner and the reader (eight at four workers). Before reading the next block, the scanner waits:

while !st.cancelled && st.issued - st.taken >= shared.slots {
    st = shared.cv.wait(st).unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner());
}

That keeps memory bounded when one slow block holds up the reader.

The scanner and the reader share one condition variable, shared.cv, though they wait for different things: the scanner for a free slot, the reader for the next block in order. Workers call notify_all() when they publish a block, and the reader calls it when it takes one. That is correct, but every notification wakes both kinds of waiter, whether or not its own condition changed. Earlier measurements suggested the reader is sometimes late to take a block that is already ready. Whether notification, the lock or scheduling causes that is still open.

items.title: 6. Measuring it without fooling ourselves
items.text:
To separate the three explanations, the next experiment joins two views of the same run:

  • The decoder's own marks, now at every boundary that matters: the attempt to take the receiver mutex, holding it, recv() returning, the guard's release, the decode, the publication, and the reader's waits and wake-ups. Each thread records into a fixed, preallocated buffer, with its operating-system thread id.
  • The kernel's scheduler events, recorded with perf on the allocated CPUs: every wake-up, every switch of a CPU from one thread to another, and every futex wait with its address.

With both, every moment a worker spends not decoding while a job is available can be classified. Was it asleep while another worker owned the receiver? Asleep in the handoff, with the mutex free? Runnable but not running, and if so, what was occupying each CPU? Or publishing, or waiting on the shared lock?

Joining them needs care:

  • Two clocks. The marks use Rust's Instant, and the kernel stamps its events with its own clock. The decoder reads CLOCK_MONOTONIC and immediately makes a recognisable system call, so the gap between the two clocks can be measured from the trace itself. On the preparation machine it is known to within 0.6 µs.
  • The instrument changes what it measures. Each instrumented run is paired with an uninstrumented one. If tracing moves throughput or CPU time by more than 3%, the result is reported as provisional.
  • The decision rules were written down before any data. An isolated multi-consumer queue experiment is justified only if receiver-specific obstruction is at least 5% of the workers' total time, in at least 80% of runs. Runnable time near the mutex is reported beside that, but never counted in it, because it may be ordinary competition for the cores.

items.title: When the instrument lies
items.text:
The preparation runs turned up a lesson worth sharing. A review of the analysis asked a pointed question: could lost kernel events pass unnoticed? Checking it showed they could. perf script prints nothing about events it dropped unless asked with --show-lost-events. Events whose thread perf couldn't resolve were printed in a form the parser skipped.

The surprise came from the kernel itself. On the virtual machine used for preparation, the kernel emitted every switch into idle on three of its four CPUs, but never a switch out of idle. perf's raw dump and ftrace showed the same, so it isn't perf or the parser.

When the instrument lies

What happenedasleeprunnablerunningasleepWhat the trace saidasleeprunnable … still “runnable”asleepAt the green line, the switch from idle into the worker was never emitted (CPUs 1–3).The worker later switched out while “runnable”: the contradiction that gave it away. On the preparation VM, the kernel recorded switches into idle on three of its four CPUs but never the switches out. Running time read as waiting. The analysis now marks such intervals unknown, and refuses a run whose idle switches don't pair.

The effect was subtle and pointed in a dangerous direction. A worker switched in from idle appeared to be woken but never running, so its running time was classified as waiting for a CPU, which is exactly the "scheduling" explanation. In one run, 19 ms of the 77 ms counted as runnable was this artifact.

Now, the analysis:

  • treats any interval the scheduler stream contradicts as unknown;
  • requires every CPU's switches into and out of idle to pair up;
  • runs a short probe before any capture, and refuses to start on a kernel that fails it.

A wrong answer delivered confidently would have been worse than no answer.

items.title: 7. Two problems, one CPU
items.text:
Even with perfect dispatch, four workers each decode less efficiently than one. On the i9, four workers spend about 30% more cycles per decoded byte than one worker, while executing almost the same instructions (1.3% more). The extra cycles go to stalls on memory: each worker's inverse-BWT table competes for the same 20 MB last-level cache, alongside the input, output and intermediate buffers.

Two problems, one CPU

Dispatch efficiencyKeep the workers supplied with jobs andwaste no time waiting.Futexes, the mutex, the scheduler, the channel, notificationsDecoding efficiencySpend fewer cycles and less memorybandwidth on each block.BWT tables, prefetch, cache residency, buffers Better dispatch uses the cores more fully; better decoding makes each core's work cheaper.

These interact. Better dispatch keeps more inverse-BWT walks running at once, which raises the competition for cache and claws back part of its own gain. That is why every experiment is judged on the whole decoder's throughput and CPU-seconds per GB, never on one stage in isolation.

items.title: 8. What happens next
items.text:
The measurement comes next. It ends in one of two places:

  • If receiver ownership really does keep free workers from available jobs, at least 5% of their time in at least 80% of runs, a multi-consumer queue becomes a justified, isolated experiment.
  • If the receiver is usually free and the delay is scheduling or backlog, that hypothesis is retired, and the effort goes to the larger problem: the inverse BWT's memory behaviour.

This post is a snapshot of an investigation in progress, and its figures come from the traces available so far. A few lines of synchronisation code can decide how well a 32-lane, latency-hiding decoder uses a whole multicore CPU. Whether they do here is a question for the evidence.

Sources:

  • the worker, scanner and reader loops: src/parallel.rs;
  • the i9 traces and the cycle accounting: the resource attribution's analysis;
  • the diagnostic's registered protocol: 2026-11-01-dispatch-causality-protocol.md;
  • the trace-completeness checks: amendment 1.

items.title: Inverse-BWT memory interference
items.text:
mibz2 · Research blog

A bzip2 file is a series of independent blocks, so four CPU cores can decode four blocks at once, each with its own data, its own working memory and its own instructions. That's what mibz2 does, and a file finishes much sooner on four cores than on one.

You'd expect the total work to stay about the same, just spread across more cores. It doesn't. With four workers instead of one, mibz2 spends about 32% more CPU time, added up over all the cores, for every gigabyte it decodes.

Little of the extra time goes on handing work between threads. Most of it is inside the decoding itself, where the decoder runs almost the same instructions per byte as before (1.3% more) but needs about 30% more processor cycles to get through them. The same instructions are running slower.

Memory is the obvious suspect. The most expensive step in decoding a block is undoing the Burrows–Wheeler transform, which means following a long chain of links through a table of about 3.6 MB. A core working alone can keep much of that table close at hand in the processor's caches. With four cores at work, four such tables, along with the buffers each worker uses to build and assemble its output, all have to share the processor's last-level cache and the hardware that serves its memory requests.

The suspected problem

One workerCore 1following its table's linksTable AShared cache:room to spareOne table in the shared cacheFour workersCore1ACore2BCore3CCore4DFour tables competing for the same cache A sketch, not a measurement of what's in the cache. Each core has its own table, but all four share the last-level cache and the path to main memory.

If that's what's happening, one worker's memory accesses push out data that another worker was about to use, so its next lookup has to fetch it from further away. Or the shared cache is simply busier, so every request takes longer to answer. Either way, the core spends more of its cycles waiting for data. That's what we mean by memory interference: workers whose logic is independent, competing for the same hardware.

The measurements point that way, but they don't settle it. This post is about two experiments proposed to find out more. One changes how the decoder reuses its memory, and measures whether the extra cost shrinks. The other keeps one decoder fixed and varies what the other cores do with memory, to see which kinds of competition reproduce the slowdown. We're starting with the first, and the rest of the post explains why.

items.title: Investigating inverse-BWT memory interference in mibz2
items.text:
Four workers finish decompression sooner, but together spend 32% more processor time per byte. We're testing whether competition for shared memory is responsible.

1 November 2026 · 14 min read · Research in progress

items.title: 1. What a worker does with each block
items.text:
Each block goes through five steps. Two of the worker's memory buffers, ll and rle, come up throughout the rest of the post.

From compressed symbols to decoded bytes

1. ll — the transformed bytesMTF decoding recovers the bytes as the Burrows–Wheeler transform left them: rearranged2. T-vector — the navigation tableBuilt by reading ll once. Each entry says where to go next, and which byte to write3. Traverse and assemble32 independent chains each rebuild a stretch of the block; the pieces are then copied together in order4. rle — the reconstructed bytesBack in the original order, but runs of a repeated byte are still stored in a short form5. RLE1 — the final expansionExpands those runs into the decompressed output, and checks the block's checksum What a worker does with each block. The worker keeps ll and rle from block to block and refills them each time.
  1. ll holds the transformed bytes. bzip2 compressed the block after rearranging its bytes with the Burrows–Wheeler transform (BWT), and the move-to-front (MTF) decoding stage recovers those rearranged bytes into ll. They are the right bytes in the wrong order: the last column of the transform's sorted table.
  2. The T-vector is built from ll. Building this table reads each byte of ll once. Each entry says which row comes next and which byte to write, so following the links from the right starting point spells out the block in its original order. An earlier post explains the table in more detail.
  3. The traversal follows the links, and assembly joins the pieces. Each lookup depends on the one before, so a single chain of lookups spends most of its time waiting for memory. mibz2 runs 32 chains at once, each rebuilding its own stretch of the block, and switches between them while one waits (the 32 lanes post covers how). The finished stretches are then copied, in order, into one buffer.
  4. That buffer is rle. The block is back in its original order, with one encoding left: before applying the transform, bzip2 had shortened every run of four or more identical bytes into a few bytes and a count.
  5. RLE1 expands those runs into the decoded output, and checks the block's checksum (CRC).

ll and rle aren't registers, and they aren't algorithms. They are two areas of memory holding the same block at different stages: ll before the BWT is undone, rle after it but before the runs are expanded. In the code they are two fields of each worker's scratch space:

ll: Vec<u8>,   // The BWT's last column, written by MTF
rle: Vec<u8>,  // The assembled sequence, before RLE1 expands its runs

items.title: 2. Where the extra time goes
items.text:
We measure efficiency in CPU-seconds per gigabyte of decoded output (CPU-s/GB): the processor time of all the workers added together, per GB produced. Four workers decode a file in much less time than one, but on this measure they cost more.

The cost of decoding on four cores

Full decoder CPU costCPU-seconds per GB of decoded output1 worker2.7074 workers3.579+32.2%CPU time per byteMore workers still increase throughput.Walk + assemblyCPU nanoseconds per BWT row · full blocks1 worker1.2344 workers1.8061.46×CPU cost in this phaseIncludes the segment-assembly copy. Measured on four physical cores. Left: the whole decoder. Right: the traversal and assembly step, on 197 matched full-sized blocks. Both measure CPU time, not elapsed time.

The whole decoder goes from 2.707 to 3.579 CPU-s/GB. Timing each step of each block separately shows where the increase lands:

Step One worker, ns per row Four workers, ns per row Increase MTF decoding 0.456 0.487 1.07× T-vector construction 0.497 0.571 1.15× Traversal and assembly 1.234 1.806 1.46× RLE1 and CRC 0.134 0.180 1.35×

Traversal and assembly take about 79% of the added time across these four steps. Over the whole file, short blocks included, they add about 0.61 CPU-s/GB.

The timing so far can't split that step in two. It covers both the link-following and the copying of the finished pieces into rle, so we don't yet know how much of the 1.46× belongs to each.

The traces also show a pattern. A block's traversal took a median 1.29× its one-worker time when no other worker was traversing at the same moment, and 1.66× when all three others were. That fits the memory story, but it doesn't prove it: a slower traversal also overlaps more of the others' traversals simply by lasting longer.

items.title: 3. Why the counters don't settle it
items.text:
The processor's performance counters narrow things down without picking a culprit.

Per decoded byte, the number of data requests that miss each core's private caches barely changes between one and four workers. Each request seems to take longer, though: by an approximate measure, it stays outstanding for about 58 processor cycles rather than 39. Traffic to main memory (DRAM) also rises sharply, especially writes.

Those clues fit several explanations:

  • The tables crowd each other out. Each worker's table pushes the others' entries out of the last-level cache (the L3, shared by all the cores), so more lookups have to go to DRAM.
  • The shared cache is congested. The lookups still find their data in the L3, but they queue for longer because four cores are asking at once.
  • The writes get in the way. To write to memory, a core first takes exclusive ownership of the cache line, and the changed line must later be written back. Writes can also push out useful data and tie up the hardware that loads and prefetches need.

These feed into each other. A little more eviction makes prefetches arrive later, later requests hold hardware resources for longer, and that slows the requests behind them. The counters can't tell us which one starts the chain.

The request-duration figure is a good example. It counts the prefetches the traversal issues in advance alongside the lookups it actually waits for, so it shows that memory behaviour changed without telling us how long any single lookup waited. And the extra DRAM writes could be a symptom rather than a cause: the same crowding that slows the traversal would produce them too. The research record has the counters in full.

So there are two ways forward: change how the decoder uses memory and see what happens, or recreate the competition under controlled conditions and see what it does. Astra and Claude each proposed one.

items.title: 4. Astra's proposal: write the output into ll
items.text:
Our research register is a list of about 165 ideas for speeding up the decoder, gathered from the project's journals, branches, issues and pull requests, each with its status and what would test it. Entry P87, "walk output in L's freed buffer", had been recorded there but never tried. Astra's experiment is a careful test of it.

The idea rests on when each buffer's contents stop mattering. Once the T-vector is built, nothing reads the bytes in ll again for that block: the traversal reads only the table. The bytes are dead, but the memory holding them, about 0.9 MB for a full block, is still allocated, and it sits idle until the next block's MTF output fills it.

P87 writes the assembled bytes into that idle memory instead of into rle. The bytes written are identical, and so is the copy that writes them. What changes is which memory the copy lands in.

The proposed P87 comparison

A · Current decoderAssembled bytes go to separate storagell: BWT last-column bytesWritten by MTF · about 0.9 MBT-vector construction reads llThe last use of ll's contentsTraversal: temporary segments32 lanes, each a stretch of the blockAssemble into separate rleIts own storage, written every blockRLE1 expands rle into the final outputB · P87Assembled bytes reuse ll's storagell: BWT last-column bytesWritten by MTF · about 0.9 MBT-vector construction reads llNow ll's contents are no longer neededTraversal: temporary segmentsThe same lanes, the same segmentsAssemble into reusable llThe same bytes, over the dead contentsRLE1 expands ll into the final outputThe assembled bytes are identical in both arms. Only the storage they are written into changes. Both arms build and traverse the same table, produce the same pieces and copy them the same way, so the assembled bytes are identical. Only the memory receiving them differs.

items.title: Why it could help
items.text:
Writing into ll means the worker touches about 0.9 MB less distinct memory per block, and so needs fewer separate cache lines in a writable state. That could mean less of the crowding, fewer ownership requests and fewer write-backs to main memory. Any saving would matter most when another worker is following its own table at the same time.

There's a subtlety in the timing. Assembly happens after the traversal it follows, so changing where the assembly writes can't speed up that same traversal. If the traversal gets cheaper under P87, the saving must come indirectly: from less competition with the other workers, from a different cache state carried into the next block, or from the steps overlapping differently. A cheaper traversal would therefore tell us more than a cheaper assembly.

items.title: Why it might not
items.text:
Both buffers are already reused from block to block. ll was written by MTF and read by the table build shortly before; rle was last read by RLE1 during the previous block. By the time assembly starts, the traversal may have pushed most of either one out of the cache, in which case reusing ll saves nothing.

The experiment measures whether the difference matters rather than assuming it does. To keep the comparison fair, both versions allocate both buffers at full size and touch their memory once in advance. Otherwise a gain could come from simply allocating less, or from the operating system mapping fewer fresh pages. Whether a production version could drop rle altogether, and save the memory, would be a separate question.

items.title: 5. Claude's proposal: vary what the neighbours do
items.text:
Claude's proposal comes at the problem from the other side. Instead of changing the decoder, it measures one decoding worker while controlling what the other three cores do.

The measured worker decodes as usual, building and traversing its tables, with counters around each step. The three neighbouring cores run one chosen kind of workload at a time.

One measured worker, three controlled neighbours

Four physical cores on the same processorCORE 1Target walkerSame decoding workMeasured every armCORE 2NeighbourControlled workloadChanges between armsCORE 3NeighbourControlled workloadChanges between armsCORE 4NeighbourControlled workloadChanges between armsShared last-level cacheCapacity, line replacement, requests and shared-cache contentionMemory controller and DRAM The measured worker is held fixed while the three neighbours run controlled workloads. The diagram shows what the cores share; it doesn't imply that each shared resource can be varied on its own.

Each workload stresses a different part of the memory system:

Neighbour workload What it tests Real decoding work Whether the setup reproduces the real slowdown at all Only traversal, or only table building Whether traversal suffers more from other traversals or from table builds Read-only data of several sizes Whether a bigger footprint in the shared cache makes traversal steadily slower Heavy writers Whether writes and write-backs are especially damaging Many L3 requests from a small footprint Whether request traffic alone, without much cache space, reproduces the slowdown Streaming to and from DRAM Whether main-memory traffic reproduces it

The results could separate the explanations from section 3. If traversal slows steadily as the neighbours' read-only data grows, even though they make few requests, cache capacity looks like the problem. If a small workload making many L3 requests slows it just as much, while large but rarely touched data does little, congestion in the shared cache looks more likely. Neighbours that only traverse, or only build, would also show whether the pattern from section 2, slower traversals when more traversals overlap, holds up under control.

items.title: The catch
items.text:
These workloads don't isolate one hardware resource each. A workload that holds data in the cache has to keep touching it, which makes requests of its own. A heavy writer changes the ownership traffic as well as the write-backs. A DRAM stream can match the decoder's average bandwidth with a quite different mix of reads, writes and bursts. So the experiment would measure how sensitive a traversal is to each kind of neighbour, rather than assign the real slowdown, fraction by fraction, to particular hardware.

It also depends on the setup behaving like the real decoder in the first place. Four independent decoding loops lack the real decoder's scanner, its buffer reuse and its mix of overlapping traversals. Claude proposed requiring real decoding neighbours to reproduce at least 70% of the real slowdown before going further. That's a sensible gate, but failing it would only show that the setup wasn't realistic enough. It wouldn't show that the real decoder is free of interference. Making the setup realistic enough is a project in itself.

items.title: 6. Why P87 comes first
items.text:
P87: reuse ll Controlled neighbours Changes Which memory the assembly writes into What the other cores do with memory Measures The whole decoder's efficiency One fixed traversal's cost Strength Directly tests a change we could ship Can identify a broader cause Limitation Tests one change only Results depend on how realistic the setup is If it succeeds Validate the change for production Design a change aimed at the resource it identifies

P87 doesn't come first because it has more to gain. The neighbour experiment may well point to a bigger opportunity, in how the tables sit in the cache or how requests compete for it. P87 comes first because it asks a smaller question whose answer changes what we do next. If it works, we have an improvement that keeps the current four-byte table and the 32-chain traversal. If it doesn't, we can drop this idea without first having to explain the whole memory system.

items.title: What would count as success
items.text:
Astra proposed measuring both versions, the current one (A) and the one that reuses ll (B), at one worker and at four. Write \(C_{X,w}\) for the CPU-seconds per GB of version \(X\) with \(w\) workers. The saving that appears only under concurrency is then

\[ D = (C_{A,4} - C_{B,4}) - (C_{A,1} - C_{B,1}) \]

which takes the four-worker saving and subtracts whatever saving B already gives a single worker. Astra suggested 0.10 CPU-s/GB as the size that would count as material.

\(D\) answers one question, and a second needs its own test:

MechanismDoes buffer reuse materially reduce theadditional CPU cost associated withconcurrency?Measured by the proposed difference-in-differencesstatistic and its uncertainty.EngineeringIs the actual four-worker decoder fasterand more CPU-efficient, withoutcompromising correctness or memoryrequirements?Measured at the full-decoder boundary.

The two can disagree. A change could make both versions slower while shrinking the gap between them, giving a positive \(D\) with a slower four-worker decoder. And reuse might make assembly or RLE1 cheaper by the same amount at one and four workers: a worthwhile small optimisation, with \(D\) near zero and nothing learned about concurrency.

To tell these cases apart, the experiment times table building, traversal, assembly and RLE1 separately. It also keeps the table building and traversal code identical in both versions, gives both the same memory, and leaves the scheduling of workers alone, so that the comparison is about where the output goes and nothing else.

The research register's original entry for P87 set a different bar, for six to ten workers. That remains a separate question from this four-core experiment.

items.title: 7. Where things stand
items.text:
Neither experiment has shown a speedup yet. P87 is the one we're running first, and the neighbour experiment remains a broader follow-up. What we'd learn depends on the result:

P87 result What it would tell us What we'd do next Faster and cheaper at four workers, with a material \(D\) Where the output goes contributes to the four-worker cost Validate the change, and look at the lifetimes of other buffers Cheaper assembly or RLE1, but \(D\) near zero Reuse helps locally without explaining the traversal slowdown Treat it as a small optimisation Fewer writes to main memory, but the same traversal cost These particular writes weren't what slowed the traversal Stop treating them as a likely cause No meaningful change This kind of reuse doesn't help under these conditions Go back to the neighbour experiment, with a realistic setup The measurement itself proves unreliable Nothing yet Fix the experiment before reading anything into it

Even a material result of 0.10 CPU-s/GB would recover only about 2.8% of the four-worker decoder's CPU cost. That's worth having, but well short of the 1.5–2× gain in throughput we're ultimately after. Getting there will probably take a deeper change to how the table is laid out in memory, how far ahead it's prefetched, or how lookups are served, and the earlier work shows how carefully that has to be done: a smaller table saves cache space for nothing if recovering each link from it becomes too slow. For now the fast four-byte table stays, and P87 leaves it untouched.

The two proposals ask different things. Changing the decoder asks whether one decision about where data lives makes it more efficient. Changing the neighbours asks what kinds of competition make an unchanged traversal more expensive. Both are sound ways to study a performance problem; they just produce different kinds of evidence. We're starting with the direct change because it's smaller, easier to interpret and bears directly on the decoder people use. If it fails, that's a better reason to invest in the broader experiment.

So the question for now is narrower than "why is four-worker decoding expensive?": can writing the output into memory the worker has finished with make concurrent decoding cheaper, without touching the traversal itself?

Research records: Inverse-BWT memory proposal and phase analysis · Research register, including P87 · Dispatch-causality investigation.

items.title: Technical appendix
items.text: ← Memory-level parallelism in mibz2

items.title: Technical appendix: MLP, ILP and the measurements
items.text: This appendix is for readers who want the qualifications and definitions that the main post leaves out to keep its argument moving. Its sections can be read in any order. Nothing new was measured for either page: every result is attributed to the experiment that produced it, and repository sources are pinned to the revisions in the source register, inspected on 2 November 2026. Numbers in square brackets refer to the register.

items.title: 1. The disagreement about ILP and MLP
items.text:
The main post reproduces the replies to Lemire's post [1] and explains the mechanism they argue about. Taking the claims one at a time:

Claim Assessment Interleaving increases available ILP. Yes. Independent loads are independent instructions. It "breaks" the hard dependencies. Imprecise: every dependency within each chain remains. Independent chains are supplied alongside them. IPC and instruction count should be measured. Sensible. They characterise the change but don't by themselves prove its cause. Allocation and cache residency matter. Yes. A random workload hitting L2 and one going to DRAM can give very different curves. The dependencies are "memory loads, not instructions". Loose: loads are instructions. The useful distinction is whether the critical delay is a memory access or ordinary computation. Superscalar execution is a prerequisite for several outstanding loads. Too strong as a general statement (section 2). An in-order processor can't benefit this way. Also too strong. It depends on the design and on the order of the instructions.

items.title: Reviewing, reproducing and explaining
items.text: Three questions are easily run together. Review asks whether the algorithm, source, method and interpretation can be inspected; here they can, as Lemire said. Historical reproduction asks whether the exact 2022 executable, machine state, page mappings, compiler output and run conditions can be recreated, which needs more provenance than source code. Causal attribution asks whether the speedup establishes the mechanism claimed and rules out the alternatives, which needs suitable measurements or interventions. Open source helps with all three and settles only the first. A fair summary: the benchmark is a legitimate way to characterise overlapping dependent traversals, and the stronger readings of its output need more evidence.

items.title: 2. What a core needs to keep several loads in flight
items.text:
Property What it describes Superscalar issue Starting more than one instruction in a cycle Out-of-order issue Starting a later ready instruction before an earlier unready one Nonblocking memory machinery Letting another request progress while an earlier miss is unresolved Memory-level parallelism Memory operations overlapping in time, at a stated level and for a stated population

A core can issue one instruction per cycle and still keep several long-lived requests outstanding across many cycles. Berkeley's original Rocket paper describes a single-issue, in-order scalar pipeline with a nonblocking data cache that supports MLP [9]. Arm's Cortex-A55 optimisation guide documents three outstanding data-cache misses under particular pipeline-spacing conditions, despite in-order issue [8].

That doesn't mean any in-order core matches an aggressive out-of-order one. An in-order design is much more sensitive to software ordering: if a dependent use blocks issue before the next independent load is reached, the independence can't help, so grouping independent loads before their uses matters. Out-of-order execution widens the processor's ability to find and exploit independence on its own; it isn't what defines MLP.

items.title: 3. The historical benchmark in detail
items.text:
The linked repository is lemire/testingmlp. Its last published revision before the article dates from January 2021. That establishes the public implementation available at the time; it doesn't prove the author's exact local checkout or command line. Reading today's changed benchmark as if it were the 2022 implementation would be unsafe. A later post by the same author [29] uses the evolved benchmark, and its settings shouldn't be conflated with the 2022 test. The 2022 post reports approximately:

Reported quantity Ice Lake system Graviton 3 system Single-lane access time 90 ns 120 ns Peak implied bandwidth 12 GB/s 9 GB/s Described simultaneous loads about 25 about 19

with Ubuntu 22.04, GCC 11 and 4 KiB pages. These are measurements of those configurations, not permanent limits attached to the processor names.

items.title: Construction
items.text:
The historical default is an array of 33,554,432 uint64_t entries, 256 MiB. A second array of the same size supports setup, outside the timed traversal. Sattolo's algorithm builds a random permutation that is one long cycle, and the lanes' starting positions are spaced along it. The test uses array-index links and several traversal states, not separately allocated list nodes [2].

The generator emits a distinct function for each lane count, with one local state variable per lane. The inner loop does one dependent lookup for each lane, then repeats. Total useful accesses are approximately fixed at \(H(K) = K \lfloor H/K \rfloor\), so adding lanes changes the schedule of roughly the same accesses rather than multiplying the work. Loop control is amortised over more accesses, and register allocation can change [3].

The timing takes the fastest of five wall-clock trials, and the traversal is kept observable through its returned result. The code collects no retired instructions, actual CPU cycles, request occupancy, cache-source information, page-walk counters or memory-controller traffic [2].

items.title: The bandwidth figure
items.text:
The program computes an implied bandwidth: completed logical accesses times 64 bytes, divided by time. Each architectural load reads eight bytes, so the calculation assumes one cache-line transfer per logical access; it doesn't measure DRAM traffic. The source divides by powers of 1024 while printing MB/s, a small ambiguity in the unit label [2].

Actual traffic differs with cache hits, several entries sharing a line, merged requests, hardware prefetches, page-table reads and other memory activity. Eight 64-bit entries fit in one 64-byte line, so a large random array doesn't guarantee a DRAM transaction for every load. And with several lanes, the ns/hit column is elapsed time divided by aggregate accesses: the reciprocal of throughput, not the service latency of one request.

items.title: Questions the benchmark leaves open
items.text: The design deliberately makes long-latency dependent loads dominant and uses independent chains to expose overlap. That's a sensible microbenchmark. A stricter review would also ask how much work the compiler adds, where requests are served, whether translation limits the result, how stable the curve is, and how loaded latency changes as lanes are added.

items.title: 4. Saturation, translation and read size
items.text:
The historical code reports a possible number of parallel paths when another lane improves time by less than one percent. A noisy point, a spill threshold or a different resource limit can produce such a knee, so a plateau is an observation that needs interpreting [2]. The four quantities often called MLP (software independence, hardware capacity, achieved occupancy, speedup) need not be equal: a program may have 32 active lanes and eight outstanding requests on average; a ten-entry resource may contribute to a system that supports a different count at another boundary; and demand loads, hardware prefetches and page walks may occupy overlapping but different resources.

Travis Downs, a collaborator on the benchmark, explains in the 2019 discussion that the core, the uncore, the memory controller and DRAM all affect the observed overlap. Taking the smallest queue capacity is insufficient because a request holds each resource for a different time. The same discussion shows page-size changes materially moving the saturation point [10].

items.title: Translation
items.text:
A 256 MiB region spans 65,536 pages at 4 KiB or 128 at 2 MiB. Those counts are arithmetic; the performance that follows depends on the TLBs and page walkers. A TLB miss may need memory accesses of its own before the data access can go ahead.

The historical README warns about this and recommends transparent huge pages. The source requests MADV_HUGEPAGE, while the article says the tests used small pages. These aren't in conflict: a request for huge pages doesn't establish the pages obtained, Linux can fall back to ordinary pages, and the effective backing has to be checked [4, 30].

For an application comparison, default page behaviour can legitimately be part of the system being compared. To isolate a core's data-miss machinery, translation has to be controlled or measured separately. Both are useful experiments; they answer different questions.

items.title: Read size
items.text:
There are several granularities: the operand size, the cache-line fill, the useful payload consumed, and the page used for translation. A four-byte lookup can need a 64-byte fill, two adjacent four-byte values may share that line, and an access crossing a line boundary may need two. Widening an operand from four to eight bytes doesn't automatically double the memory cost, while growing a node from one line to two can matter a great deal.

The right bandwidth denominator depends on the question. Useful decoded bytes describe the application's productivity; transferred cache lines describe a memory interface; retired loads describe instructions. None substitutes for the others.

items.title: A lower-bound envelope
items.text:
With \(K\) independent chains, recurrence latency \(L\), core execution work per step \(u\), sustainable issue or execution rate \(P\), bytes transferred per step \(b\) and sustainable bandwidth \(B\), an optimistic envelope is

\[ \text{cycles per useful step} \ge \max\left(\frac{L}{K},\ \frac{u}{P},\ \frac{b}{B}\right) \]

with \(L\) in cycles, \(P\) in operations per cycle and \(B\) in bytes per cycle. Separate port limits may matter more than a single aggregate \(P\). It's a reasoning aid, not a calibrated simulator: it leaves out branch recovery, burstiness, queueing and imperfect scheduling.

For a specific resource \(j\), if a useful step needs \(m_j\) requests that each hold the resource for \(W_j\) seconds, and it has \(Q_j\) entries, then

\[ \text{useful steps per second} \le \frac{Q_j}{m_j W_j} \]

That is why taking \(\min(Q_j)\) across unrelated queues is wrong: their occupancy times and request populations differ. A small queue passed through quickly can sustain more throughput than a large one whose entries stay occupied.

items.title: How fewer instructions can help
items.text:
Once enough chains are exposed that \(L/K\) no longer dominates, an instruction change may:

  • shorten the dependency that produces the next address;
  • reduce load/store or address-generation pressure;
  • reduce front-end work;
  • reduce register pressure and spills;
  • fit more useful independent loads into the finite instruction window;
  • reduce branch or bookkeeping overhead;
  • change prefetch timing.

These are different mechanisms. The finite window is the most relevant here: with many independent chains in the source, the processor still has to reach their loads before its tracking resources fill, so removing intervening work can raise the MLP achieved without changing the memory hierarchy. This interaction is central to the ISCA MLP work and to Cimple [5, 7].

More lanes can also make things worse. Lane state may spill to memory, code may grow, output streams may take cache space and write buffers, scheduling can get more expensive, and more concurrency may raise memory queueing and so \(L\) itself. AMAC and Cimple arrange independent memory-bound tasks within one thread and confront exactly these costs. Their value here is the mechanism and the experimental framing, not their headline speedups or optimal group sizes [6, 7].

items.title: IPC is a ratio, not a score
items.text:
Over one interval, \(\mathrm{IPC} = I/C\), and cycles per useful byte \(= (I/B)/\mathrm{IPC}\), where \(B\) is useful output. A hypothetical change:

Version Instructions/byte IPC Cycles/byte A 12 3.0 4.0 B 8 2.5 3.2

B uses 20% fewer cycles per byte with lower IPC. Conversely, extra easy work can raise IPC without raising useful throughput. A rule like "IPC below one means memory-bound" is too crude; Intel's and Arm's methodologies use several categories and follow-up measurements [14, 31].

An instruction can expand into several back-end operations, and fusion can change some of the accounting without removing all of the work, so two sequences with similar instruction counts can load the ports, store machinery and front end quite differently. For the walk, the useful questions are which instructions delay the next table address, which consume the resource that currently limits it, which make memory accesses only to maintain lane state, and which occupy the window while more useful loads wait to become visible.

Misses per thousand instructions can mislead during an instruction optimisation: halve the instructions with misses per output byte unchanged, and MPKI doubles. Track misses and requests per BWT row or per final output byte as well.

items.title: Little's law needs a boundary and a population
items.text: For a stable, consistently measured request population, \(\overline{N} = \lambda \overline{W}\): average outstanding requests equal the completion rate times the average residence time. If each counted request transfers one line of \(S\) bytes, line bandwidth is about \(\overline{N} S / \overline{W}\). But a retired load, a fill-buffer allocation, an L2-miss transaction and a DRAM read needn't be the same population, and the latency of a lightly loaded serial chain needn't be the latency of a heavily loaded multi-chain test: queueing, the source of the line and prefetching all change it. Higher occupancy can mean more useful overlap, or slower service.

items.title: 6. Counter definitions and their populations
items.text:
Let \(O\) be an occupancy counter that adds the number of qualifying outstanding requests every cycle, \(A\) the number of matching requests, \(P\) the cycles with at least one pending, and \(C\) all relevant cycles.

Ratio Units Meaning \(O/A\) cycles per request Average residence time \(O/P\) requests Average occupancy, given that a request is pending \(O/C\) requests Average occupancy over all measured cycles

These follow from what is accumulated. Before applying them, check that numerator and denominator cover the same requests, interval, privilege filters and hardware scope, and handle requests already outstanding at the start of a short window or still outstanding at its end.

items.title: The L1 demand-associated metric
items.text:
Intel defines an MLP metric as L1D_PEND_MISS.PENDING divided by L1D_PEND_MISS.PENDING_CYCLES [11, 12]. Its event definition concerns demand-associated fill buffers. A fill a prefetch started may begin to count once a demand access joins it, and page-walk reads and split accesses complicate the correspondence with source-level loads. It isn't a count of independent BWT chains, of total prefetch concurrency or of DRAM requests.

In our archive the conditional value stays near 2.18 from one worker to four while the share of cycles with a pending demand miss rises from about 12% to 30% [24]. As an illustration, \(2.18 \times 0.12 \approx 0.26\) and \(2.18 \times 0.30 \approx 0.65\): an unchanged conditional average beside a large rise in occupancy over all cycles. Exact aggregation should use the matching raw totals, and because these are process-wide figures, a shift in the time spent in each phase moves them too.

When comparing workers, sum the numerators and denominators before forming a weighted aggregate. That gives a cycle-weighted average per logical processor, not the total number of requests outstanding at once across the machine. An unweighted average of per-thread ratios can give short-lived or lightly loaded threads too much weight.

items.title: The offcore ratio
items.text:
For the relevant Intel event family, OFFCORE_REQUESTS_OUTSTANDING.ALL_DATA_RD integrates outstanding data reads from an L2 miss to completion at the superqueue boundary. Divided by OFFCORE_REQUESTS.ALL_DATA_RD, it gives cycles per request. The population mixes demand reads, prefetches and relevant page-walk reads, and can include requests served by the LLC, so it isn't automatically DRAM latency [11].

Our archived median rises from roughly 39 to 58 cycles per request with four workers (an arithmetic mean gives about 41 to 58) [24, 25]. That's consistent with a longer average residence for the counted population. It doesn't prove that an unchanged set of useful BWT requests each became slower by that amount: the source mix, phase mix and request mix can all change.

items.title: Prefetch and demand-only counts
items.text: A line can arrive before its demand use, or a demand access can join a fill already in flight. A retired demand-load classification describes that load's encounter with the hierarchy, not necessarily the line's full history. MEM_LOAD_RETIRED.FB_HIT says a load merged into a still-pending fill for the same line; the initiating request may have been demand or prefetch, so it doesn't show that the corresponding share of work was supplied by prefetch [11]. For the walk, which prefetches every next row, counting only demand loads that miss in L3 can leave out much of the expensive traffic.

items.title: Two withdrawn readings
items.text: The corrected mibz2 memory proposal withdraws an earlier estimate that about 98% of walk traffic was prefetch, because retired demand loads reaching L3 and all offcore reads are different populations. It also withdraws reading an inferred count near six as measured, constant walk MLP: the assumed request rate, a mixed process-wide latency proxy and the stage time partly constructed the apparent agreement [25]. Those corrections stand.

items.title: Counter values need causal context
items.text: More outstanding requests might mean more useful parallel work, or slower service. More DRAM writes might cause contention, or result from evicting dirty data. Fewer retired demand misses might reflect effective prefetching while total traffic grows. Events can also overlap or nest, so adding several stall counts is invalid when one cycle belongs to more than one; and sampling has different semantics from counting. A coherent set of counters is evidence for distinguishing hypotheses, not a self-interpreting explanation.

items.title: 7. A measurement programme for mibz2
items.text: The aim is to resolve the remaining ambiguity without repeating experiments that are already closed, such as the 32-lane unroll.

items.title: Objectives, phases and axes
items.text:
For the production decoder the objectives are wall-clock decoded throughput, CPU-seconds per GB, behaviour across blocks and memory footprint; for understanding the walk, actual cycles, nanoseconds, requests, instructions and traffic per BWT row. A stage improvement and a decoder improvement are separate results.

Measure table construction, traversal, segment assembly and the later RLE and CRC work separately, and keep the whole-decoder test, using the production sequence of blocks and buffer lifetimes: a prebuilt table traversed repeatedly can be much warmer than one met during real decoding. Keep lane count, segment count, prefetch policy, worker count, lane-state layout and output-buffer lifetimes as separate axes. More lanes try to improve overlap within a core; more workers add cores and pressure on shared resources.

items.title: What to collect
items.text:
Measurement What it helps answer Actual cycles and ns per BWT row Did useful service improve, and did the frequency change? Retired instructions per row Did dynamic instruction work fall? Branch misses per row Did recovery costs change? Load/store and resource-pressure evidence Did the change reduce the resource that matters? Requests and supplier information per row How much counted traffic is there, and where is it served? Conditional occupancy How many requests overlap when any is pending? Pending-cycle fraction and unconditional occupancy How much of the time is that activity going on? Matching residence-time estimate Are requests taking longer to finish? Whole-decoder throughput and CPU cost Does the change improve the actual program?

No single row is a verdict; the combination should support or contradict a prediction written down beforehand:

Hypothesis Result that would support it Too few independent loads become visible Better scheduling raises the useful request rate and cuts stage time, without extra traffic. Lane bookkeeping consumes a limiting resource A controlled layout or instruction change reduces that resource and the native stage cycles, with similar request behaviour. Translation is significant Verified mapping changes move page-walk activity and stage time together. LLC residency deteriorates Supplier and replacement evidence changes with a controlled live footprint. Shared request service is congested Residence time and slowdown respond to request pressure even with the footprint controlled. Output traffic interferes with traversal A targeted change to output lifetime or write traffic improves the affected stage and the decoder.

None of these interventions is pure: changing instructions changes request timing, changing page size can change placement, and changing traffic changes queueing. Record those consequences rather than assume them away.

items.title: Track A: the machine and the method
items.text: Compare a single chain, an unrolled version of that same chain, and several interleaved independent chains, holding useful accesses fixed. That separates amortised loop control from inter-chain overlap more cleanly than comparing one chain only with many. Sweep the active working set through the cache levels and beyond the LLC, saying whether total footprint or footprint per chain is held fixed; vary node spacing independently of payload size; compare verified page mappings, not just allocation requests; and establish single-core behaviour before adding cores. Inspect the generated loop at each important lane count, and keep the executable, compiler flags, the input permutation or its hash, affinity, page backing and raw timings.

items.title: Track B: the decoder's limiting work
items.text: Use the production workload for any shipping decision, keep cold and warm microbenchmarks if useful and label them, and keep the whole-decoder benchmark beside every stage measurement, because removing a copy, changing a buffer or growing the code can affect another phase or the other workers.

items.title: Counter mechanics and the existing harnesses
items.text:
Small Linux perf event groups can collect matching counters together. For per-thread phase measurements, bracket a substantial block or batch, use consistent filters, keep the enabled and running times, and reject unscheduled groups. Subtract the time metadata as well as the counts when taking interval deltas: resetting counts doesn't reset all the time accounting. Measure the cost of an empty bracket and keep the uninstrumented timing [17, 18]. Prefer a few purpose-built groups to one oversized collection that multiplexes heavily, since a scaled count assumes the scheduled intervals represent the whole interval.

The current sweep covers several lane counts, prefetch hints, and room against flagged walkers; it keeps decode order and has an optional separate PMU pass, and its byte denominator is BWT rows. The phases example reports per final decoded byte. Both report c/B by converting elapsed seconds with a supplied nominal clock, which isn't a PMU cycle count; a fixed multiplier cancels in a ratio, but those values shouldn't be mixed with PMU cycles or across byte definitions [26, 27].

items.title: 8. What the tools can establish
items.text:
Disassembly shows whether independent loads stay visible, whether lane state is reloaded, whether bounds checks or spills remain, and where code grew. It can't show the cache residency or service time a run experiences. Static intuition from the source is especially unreliable for a compiler-managed array of lane state, so archive the binary behind each timed result.

LLVM-MCA helps investigate dependencies and execution-resource pressure, but it doesn't predict a workload's cache behaviour and its default load latencies are optimistic [15]. Treat it as a source of candidate explanations and lower bounds; a prediction that disagrees with measured time tells you about the model's assumptions.

Cachegrind gives reproducible instruction counts that make regressions easy to catch, but its cache and branch simulations are basic [16]. A deterministic instruction-count improvement is evidence of less work executed under that tool, not of native overlap, prefetch timeliness or contention.

Hardware counters observe defined events; they don't label causes. The CPU model, event definition, filtering and errata all matter, and Intel and Arm events with similar names needn't count equivalent things [13, 14]. Cross-ISA IPC is unsuitable as a standalone score, since x86 and AArch64 express the same work in different instruction sequences. Top-down categories narrow a problem without replacing a study of the useful work and the intervention [31].

items.title: 9. Open questions
items.text:
Prefetch lead time is coupled to everything else. The walk prefetches one link ahead, but the time before demand returns to a lane depends on the lane count and on the time spent advancing the other lanes. Removing bookkeeping shortens that interval, so an optimisation may consume a prefetched line sooner and expose more of its latency even while cutting instructions. That is a hypothesis drawn from the schedule, not a claim that it caused the archived unrolling result; testing it needs timing and request-population evidence. A second unknown hop can't be prefetched by adding another hint: its address has to be discovered first, or a representation has to precompute a shortcut, with its own build cost, footprint and cache behaviour.

Local and end-to-end objectives diverge. For a phase taking fraction \(f\) of total time, speeding it up by \(s\) gives an idealised whole-program speedup of \(1 / ((1 - f) + f/s)\), if nothing else changes, and in a concurrent decoder something else usually does. Wall throughput and CPU cost can also diverge: four workers finish sooner while using more CPU-seconds per GB.

What remains unknown. The public article doesn't establish the exact 2022 binary and runtime configuration, and its measured knee can't identify a hardware queue's capacity. For mibz2, the archived evidence doesn't yet divide the four-worker penalty among LLC capacity, request congestion, writeback interference, prefetch timing and translation, and the static address-port model alone doesn't establish the limiting resource of the unrolled candidate.

items.title: 10. Further reading
items.text:
Kärkkäinen, Kempa and Puglisi, Slashing the Time for BWT Inversion [19]. The algorithm itself: reducing costly accesses and overlapping inversions from several starting positions, which separates how much expensive work there is from how it's scheduled.

Chou, Fahs and Abraham, Microarchitecture Optimizations for Exploiting Memory-Level Parallelism [5]. Why finite instruction windows, execution structure and branches bound the memory overlap a core can expose.

Kocberber, Falsafi and Grot, Asynchronous Memory Access Chaining [6]. Suspended memory-bound tasks, uneven progress and the cost of scheduling them. Its speedups aren't predictions for BWT.

Kiriansky et al., Cimple: Instruction and Memory Level Parallelism [7]. ILP and MLP as working together, including the limits from intervening instructions and execution windows.

Travis Downs on the earlier benchmark [10]. Several resources along the path, different occupancy times, and translation, for this same benchmark family.

Intel's event and metric definitions [11, 12]. What each ratio counts. Reading the exact numerator and denominator is worth more than any secondary name for a metric.

items.title: Instructions, overlap and evidence
items.text:
mibz2 · Research blog

To decode a bzip2 block, mibz2 eventually performs an odd kind of memory access. It reads an entry from a table, and the value it gets back says which entry to read next. Each 4-byte entry packs two things: its low 8 bits are one decoded byte, and the bits above them are the number of the next row to read.

let q = t[row];    // read this row's entry
row = q >> 8;      // the upper bits: the next row to read
out.push(q as u8); // the low 8 bits: one decoded byte

Suppose the walk is at row 7, and row 7's entry says that row 12 comes next. Only once that entry has arrived does the CPU know to read row 12, whose entry might point to row 4, and so on. The CPU isn't short of instructions it could run. It's short of an address. And when the entry isn't in a nearby cache, every step waits for memory.

So mibz2 doesn't walk one chain at a time. It picks about 500 starting rows spread across the table, which cuts the traversal into segments, and advances 32 of those segments in turn, so that while one lane waits for its load the others can issue theirs. In 32 lanes, 8.6 chains we measured what that buys: the 32-lane walk runs about 8.6 times as fast as a single chain.

What made it faster? It's tempting to say we'd found how many memory requests the CPU can keep in flight at once, its memory-level parallelism (MLP). But the same change also handed the CPU's scheduler far more independent instructions, which is instruction-level parallelism (ILP). Which of the two explains the speedup, and does the answer change what we should try to make faster?

The same question came up in 2022, in replies to Daniel Lemire's post Memory-level parallelism: Intel Ice Lake versus Amazon Graviton 3. Lemire measures MLP with a benchmark much like our walk: a long pointer chase through a large array, then the same accesses shared among more and more independent chains. Ivica Bogosavljevic replied that the speedup comes from ILP as well; Lemire, that the waits are memory loads, not instructions.

They were both right, because ILP and MLP aren't rival explanations here: the independent instructions are what let the memory requests overlap, so the two names describe one mechanism from its two ends. The more useful question is what a speedup like our 8.6 can tell you about the part of the machine that limits it. It shows that overlapping the chains pays, but not what stops the gain from growing, and so not what to make faster next. We found that out on our own walk: removing a third of its instructions made it about 12% faster on its own, and left the decoder no faster with four workers.

The sections below take that argument in order: why one chain stalls; how ILP and MLP fit together; what Lemire's curve can and can't measure; what happened when we cut the walk's instructions; and where the four-worker decoder's extra time goes instead.

items.title: Memory-level parallelism in mibz2: instructions, overlap and evidence
items.text:
Interleaving pointer chases lets memory waits overlap. The speedup shows that this pays, but not what limits it: a 2022 exchange about Daniel Lemire's benchmark, read against mibz2's inverse-BWT walk.

2 November 2026 · 15 min read · Research synthesis

items.title: 1. Why a pointer chase stalls
items.text:
Stripped of the decoding, the walk is the classic pointer chase. Written in C, with next standing for the table, each step is

p = next[p];

and the value each load returns is the address of the next. An out-of-order CPU looks far ahead in the instruction stream for work it can start early, but it can't issue a load whose address it doesn't know yet, and no amount of lookahead can supply a value that hasn't arrived.

Unrolling the loop, writing the step out four times, doesn't change that:

p = next[p];
p = next[p];
p = next[p];
p = next[p];

That saves a little loop bookkeeping, but the four loads are still one chain, each waiting for the last. What does help is giving the loop four independent chains:

p0 = next[p0];
p1 = next[p1];
p2 = next[p2];
p3 = next[p3];
