The first four are one stdlib script, coord.py, added in #186, and the repository's CLAUDE.md says when the Coordinator runs each one. (TYPE: QUEUED is a staging label added with the inboxes: work for a busy role waits on #145 until the Coordinator dispatches it.) The script only reads: it never posts, edits or deletes. The tripwire can't stop a misroute, only report it. It never edits, moves or re-posts a comment, and never dispatches anything itself, so it can't create work of its own.

The tripwire needed the same treatment as everything else. A workflow started by a comment runs only from master, so each version could be tested only after it merged. The Coordinator tested each one with a deliberate, labelled misroute on #145, and each test found something that the code and its unit tests hadn't. (A check run is one line in a PR's list of checks. GitHub groups a workflow's check runs into a check suite, and the Coordinator's subscription hears only when a suite finishes.)

  • The first was classified correctly, and then its warning couldn't be posted: #145 is locked, and the Actions bot can't comment on a locked conversation.
  • The second raised a failing check run on #145 instead. The check showed red, but nothing woke the Coordinator.
  • The third made its check run start in progress and then fail, to reopen the suite. The suite stayed green and sent no event: a GitHub Actions suite follows its workflow run, not check runs added to it.

One of these tests refuted a claim that had already merged: #188 went in saying its check run would wake the Coordinator, and its test showed within a minute that it didn't.

So the tripwire is a record, not an alarm. It leaves a failing check on #145's head commit, independently of the Coordinator, and the check shows on #145 until the next commit to the channel branch. The Coordinator finds the misroute itself, by running audit at the start of each session and every time it wakes.

The merge guard needed the same treatment, and got it only while this post was being checked. A reviewing agent pointed out that GitHub refuses a mismatched head, and it does: a merge of #139 was refused with a 409 on 2 November. The guess had never reached GitHub. The merge tool takes the expected head as expectedHeadSha, and the Coordinator had been passing it as sha, a name the tool doesn't have and drops without a word. The prefix refused earlier had met the tool's own format check, under the right name. Read back, eight merges between 02:12 and 09:36 had passed the head that way, among them an earlier guess on #167 and four merges made after head-sha existed. Each merged its PR's final head, so nothing wrong landed, but none was checked. head-sha had checked the value; nothing had checked that the value reached the merge. #190 adds the missing step: the SHA goes in expectedHeadSha, and head-sha --merged reads the merge back and passes only if the PR merged at exactly that head.

Three gaps remain. The checks are run by the Coordinator on itself: CLAUDE.md says when, but nothing outside its session makes it run them, and the tripwire, the one check outside it, can only leave a mark. The Coordinator can't see the Astra tasks' run history; it infers a run from receipts in the cursors, which route reads. And a brief that was delivered but never started, one with no receipt half an hour after it was posted, is still caught only by the Coordinator noticing a quiet record (section 7). A mechanical check for it would close the loop from sent to started. It isn't built.

items.title: 10. Where it stands
items.text:
The channel log records each step. The trigger was first tested on the Guardian: a comment started its run, it published an assessment, and its review woke the Coordinator. The first real cycle followed on a checkpoint covering two prototypes. The Guardian's run started nine seconds after it was posted, checked both prototypes against the gates, and asked for the independent review.

That review came back while this post was being finished. The Researcher launched the isolated reviewer, and its report arrived as a comment on the channel. Both prototypes pass on correctness and safety, and so does v3's finaliser. Two things need fixing before anything is combined: some changed paths still need their own execution counters, and both prototypes remove the same instruction, so their savings overlap. That is the next checkpoint.

On 5 November the redesigned setup ran its first full round:

  • The Optimiser ranked the whole decoder's candidates from its inbox. It put P87, a production-shaped change that writes the walk's output over a buffer it has already consumed, first.
  • The Coordinator built P87 and registered a decision rule before measuring it.
  • The Guardian and the Researcher reviewed that rule from their inboxes before the benchmark finished. The Guardian's review changed it.
  • The change made the four-worker Wikidata decode 2.2% faster in one run, and favourable but inconclusive in a second, with 6.8% less memory and no slower row. It merged.

Then all three agents took their next assignment under the new specs:

  • each woke only on its own inbox;
  • each committed a receipt within a minute or two, and published its review on #145;
  • the Guardian also moved itself onto its current operating spec.

The first reviews under the new design corrected the Coordinator's write-up before it was published.

The rest of that night was the first long test. At 02:52 UTC, at my instruction, the Coordinator's mode note was amended to tell it to fan out hard on the hard research, and to do tests, CI and documentation itself rather than spend agents on them. From then until my morning check it ran with nobody watching. Only the Optimiser was in the loop: the Guardian and the Researcher received no work after 00:36.

The Coordinator's Claude Code workflows put several agents on one question at once. In one, three agents mined an old CI sweep, modelled each runner's per-core miss resources and built a walk keyed on SMT co-residency, and three sceptics each refuted part of that work. Another reviewed the fused post-walk change through three lenses, one of them a differential of about 14,600 valid and corrupt inputs against master, which found no divergence. The workflows' own records stay in the Coordinator's session; the journal keeps what they found. Every decoder change that reached a pull request still went through the CI benchmark, under a decision rule registered before its first run, without review by the Guardian or the Researcher.

Five decoder changes merged. Two trimmed the move-to-front stage (#170, #172). #171 staged the walk's output through one tile, for a four-thread wall 5% to 14% faster over five runs. #180 widened the window of blocks in flight, for 8% to 10% in three runs, at a cost of 4% to 6% more CPU and 8 MB more memory. The Coordinator weighed that in the journal and accepted it, noting that the extra CPU still has to be measured in wikidata-pq's pipeline, where the decoder shares its cores. #181 removed the deferred flags that #171 had carried with it: the decoder ran about 4% more instructions and still got faster. That fits the reading that the walk is bound by memory requests in flight rather than by instructions, though no hardware counter has shown it. The benchmark history, which chains each merge's own paired run, now puts the four-thread Wikidata wall at 0.75× its value at #69 (95% band 0.69–0.82), against 0.85× before #180. The chain assumes that a change measured on one runner holds on another.

As much again was tested and rejected. The 32 KiB tile, 1024 offsets a lane, filled the whole of Zen 4's L1D and ran 23.5% slower even at one thread (#177, #178). The fused post-walk pass (#183) halved the simulated cache misses after the walk, but the four-thread wall wasn't shown to follow: neither PR run was faster there beyond noise, though the fusion alone was, by 1.5%. October's four-copy win for a walk keyed on SMT co-residency reversed on today's staged walk. Split condition variables were rejected on a count of wasted wakes before anything was built.

Each is written up in the journal with its runs. The walk round had already redirected the work: since the 06:03 checkpoint the Optimiser has ranked candidates by the memory traffic of four workers on two SMT cores, not by instruction counts, and the fused pass and split condition variables were its first and third picks. Their failures narrowed the search to the walk's random reads and its table's footprint. The next build the Optimiser proposed is a retest of compact30's smaller table under today's staged walk, though its own prior on it is weak.

So the work moves without me relaying it. When a message went to the wrong address, the record showed it, and the Coordinator corrected it without my carrying anything across, though it took me to notice. Now the Coordinator reads each message and each merge back rather than assume they landed, and a misroute leaves a failing check on #145 that the Coordinator didn't write. Whether all of this makes the research faster will keep showing in the benchmark history.

If you want to set up something similar:

  • give each agent its own inbox, and one shared place to publish;
  • have each run commit a receipt before it works, and its progress as it goes;
  • point every message at an exact commit;
  • wake agents with events rather than timers, and keep those events few;
  • keep every agent's instructions in the repository at a pinned commit;
  • write down what a message is allowed to authorise;
  • decide what an independent reviewer gets to see;
  • check effects, not reports: read every message back where it should have landed, and every merge back after it lands.

My own part is choosing the scope and making the decisions the charter keeps for me.

items.title: Technical appendix: the ideas behind building a smaller bzip2 decoding table
items.text:
The main post moves quickly through ideas that come from several fields at once: the Burrows–Wheeler transform, sorting, compact integer formats and machine code. This appendix introduces them one at a time, for a programmer who hasn't met them before. Simple things get simple explanations. The sections build on one another, but each can be read on its own. A glossary is at the end.

All code is quoted from the frozen sources:

  • the record format and the walker, examples/c30walk.rs at e003a32;
  • the first builder, examples/c30walk/ctor.rs at e003a32;
  • the second builder, examples/c30walk/ctor2.rs at 8beffe2.
path: Building a smaller bzip2 decoding table

items.title: 1. A table of next steps
items.text:
Imagine an array in which every entry says which entry to visit next:

index:      0  1  2  3  4  5
next[i]:    3  4  5  2  0  1

Start at index 3 and follow it: \(3 \to 2 \to 5 \to 1 \to 4 \to 0 \to 3\). Every index appears exactly once as a destination, so the table is a permutation: it reorders the indices without losing or repeating any.

Undoing the Burrows–Wheeler transform comes down to following a permutation like this one, emitting a byte at each step. mibz2's conventional table stores one 4-byte entry per row. Compact30, named for the thirty rows it packs into each 64-byte record, stores the same permutation in less memory. The catch, and the subject of the main post, is that the compact table has to be built first, and building it must not cost more than it saves.
path: Building a smaller bzip2 decoding table

items.title: 2. The BWT in one example
items.text:
The Burrows–Wheeler transform (BWT) is the reversible reordering at the heart of bzip2. Section 1 of the space–time post animates it. The short version: write down every rotation of the block, sort them, and keep the last column. For \(\mathtt{banana}\):

Row Sorted rotation First column \(F\) Last column \(L\) 0 abanan a n 1 anaban a n 2 ananab a b 3 banana b a 4 nabana n a 5 nanaba n a

So \(L = \mathtt{nnbaaa}\) and \(F = \mathtt{aaabnn}\). The original block is in row 3, and the decoder is given that row number along with \(L\). Decoders never build the rotations; the table only explains the idea. The fact everything below uses is that \(F\) holds exactly the bytes of \(L\), sorted. That is what makes counting sort work.
path: Building a smaller bzip2 decoding table

items.title: 3. Counting sort, buckets and cursors
items.text:
A bucket is a contiguous range of positions reserved for one kind of item. Because \(F\) is sorted, each byte's occurrences are adjacent: in \(\mathtt{aaabnn}\), the a's occupy positions \([0, 3)\), the b position \([3, 4)\) and the n's \([4, 6)\). The notation \([0, 3)\) means 0, 1 and 2: the start is included and the end isn't, as in Rust's 0..3.

Counting sort sorts values from a small known range without comparing them:

  1. Count each value. A byte has 256 possible values, so the counts fit in an array of 256.
  2. Turn the counts into bucket starts. Byte \(c\)'s bucket starts at the number of bytes smaller than \(c\); for \(\mathtt{banana}\), a at 0, b at 3, n at 4. This running total is a prefix sum, and the code calls the array of starts \(C\).
  3. Place each item at the next free position of its bucket.

The cursor in step 3 is nothing special: it is a variable holding the next free position in one byte's bucket. Place an item there, then add one:

let mut next = bucket_starts;          // C: one cursor per byte value
for (i, &c) in l.iter().enumerate() {
    let r = next[c as usize];          // this row's destination
    next[c as usize] += 1;
    table[r] = i as u32;               // store the source row at the destination
}

For \(\mathtt{banana}\) the scan assigns:

Source row \(i\) \(L[i]\) Destination \(r\) 0 n 4 1 n 5 2 b 3 3 a 0 4 a 1 5 a 2

This placement is stable: equal bytes keep their original order. The three a's come from rows 3, 4 and 5 and go to positions 0, 1 and 2, in that order. A left-to-right scan with a cursor per byte gives stability for free. The builders rely on its consequence: within one byte's bucket, consecutive destinations hold increasing source rows.
path: Building a smaller bzip2 decoding table

items.title: 4. The navigation table
items.text:
Store the source row at each destination, as the loop above does, and you have the table the walk follows:

Destination row \(F\) Next row 0 a 3 1 a 4 2 a 5 3 b 2 4 n 0 5 n 1

That is the permutation of section 1. Start at row 3, emit \(F\) at each row, and move to the next row. The output is b, a, n, a, n, a: \(\mathtt{banana}\).

The space–time post calls this table \(T^{-1}\), because Seward's \(T\) runs the other way. bzip2's decoder, and mibz2's, store \(T^{-1}\) so that the walk emits the block forwards. The research journals call the same table ψ. Compact30 changes how this table is stored, not the permutation itself.

Two coordinates are easy to confuse here:

  • a destination \(r\) is which entry of the table is being filled;
  • a source row \(i\) is which position of \(L\) supplied it, and so which row the walk visits next.

The builder decides where to write from \(r\), and what to write from \(i\).
path: Building a smaller bzip2 decoding table

items.title: 5. Labels: numbering rows thirty to a block of 32
items.text:
Compact30 doesn't store a next row \(i\) as a plain number. It stores the row's label:

\[ \varphi(i) = 32\left\lfloor \frac{i}{30} \right\rfloor + (i \bmod 30) \]

(in Rust, 32 * (i / 30) + i % 30). It isn't a hash or an identifier; it's just a renumbering in which each group of 30 rows uses 30 of a block of 32 numbers:

Row \(i\) \(\lfloor i / 30 \rfloor\) \(i \bmod 30\) Label \(\varphi(i)\) 0 0 0 0 29 0 29 29 30 1 0 32 42 1 12 44 59 1 29 61 60 2 0 64

Labels 30 and 31 are never used, nor 62 and 63, and so on. The gaps are deliberate. A record holds 30 two-byte fields and a 4-byte header, the size of 32 two-byte slots, and the two unused labels in each block line up with the header. Because 32 is a power of two, the walk can split a label \(y\) into its record and its field with two cheap operations:

  • y >> 5, a shift right by five bits, divides by 32: the record;
  • y & 31 keeps the low five bits: the field.

With plain row numbers, it would have to divide by 30, which is much slower. The label function exists to make the walk cheap; the builder has to work with it.
path: Building a smaller bzip2 decoding table

items.title: 6. Records, offsets and RAW groups
items.text:
The record is:

#[repr(C, align(64))]
struct Rec {
    f: [u16; 30],   // bytes 0–59: one 16-bit field per row
    h: u32,         // bytes 60–63: the header
}

u16 and u32 are unsigned 16- and 32-bit integers. align(64) places every record at a multiple of 64 bytes, so each record fills exactly one 64-byte cache line, the unit in which the processor moves memory into its caches.

Each record holds 30 consecutive destinations: destination \(r\) is in record \(\lfloor r/30 \rfloor\), field \(r \bmod 30\).

Ordinary records. All 30 rows output the same byte, and their next rows' labels are close together. The header holds the byte and a base, the first row's label:

\[ h = (\text{base} \ll 8)\ \text{|}\ c, \]

so h & 255 is the byte and h >> 8 is the base. Each field holds its row's label minus the base, so the walk computes the next label as base plus field. Because of section 3's ordering, the first row has the smallest label and the last row the largest.

RAW groups. Two situations break the ordinary form:

  • crossing: the record's 30 destinations straddle two buckets, say 18 a's and 12 b's, so no single header byte fits;

  • wide: the labels are too far apart for 16-bit offsets.

Such a group is stored as a RawG, 32 four-byte entries (128 bytes), of which 30 are used. Each entry is (label << 8) | byte, so every row can have its own byte and its own full label. The record keeps all fields at 0xFFFF, and its header becomes RAW_BIT | index: bit 28 set, and the RAW group's index in the low 20 bits. RAW doesn't mean uncompressed input; it means this group's navigation is spelled out in full.

A third kind, forced RAW, exists only for testing. The research harness can force a fraction of groups to RAW to exercise those code paths. The measured configuration forces none.

Why the limit is 65,533. A u16 holds 0 to 65,535, but compact30 reserves the top two values. 65,534 (0xFFFE) marks the row where one of the walk's segments starts, and 65,535 (0xFFFF) fills RAW records, padding and the parking record. An ordinary offset can therefore be at most 65,533, and the code's MAX_OFF is that. A group whose labels span more is wide.

Parking. After the last group comes one more record, all 0xFFFF. When one of the walk's lanes reaches a RAW row, it starts fetching the RAW entry and moves to this record's label for a turn. It resumes from there once the entry has had time to arrive.

A note on the toy example: \(\mathtt{banana}\)'s six destinations all fall in record 0, but they belong to three buckets. So its one record would be crossing RAW. The ordinary record above is the common case in real blocks, not something this toy example can show.
path: Building a smaller bzip2 decoding table

items.title: 7. Epochs and snapshots
items.text:
An epoch here is simply a fixed stretch of source rows: 61,440 of them. It has nothing to do with time.

The number isn't arbitrary; it falls out of the label function. The second builder stores only a label's low 16 bits, so it wants to know where the high 16 bits go up by one, every \(2^{16} = 65536\) labels. Each 30 source rows use 32 labels, so 65,536 labels are \(65536 / 32 = 2048\) groups, and \(2048 \times 30 = 61440\) source rows. Therefore

\[ \varphi(i + 61440) = \varphi(i) + 65536. \] Source row Label 0 0 61,439 65,533 61,440 65,536 61,441 65,537 122,880 131,072

Within epoch \(e\), every label equals \(65536 \cdot e\) plus its low 16 bits. The useful low values stop at 65,533, because of the two unused labels per block of 32.

The builder can't afford to store an epoch for every row. It doesn't need to, because of the ordering in section 3: the rows arriving in one bucket come in source order. So at the start of each epoch it saves a snapshot, a copy of the 256 cursors: each byte's next free destination. Write \(A_e[c]\) for byte \(c\)'s cursor at the start of epoch \(e\). Then

\[ A_e[c] = C[c] + \text{the number of } c\text{'s before source row } 61440\,e. \]

These are exact counts, not estimates. Suppose byte a's snapshots are:

Epoch \(e\) \(A_e[\mathtt{a}]\) 0 100 1 104 2 104 3 106

Four a's arrived in epoch 0 (destinations 100–103), none in epoch 1, and two in epoch 2 (104–105). Which epoch filled destination 104? Epoch 2: the latest epoch whose snapshot is at most 104,

\[ h(r) = \max\{\, e : A_e[c] \le r \,\}. \]

Choosing the first epoch with the value 104 would give epoch 1, wrongly. Repeated snapshot values mean the byte was absent for a while, and the latest one is right. The code's epoch_of searches backwards from the newest snapshot for exactly that.

If destination 104 holds the 16-bit value 12, its full label is \(2 \times 65536 + 12 = 131084\). The builder recovered it from a value already sitting in the final record, a destination it already knows, and a small table of counts.

A 900,000-row block spans 15 epochs, so its snapshots take \(15 \times 256 \times 4\) bytes, 15 KiB, against 3.6 MB for a 32-bit temporary per row. The general trick is worth remembering: periodic summaries of state you already keep can replace per-item metadata.
path: Building a smaller bzip2 decoding table

items.title: 8. Descriptors and portions
items.text:
A descriptor is a small struct holding what an operation needs to carry on. The second builder keeps one per byte value, Desc:

struct Desc {
    write: *mut u16,   // the next field to write
    end: *mut u16,     // one past the last field of the current portion
    w0: *mut u16,      // the portion's first field
    r0: u32,           // the destination of that first field
    lim: u32,          // the end of the byte's bucket
    g: u32,            // the record the portion is in
    raw: u32,          // its RAW index, if the record is RAW from the start
}

The *mut u16 fields are raw pointers, memory addresses. With them ready, the per-row path writes through write and bumps it, without recomputing a record and field from a destination. Each descriptor is 40 bytes: three 8-byte pointers and four 4-byte integers.

A portion is one byte's share of one record. Usually it is the whole record. But if record 10 covers destinations 300–329 and a's bucket ends at 320, then a's portion is 300–319 and the next byte's is 320–329. That record is crossing RAW, and each portion is finished into its RAW block separately.

A portion isn't always finished the moment its last field is written. It's finished when the byte next turns up and finds its portion full (refill), when a run continuing past it closes it, or at the end of the block, whichever comes first. The snapshot rule still works then, because a snapshot counts the rows already written to open portions.
path: Building a smaller bzip2 decoding table

items.title: 9. Finishing a group
items.text:
When an ordinary candidate's portion is full, finish does four things:

  1. It recovers the full labels of the group's first and last rows (section 7). In the common case the whole group arrived in the latest epoch, so no search is needed.
  2. It classifies the group. The labels increase through the group, so the first is the smallest and the last the largest, and their difference is the group's whole span. No scan of all 30 is needed.
  3. If the span is at most 65,533, it writes the header and converts the fields to offsets.
  4. If not, it builds a RAW block from the 30 full labels.

Why classify from full labels. Take first label 2 and last label 65,536. Their true span is 65,534, too wide. Their low 16 bits are 2 and 0, which would make the group look tiny, or backwards. Only the full labels give the right answer. The test suite pins the exact boundary: source rows 3 → 61,440 span 65,533 (ordinary), and rows 2 → 61,440 span 65,534 (RAW).

Why 16-bit subtraction is then enough. Normalisation here just means subtracting the group's first label from each label, turning absolute labels into offsets: \([1000, 1004, 1009]\) becomes \([0, 4, 9]\). Suppose a group crosses an epoch boundary, with labels 65,530 and 65,540. In the fields they're stored as 65,530 and 4. Ordinary arithmetic gives \(4 - 65530 = -65526\), which is nonsense. But 16-bit unsigned subtraction wraps around modulo 65,536:

\[ (4 - 65530) \bmod 65536 = 10, \]

the true offset. So once step 2 has shown that the span fits, wrapping_sub on the 16-bit fields gives every offset correctly. The builder never needs the 30 full labels of an ordinary group, only two.

Where SIMD comes in. Normalisation does the same subtraction 30 times. Modern processors have SIMD (single instruction, multiple data) instructions, which do one operation on several values at once. x86's psubw subtracts eight pairs of 16-bit numbers held in a 128-bit register. The compiler turned the builder's plain Rust loop into five of them:

movdqu (%rdi),%xmm2       ; load 16 bytes: eight fields
psubw  %xmm1,%xmm2        ; subtract the first label from all eight
movdqu %xmm2,(%rdi)       ; store them back

Three such groups of eight cover 24 fields, and two narrower loads, of 8 bytes and 4 bytes, cover the last 6. The arithmetic is cheap. The loads and stores aren't free: the fields are read and rewritten after already being written once as labels.
path: Building a smaller bzip2 decoding table

items.title: 10. RAW groups and their canonical order
items.text:
Canonical means "the one agreed form" of something that could be written several equivalent ways, as a set is often listed sorted so that {3, 1, 2} and {2, 3, 1} both appear as [1, 2, 3].

Compact30's agreed form puts RAW blocks in record order. Record 2's RAW block comes before record 5's, which comes before record 9's, and each RAW record's header holds its block's position. The builder doesn't find RAW groups in that order, though:

  • crossing groups are known from the byte counts before the scan, and get blocks in advance;
  • wide groups are found during the scan, when they finish, and get the next free block.

So the blocks might come out as [record 9, record 2, record 5]. The walk would cope with any consistent numbering, but the builder must match the reference byte for byte. A different order would be a different output.

The canonicaliser, the same in both builders, does three things:

  1. Ranks the RAW records. A bitmap, one bit per record set if the record is RAW, is scanned in record order. Each RAW record's rank becomes its block's final position, and is written into the header.
  2. Tags each block with its destination. Each RAW block has two spare entries, and the last one, word 31, temporarily holds the block's final position.
  3. Moves the blocks into place. It follows permutation cycles: pick up a block, put it where its tag says, pick up the block it displaces, and carry on until the cycle closes. This moves the blocks in place with one spare block of memory, then clears every word 31.
path: Building a smaller bzip2 decoding table

items.title: 11. Runs, fragments and the bulk emitter
items.text:
A run is a stretch of equal bytes, like the b's in aaaabbbbbbbbbcccc. BWT output has many, which is why bzip2 compresses it well.

A run's rows go to consecutive destinations of one bucket, because each takes the cursor's next value. Their labels are consecutive source labels, which follow a fixed pattern determined only by where the run starts within a block of 30 rows. So when a run covers a whole record, aligned to its start, the final offsets and the header are known in advance. The builder writes the record directly from one of thirty precomputed patterns, with no labels and no finish. That is the bulk emitter. It handles 74.3% of rows on the main corpus.

A run rarely starts exactly at a record boundary. Its first few rows may complete a record that was already part-filled, then come whole records, then a remainder:

prefix fragment → complete records → suffix fragment

The fragments go through provisional labels, written in bulk by fill, and are finished later like any other portion.

The builder finds runs by testing 16 bytes of \(L\) at a time for uniformity. A 16-byte tile that isn't uniform is handled one row at a time. The tile's labels are generated from its starting label, with one adjustment for the gap after each 30th row, so the source position is advanced once per tile, not once per row.
path: Building a smaller bzip2 decoding table

items.title: 12. Instructions, dependencies and time
items.text:
The research reports discuss the builder at three levels, which are related but not the same:

  • Mathematics: which output must be produced. Every destination needs the right next label and byte.

  • Algorithm: how it's produced, for example by stable counting sort, provisional labels and a finish per group.

  • Machine code: the instructions the compiled program actually runs: loads, stores, arithmetic, comparisons, branches, SIMD.

A change at one level shows up at the levels below. Removing a class of work from the algorithm removes many instructions. A change to how the Rust is written can remove a redundant load without changing the algorithm. A bottleneck in the processor can survive both.

Rust becomes assembly through the compiler. Two lines like

d.write.write(u);
d.write = d.write.add(1);

don't map one-to-one onto two instructions. The compiler decides what lives in registers, which loads it can drop, which branches to keep and which loops to vectorise. That is how the builder gets psubw without any hand-written SIMD, and why restructuring the Rust, or the algorithm, is how the instruction count goes down.

A dependency chain is a sequence of operations in which each needs the previous result. The first builder's per-row path was roughly: load the cursor, compute the record, load its header, extract the base, subtract, compare with the limit, store. No step can start before the one it depends on finishes. Independent operations can overlap, because a modern core runs several at once. So removing one link of a long chain can matter more than removing several independent instructions.

Fewer instructions needn't mean less time. An instruction count says how long a code path is, not how long it takes:

  • instructions differ in cost, and some split into several internal operations (micro-ops);
  • independent instructions can run at the same time;
  • a load can wait a long time for memory;
  • a mispredicted branch throws work away;
  • a short path that runs millions of times can still dominate the total.

So the reports weight each path by how often it runs on the real corpus. Even then they keep the result as an estimate until it's measured.

Lockstep steps. In the construction measurement, four workers each build a block, and the next step starts only when all four have finished. A step's time is its slowest worker's time. So a builder whose cost varies a lot from block to block loses time even if its average cost is unchanged: the slow blocks set the pace.

The instruction floor. A floor is the cost that remains once unnecessary work is gone. The current question is how much of the second builder's machine-level work the frozen output truly requires, and how much is removable. Some work is required: the right labels must reach the right fields. Some is removable, such as recomputing state that is already known, or reloading a value already in a register. Some is a trade, like provisional labels, which shorten the per-row path but add a second pass over the fields. And some costs, like cache misses, can't be read off the assembly at all.
path: Building a smaller bzip2 decoding table

items.title: 13. Four groupings, three numbers
items.text:
The builder juggles four different ways of dividing up the same rows:

Grouping Rows in it share It decides Bucket one byte value in \(F\) where each row goes Record 30 consecutive destinations how the output is laid out Epoch 61,440 consecutive source rows how full labels are recovered Run consecutive equal bytes in \(L\) when the bulk emitter can be used

They don't line up. A run can feed several records, a record can straddle two buckets, and one record's rows can come from several epochs. Most of the builder's complexity comes from reconciling these four without a full-sized temporary table.

And three numbers that are easy to confuse:

Symbol What it is Example \(i\) a source row: a position in \(L\) 42 \(r\) a destination: a position in \(F\), and a slot in the records 67 \(y = \varphi(i)\) the label of the row the walk visits next 44

If source row 42 is placed at destination 67, the builder writes information derived from label 44 into the field for destination 67, field 7 of record 2. Where the value goes comes from \(r\), and what it is comes from \(i\). Keeping those two apart is most of what it takes to read ctor2.rs.
path: Building a smaller bzip2 decoding table

items.title: 14. Glossary
items.text: Term Meaning BWT Burrows–Wheeler transform: the reversible reordering bzip2 is built on \(L\), \(F\) the last and first columns of the sorted rotations; \(F\) is \(L\) sorted Bucket the positions in \(F\) that hold one byte value Prefix sum a running total, used to turn counts into bucket starts Cursor the next free position in a bucket Stable equal items keep their original order \(T^{-1}\), ψ the navigation table: for each row, the next row of the walk Label, \(\varphi\) a row number recoded as 30 of every 32 values Record 64 bytes: 30 16-bit fields and a 4-byte header Base, offset a group's first label, and each row's label minus it RAW group 30 full entries, each a label and a byte, for a group that can't be ordinary Crossing, wide, forced RAW because of two buckets, because of too large a span, or because a test says so Portion one byte's share of one record Descriptor one byte's write state: pointers into its current portion Epoch 61,440 consecutive source rows, over which a label's high 16 bits are fixed Snapshot the 256 cursors saved at an epoch's start Normalisation subtracting a group's first label from each label Bulk emitter writes whole records for aligned runs directly from patterns Fragment the part of a run that doesn't fill a whole aligned record Canonicalisation putting RAW blocks into record order and renumbering their references SIMD instructions that work on several values at once Oracle the reference builder whose output must be matched byte for byte Dependency chain operations that each need the previous one's result
path: Building a smaller bzip2 decoding table

items.title: 15. Where the design comes from
items.text:
No single obscure primitive explains the builder. Each ingredient is a standard technique, and the combination is specific to compact30:

  • The navigation permutation and counting sort are as old as the BWT. Burrows and Wheeler's 1994 report already builds the table from counts, as the space–time post describes.

  • Base-plus-offset encoding is common in compressed integer formats and databases.

  • The record layout follows from fitting a group's offsets and a header into one cache line: 60 bytes leave 30 two-byte fields. Addressing them in blocks of 32 gives the label function, and \(2048 \times 32 = 65536\) gives the epoch, 61,440 rows. Each constant follows from the one before.

  • Bulk emission exploits the runs that make BWT output compressible.

  • Deferring the offsets came from asking whether each row's final offset had to be known when the row arrived. Answering no, and recovering the lost high bits from snapshots, is the second builder's design.

Seward's 2001 paper, discussed in the space–time post, is the background to the space–time trade-off itself. It doesn't propose this builder.

items.title: From 49 instructions to 12
items.text:
mibz2 · Research blog

The last post ended with a smaller navigation table, compact30 (named for its thirty rows to each 64-byte record), beating mibz2's conventional one when four workers walk at once, and a warning: the table still has to be built. The records in that comparison came from a reference builder that computed every row's successor in a full-sized temporary array first. A decoder can't afford that. It needs a builder that goes straight from the block's last column \(L\) and its byte counts to the final records, and costs about as much as the builder mibz2 uses today.

This post follows that builder through two versions. The second one's inner loop is a quarter the length of the first's, and the change behind it wasn't hand-written assembly. It was a different order of work, which let the compiler emit a much shorter loop. The second builder still costs too much with four workers, so the post ends with what we're doing about that.

The ideas a reader may not have met before, such as stable counting sort, the row labels, epochs and RAW canonicalisation, are introduced slowly in the technical appendix. It works through a small example from scratch, and its sections can be read on their own.
path: Building a smaller bzip2 decoding table

items.title: Building a smaller bzip2 decoding table: from 49 instructions to 12
items.text:
Writing a cheap placeholder for each row, and finishing each 30-row group once, shrank the inner loop. It still builds too slowly.

4 November 2026 · 12 min read · Research in progress
path: Building a smaller bzip2 decoding table

items.title: 1. What the builder has to produce
items.text:
The navigation table says, for each row of the block, which row the walk visits next. mibz2's conventional table stores that as a 4-byte entry per row. Compact30 groups the rows thirty at a time. Each group gets a 64-byte record, the size of one cache line: thirty 16-bit fields (60 bytes) and a 4-byte header.

In an ordinary record, all thirty rows output the same byte, and their next rows lie close together. The header holds that byte and a base, the first row's successor. Each field holds its own row's successor minus the base:

\[ \text{successor}(j) = \text{base} + \text{offset}[j]. \]

If a group's first three successors are 40, 44 and 49, the base is 40 and the first three fields are 0, 4 and 9. That's base-plus-offset encoding, used in many compressed integer formats. Compact30 keeps every offset directly addressable, so the walk reads one field instead of decoding packed bits.

Two kinds of group can't be ordinary, and are stored instead as RAW groups, thirty full 4-byte entries in a separate 128-byte block:

  • a crossing group holds the end of one byte's rows and the start of the next byte's, so no single header byte fits it;

  • a wide group's successors are too far apart for 16-bit offsets: more than 65,533 apart, because the two largest field values are reserved as markers.

The builder must produce the reference builder's output exactly, byte for byte. That includes every header, the padding in the last record, a final "parking" record, and the order of the RAW groups.

The successors themselves come from counting sort: each row of \(L\) goes to the next free position in its byte's bucket, the run of positions in the sorted first column \(F\) where that byte lives. The free position is tracked by a cursor per byte. Because the scan goes left to right, the rows that land in one bucket arrive in increasing order. Section 3 of the appendix works this through for \(\mathtt{banana}\). For the builder, it means that within one ordinary group the first row has the smallest successor and the last row the largest. So a group fits an ordinary record exactly when its first and last successors are at most 65,533 apart.
path: Building a smaller bzip2 decoding table

items.title: 2. The first builder: final offsets, one row at a time
items.text:
The obvious way to build the records is to scatter rows as counting sort does, and to write each row's final offset as it lands. That is what the first builder did. Abbreviated:

let x = self.x[ci];                         // byte c's next slot, in record coordinates
self.x[ci] = x + 1 + 2 * ((x & 31) == 29) as u32;
let (g, j) = ((x >> 5) as usize, (x & 31) as usize);
let idx = if j == 0 {
    // first slot of a group: start the record's header, unless it's RAW
    ...
} else {
    let h = self.header(g);                 // read the record's header back
    if h & RAW_BIT != 0 {
        Some(h & M20)                       // already RAW
    } else {
        let d = y - (h >> 8);               // offset from the record's base
        if d > MAX_OFF {
            Some(self.promote(g, j, h, true)) // too wide: turn the group into RAW now
        } else {
            self.fields(g).add(j).write(d as u16);
            None
        }
    }
};

Every row that isn't part of a long run goes through this. It reads the record's header back from memory, tests whether the group is RAW, subtracts the base, compares the result with the 16-bit limit, and only then writes. Most of those steps depend on the one before. The compiled loop for one row was 49 instructions long.

The first builder was correct: it matched the reference byte for byte, and passed an independent source audit. But a measurement on the i9 workstation put it at about 1.32 times production's CPU cost with four workers, against a budget of at most 1.067. That measurement was formally invalid: on one core the production builder it was compared with didn't stay stable from round to round, and one synchronised step started unevenly. But its figures left no doubt that the first builder was far over budget.
path: Building a smaller bzip2 decoding table

items.title: 3. The second builder: write a provisional label, finish later
items.text:
The second builder, designed by Astra, asks a different question: does the builder need to know a row's final offset when the row arrives? It doesn't. The offset depends on the group's base and on whether the group stays ordinary, and neither is known until the group is complete. So the builder writes something cheaper now, and does the rest once per group.

What it writes is the row's label. Compact30 numbers the rows so that each group of thirty uses thirty of a block of 32 consecutive numbers:

\[ \varphi(i) = 32\left\lfloor \frac{i}{30} \right\rfloor + (i \bmod 30). \]

Row 42 is the 13th row of group 1, so \(\varphi(42) = 32 + 12 = 44\). The two unused numbers in each block of 32 line up with the record's 4-byte header. With 32 a power of two, the walk can split a label into record and field with a shift and a mask. Successors are stored as labels; that is why a 30-row record can be addressed so cheaply.

The second builder takes the low 16 bits of the label, \(\varphi(i) \bmod 65536\), and writes them straight into the field where the row's final offset will eventually go. It uses no temporary array: the fields of the final records are the workspace.

To know where that field is, it keeps a small descriptor for each of the 256 byte values: a pointer to the next field to write, a pointer to the end of the current stretch of fields, and some bookkeeping. The per-row work, one, is then:

unsafe fn one(&mut self, c: u8, u: u16) -> bool {
    let ci = c as usize;
    if self.desc[ci].write == self.desc[ci].end && !self.refill(ci) {
        return false;                   // the byte's bucket is full: malformed counts
    }
    let d = &mut self.desc[ci];
    d.write.write(u);                   // the provisional label, into its final field
    d.write = d.write.add(1);           // and on to the next field
    true
}

It has no header read, no RAW test and no span check. When the descriptor's current stretch is full, refill finishes it and opens the next. refill is marked #[cold], which tells the compiler to keep it out of the way of the common path.

Writing only 16 bits loses information. A bzip2 block can hold 900,000 rows, and their labels run far past 65,535. The next section is about how the builder gets the missing high bits back without storing them.
path: Building a smaller bzip2 decoding table

items.title: 4. Getting the high bits back: epochs and snapshots
items.text:
The label function has a convenient period. After 2,048 groups of 30 rows, which is 61,440 rows, the label has advanced by exactly \(2048 \times 32 = 65536\):

\[ \varphi(i + 61440) = \varphi(i) + 65536. \]

So the builder splits the scan of \(L\) into epochs of 61,440 source rows. Within one epoch, every label's high 16 bits are the same number, the epoch's index \(e\), and

\[ \text{full label} = 65536 \cdot e + \text{the 16 bits in the field}. \]

The builder still has to know which epoch each row came from, and it can't afford to store an epoch per row. It doesn't need to. At the start of each epoch it saves a snapshot: the 256 byte cursors, each one the next free position in that byte's bucket. Rows land in a bucket in scan order, so the snapshots divide each bucket into epochs. A row of byte \(c\) at position \(r\) came from the latest epoch whose snapshot for \(c\) is at most \(r\):

\[ h(r) = \max\{\, e : A_e[c] \le r \,\}, \]

where \(A_e[c]\) is byte \(c\)'s cursor at the start of epoch \(e\). "Latest" matters. If \(c\) doesn't occur at all in some epoch, its cursor doesn't move, and two snapshots hold the same number. The row at that position arrived in the later of the two epochs.

A full 900,000-row block spans 15 epochs, so its snapshots take \(15 \times 256 \times 4\) bytes, 15 KiB. A temporary 32-bit successor for every row would take 3.6 MB. Both the snapshot and the epoch search are a few lines each. Section 7 of the appendix has a worked example.
path: Building a smaller bzip2 decoding table

items.title: 5. Finishing a group once
items.text:
When a group's thirty fields are full, finish turns it into its final form. It recovers the full labels of the first and last rows from the snapshots. In the common case it doesn't search at all, because the whole group arrived in the latest epoch. It then classifies the group from those two full labels:

  • If they differ by at most 65,533, the group is ordinary. The header becomes y0 << 8 | c, the first full label and the byte, and each field becomes its offset from the first.

  • If not, the group is wide. Its thirty full entries are rebuilt into a new RAW block, and the record is replaced by a reference to that block.

The classification has to use the full labels. The 16-bit values can mislead: a first label of 2 and a last of 65,536 are 65,534 apart, one too many for an ordinary group, but their low 16 bits are 2 and 0. The tests check that exact boundary. Rows 3 to 61,440 span 65,533 and stay ordinary; rows 2 to 61,440 span 65,534 and become RAW.

Once the group is known to be ordinary, though, the 16-bit values are enough for the offsets. Subtracting in 16-bit arithmetic that wraps around gives the right answer even across an epoch boundary. A first label whose low bits are 65,530 and a later one whose low bits are 4 differ by \((4 - 65530) \bmod 65536 = 10\), which is the true difference. In Rust, the normalisation is a short loop over the thirty fields:

let mut f = fp.read();               // all 30 fields, 60 bytes
for x in f.iter_mut() {
    *x = x.wrapping_sub(u0);         // u0: the first field's 16 bits
}
fp.write(f);

The compiler turned that into SIMD code. psubw subtracts eight 16-bit numbers at once, so three of them cover 24 fields, and two narrower ones cover the last 6. There is no hand-written vector code in the source. The arithmetic is cheap, but the 60 bytes of fields are still read and written a second time. That matters in section 8.

Crossing groups are known from the byte counts before the scan starts, so their RAW blocks are made in advance, and each byte's share of a crossing group is finished into its block separately. RAW groups found to be wide during the scan are numbered in the order they're found, which isn't record order. So at the end, a canonicalisation pass, unchanged from the first builder, permutes the RAW blocks into record order in place and rewrites each record's reference. Section 10 of the appendix explains it.
path: Building a smaller bzip2 decoding table

items.title: 6. Most rows never take the per-row path
items.text:
Long runs of one byte are common in a BWT's last column. A run's rows land in consecutive positions of one bucket, and consecutive source rows have labels that follow a fixed pattern. So when a run covers a whole group, aligned to the group's start, the builder can write the final record directly from one of thirty precomputed patterns, header included. It writes no provisional labels and needs no later finish. This bulk emitter, complete, was carried over unchanged from the first builder. Before a run fills whole groups, and after, the builder writes its leftover rows with fill, which still produces provisional labels.

On the main Wikidata corpus, 207,006,515 rows in 434 blocks:

Path Rows Share Bulk emitter: 5,127,300 complete records 153.8 million 74.3% Run fragments, through provisional labels 14.9 million 7.2% One row at a time, through one 38.3 million 18.5%

So the 12-instruction loop of the next section handles about a fifth of the rows. The builder also finishes 1,723,371 full ordinary groups and 30,949 wide ones.
path: Building a smaller bzip2 decoding table

items.title: 7. How the Rust becomes twelve instructions
items.text:
Nothing in either builder is hand-written assembly. Both are Rust, compiled by rustc with LLVM. The method is to read what the compiler produced, find work that doesn't need doing, and change the Rust so that the compiler has less to emit. The first builder's 49-instruction loop wasn't badly compiled; it was doing a lot. The second builder asks for less, so it gets a shorter loop.

This is that loop, from the prototype's build, in the AT&T syntax objdump prints by default (source first, destination last). The build that was measured has the same instructions at different addresses.

movzbl (%r15),%esi              ; c = the next byte of L
lea    (%rsi,%rsi,4),%rcx       ; 5c
lea    (%r8,%rcx,8),%r14        ; &desc[c]: descriptors are 40 bytes, 8 × 5c
mov    (%r8,%rcx,8),%rax        ; desc[c].write
cmp    0x8(%r8,%rcx,8),%rax     ; == desc[c].end ?
je     3440d                    ;   then refill (out of line)
mov    %bx,(%rax)               ; *write = the 16-bit label
addq   $0x2,(%r14)              ; desc[c].write += 2 bytes
inc    %r15                     ; next byte of L
inc    %ebx                     ; next label
cmp    %r12,%r15                ; end of this stretch of L?
jne    343e0
Instructions What they do movzbl read one byte of \(L\) two lea compute that byte's descriptor address: lea does arithmetic on addresses without touching memory mov, cmp, je load the write pointer, compare it with the end pointer, leave if full mov, addq store the label, advance the pointer inc, inc, cmp, jne next byte, next label, loop

A few Rust details helped:

  • #[inline(always)] on one puts its body in the loop.
  • #[cold] and #[inline(never)] on refill keep the rare case out of it.
  • The builder is generic over a constant, build::<COUNT>. With COUNT = true it keeps structural counters for analysis, and with false, the version that is measured, every counting branch disappears at compile time.

You can see all of this yourself on an x86-64 Linux machine. Build the frozen source and disassemble it:

git clone https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2 && cd mibz2
git checkout 8beffe2   # the frozen second builder
rustup toolchain install 1.97.0 --profile minimal
cargo +1.97.0 build --locked --release --example c30walk
objdump -d -C --no-show-raw-insn target/release/examples/c30walk > c30walk.asm

Then search c30walk.asm for ctor2::Ctor2>::build::<false>. The annotated excerpts are a shorter place to start. They pick out the two one-row loops, the bulk emitter and the fast path through finish. Addresses will differ from build to build. The archived listings are the reference for the counts quoted here.

items.title: 8. Fewer instructions, not yet a cheaper build
items.text:
The second builder passed the same checks as the first, and more:

  • byte-for-byte equality with the reference builder on 11 corpora and 53,924 synthetic cases, chosen to hit epoch boundaries, absent bytes, crossing groups, both span limits and malformed counts;

  • an independent audit of its unsafe code;

  • 542 cases run under Miri, Rust's checker for undefined behaviour, including targeted runs of the cases a first, interrupted run hadn't reached.

Then it was timed against production's builder on the i9 workstation, under a protocol fixed in advance. That measurement is also formally invalid. Production's own four-worker cost wasn't stable enough across its 20 rounds, almost entirely because of one slow round. Read only as descriptions, the figures are:

Four workers, compact30 ÷ production First builder Second builder Limit CPU cost of building 1.316 1.086 1.067 Time until all four have built 1.364 1.114 1.02

The two builders were measured in separate runs, so the drop isn't a controlled comparison. But it's large, and every one of the 19 normal rounds showed the second builder taking between 1.110 and 1.144 times as long as production. Re-running the same measurement just to turn "invalid" into "fail" wasn't worth the workstation's time.

The figures point to two reasons the shorter loop wasn't enough.

The work moved rather than vanished. Each row that goes through a provisional label is written twice, once as a label and once as an offset, and read in between. Across the corpus, normalisation reads about 103 MB of fields and writes about 103 MB back, roughly one extra byte each way per row. The first builder did almost none of that: its field loads were 0.002 per row, against the second's 0.274. The fast path through finish is 81 instructions, and a group that rolls over through refill adds another 62. That's about 143 per group, against 12 per row in the loop.

The slowest worker sets the pace. The second limit is about completion. The four workers build in lockstep, and a step ends when the last of them finishes. If three take 9 ms and one takes 11 ms, the step takes 11 ms, and speeding up the other three changes nothing. The second builder's cost varies more from block to block than production's does: blocks that use the bulk emitter less are relatively more expensive. On the full blocks, about 1.18 times production's cost in the quarter with the least bulk coverage, against about 0.98 times in the quarter with the most. So the slowest worker in a step falls further behind the average under compact30. Weighted by time, the slowest worker took 1.073 times the mean worker's time with the second builder, against 1.047 with production's. That difference is enough, as arithmetic, to turn a CPU ratio of 1.086 into a completion ratio of about 1.114. It is a description, not a diagnosis: the records can't tell whether those builds are slower because of more instructions, cache misses or something else.

An assembly-level review of the second builder found more removable work. One example is in the loop above. mov (%r8,%rcx,8),%rax has already loaded the write pointer into a register. But addq $0x2,(%r14) adds to the copy in memory, which means reading the pointer again. The compiler could instead store the incremented register value, removing one load from each of 38 million rows. Whether that would save time depends on what the processor was waiting on, which an instruction count can't tell you.

The review's strongest candidate was a specialised path for the common case of an ordinary group followed by another group of the same byte. The candidate would finish one and set up the next without the general machinery, removing perhaps 40 to 50 instructions per group. The review modelled what that would buy, using the measured records. To reach just the completion limit, without the margin a valid pass needs, it would have to save about 6.6 ns, around 33 cycles, on every one of the 1.65 million fast group finishes. The assembly doesn't show that much removable time. So the review advised against building that change on its own.

That leaves the question this work is now on. A single local change won't close the gap. Would all the removable work together, counted across the whole builder without counting any saving twice, be enough? A fuller accounting of the builder's machine code is under way, weighted by how often each path runs and by which workers finish last. Until it reports, the second builder stays as it is. It is correct, and much cheaper than the first, but it doesn't yet meet the budget the traversal result set.

The general lesson outlasts this builder. A computation that is expensive done once per element can become cheap if its results are held in a different form for a while, and the expensive part is done once per group. The cost doesn't disappear, though: it moves, and it has to be found again where it went.

items.title: Huffman decoding: the bit buffer in a register
items.text:
mibz2 · Research blog

A decoder reads a compressed file one byte at a time, but the codes inside a bzip2 file aren't whole bytes. They are Huffman codes: each is a run of bits of its own length, one bit for a very common symbol and a dozen or more for a rare one, packed end to end with nothing between them. So a decoder keeps a bit buffer, a small holding area for bits it has read from the file but not yet decoded. In mibz2, our bzip2 decoder written in Rust, the buffer is a single 64-bit integer. The decoder reads each code off its top end, shifts the rest up behind it, and tops it up with more bytes from the file when it runs low.

This post is about where that integer was kept. It held the same bits and the decoder did the same work, but the compiled code wrote the buffer to memory after every code and read it back before the next. Even from the processor's nearest cache, a read of a value just written waits several cycles for the write, and every code waited that long. Rearranged so the compiler could keep the buffer in a register, the thread that reads the codes, which mibz2 calls the scanner, ran 12.9% faster on an Intel Xeon 8370C CI runner and 5.0% faster on an AMD EPYC 9V74.

The benchmark decodes a fixed sample of the Wikidata dump: 12 slices of it, 210 MB once decoded. On the Intel runner a one-thread decode of that sample ran 2.7% faster. The scanner is about a tenth of the decode, so its own saving accounts for about half of that figure; the rest is within the noise of the other stages. On the AMD runner no change in the whole decode was detected. Some AMD cores can serve a read of an address just written without the usual wait, which leaves less to remove there. On Intel the cut fell short of the 15–25% predicted for it.

Section 1 shows a bit buffer at work on a small example and as mibz2's code. Section 2 is how the decoder reads a code with a lookup table, and why each code waits for the last. Section 3 places this in bzip2's format and in mibz2's decoder. Sections 4 to 6 are how the stored buffer was found, why the compiler put it there, and the change. Sections 7 to 9 give the prediction, the correctness checks and what the benchmark measured, run by run.
path: Huffman decoding: the bit buffer in a register

items.title: Huffman decoding in mibz2: keeping the bit buffer in a register
items.text:
The Huffman decoder wrote its bit buffer to memory and read it back at every lookup. Kept in a register, the stage ran 13% faster on Intel and 5% on AMD.

5 November 2026 · 16 min read · Research result
path: Huffman decoding: the bit buffer in a register

items.title: 1. What a bit buffer is
items.text:
Huffman coding gives each symbol a code of its own length: short for common symbols, long for rare ones. The codes are chosen so that no code is the beginning of another, which is what lets them be packed end to end with no separators. Reading from the start, the bits seen so far can only ever be the beginning of one code.

Reading a toy Huffman code

The codeA 0B 10C 110D 111A is the most common symbol,so it gets the shortest codeThe bits, and how they read01 1 01 001 1 1ACBADeach arrow: where the nextcode starts is known onlyonce this one has been read A made-up code, not one of bzip2's. The ten bits 0110100111 hold five symbols. Their boundaries are found only by reading the codes in order.

Take a made-up alphabet of four symbols, A to D, where A is the most common: A gets 0, B 10, C 110 and D 111. The ten bits 0110100111 then read as A, C, B, A, D. Notice what the reader had to do. It could only tell that C began at the second bit once it had read A, and only tell where B began once it had read C. Where a code starts depends on the lengths of all the codes before it.

A computer, though, reads the file in bytes, eight bits at a time, and these codes don't line up with bytes. The bit buffer bridges the two. mibz2 loads the file's next bytes into a 64-bit integer, buf, with the first unread bit at the top (the left end, written in binary). Two more numbers go with it, and together they are the reader's whole state, Bits:

Field Type What it holds pos usize the next byte of input to load buf u64 the stream's next bits, the first of them in the most significant bit live u32 how many of buf's top bits are valid

Three operations act on it, each a line or two of Rust:

  • Peek at the next \(n\) bits without consuming them: buf >> (64 - n). For the next three bits that is buf >> 61, which moves the top three bits to the bottom of the number.
  • Skip \(n\) bits once a code of that length has been read: buf <<= n; live -= n;. The code's bits fall off the top, and the next code moves up to take their place.
  • Refill when the buffer runs low: load the eight bytes at pos, OR them into buf just below the bits still live, and advance pos by as many whole bytes as fitted. That leaves at least 56 bits live.

The figure below runs the toy bits through a ten-bit buffer. Each press of its button is one peek and one skip: it says which code the bits at the front begin with, and then shifts that code out, so the next one moves to the front.

Try it: decode the toy bits one code at a time

The code: A = 0 B = 10 C = 110 D = 111

  1. 0
  2. 1
  3. 1
  4. 0
  5. 1
  6. 0
  7. 0
  8. 1
  9. 1
  10. 1

The buffer, its next unread bit on the left. In green: the bits of the code at the front, and that code in the key above. Dotted: room left by bits already shifted out.

Decoded so farnone yetUnread bits (live)10The last shift, in Rustnothing shifted yet Read the next code →Reset

Read in order: the buffer starts 0, which is A. Shifting A's one bit out brings 110 to the front, which is C. Then 10 is B, 0 is A and 111 is D. Each shift moves the buffer left by the length of the code just read.

In mibz2 the buffer is 64 bits wide, not ten, and a refill tops it up long before it runs out.

So the buffer is just an integer and a few shifts. It isn't an array or a special piece of hardware, and the whole state is three numbers: pos, buf and live.
path: Huffman decoding: the bit buffer in a register

items.title: 2. Reading a code with a lookup table
items.text:
In the figure, each symbol was found by matching the front of the buffer against the four codes. A simple decoder makes that match a bit at a time. It looks at the first bit: if it is 0, the symbol is A. If not, it looks at the second bit: if that is 0, the symbol is B. If not, it looks at the third. Each bit of a code costs a step, so the toy's ten bits take ten.

Fast Huffman decoders, mibz2 among them, replace those steps with a single lookup in a table made before decoding starts. The toy's longest code is three bits, so peek at the next three bits, whatever they are: buf >> 61, the peek from section 1. No code is longer than three bits, so the first code is always inside them. A shorter code leaves bits over, and those belong to the codes after it. Three bits have only eight possible values, and for each one we can work out in advance which codes it begins with:

Next three bits They begin with Bits to skip 000 A, then A 2 001 A, then A 2 010 A, then B 3 011 A 1 100 B, then A 3 101 B 2 110 C 3 111 D 3

The three bits, read as a number from 0 to 7, pick the row. Many rows hold more than one code: 010 is A's code 0 followed by B's code 10. So a row can name two symbols, and one lookup then decodes both. The bits to skip are the lengths of the codes the row names, added up: A and B are 1 + 2 = 3 bits. When the bits after the first code don't make a whole code, the row names just the one symbol. 011 is an example: its 11 is only the start of C or D, so the row says A and skips one bit, and the next lookup sees the rest.

With this table the toy bits 0110100111 take four lookups instead of ten steps:

Lookup Next three bits The row says Bits to skip Decoded so far 1 011 A 1 A 2 110 C 3 A C 3 100 B, then A 3 A C B A 4 111 D 3 A C B A D

mibz2's table works the same way, at a larger size. A bzip2 code can be up to 20 bits long, and a table with a row for every 20-bit value would have about a million rows, 4 MB of them: far too large for the processor's nearest cache, which holds tens of kilobytes. So mibz2 peeks at ten bits instead. Its table has 1,024 entries of 32 bits each, 4 KB in all. Ten bits is a balance: with fewer, more codes would be too long for the table; with more, the table would outgrow the cache. Most of bzip2's codes are shorter than ten bits, so most entries are like the toy table's rows: one or two symbols, and how many bits to skip.

Ten bits can't settle every case, and two other kinds of entry cover the rest. A code longer than ten bits only begins in those ten bits. Its entry says so, and the decoder reads that code a bit at a time on a slower path, as libbzip2 (the reference bzip2 library) does. Long codes belong to the rarest symbols, so this path is seldom taken. And if no code at all begins with the ten bits, the file can't be valid bzip2, so that entry marks the block as corrupt.

The bit buffer, and one table lookup

live = 56: bits loaded and not yet usednext 10 bits46 more live bitsnot valid yetTable lookup1,024 entries of 32 bits,one for each 10-bit prefixThe entry says what those bits begin withone symbol, or two whose codes both fit, and the bits they take;or a code longer than 10 bits (slow path), or an invalid codeShift buf left by those bits; take them from livethe next lookup's index is the top 10 bits of the new bufEvery lookup needs the last one's shift: these steps form one chain.refill, after every four lookups: load the 8 bytes at pos below the live bits, andadvance pos by whole bytes until at least 56 bits are live Conceptual, drawn just after a refill. The divisions in the bar are bytes. A refill leaves 56 to 63 bits live; four lookups use at most 40 of them.

On the Wikidata sample, about 83% of lookups decode two symbols at once (our counts). A refill leaves at least 56 bits live, and four lookups use at most 40, so the fast loop refills, makes four lookups, then refills again.

One lookup is four steps:

  1. take the top ten bits of buf;
  2. load the table entry they index;
  3. take the code's length from the entry;
  4. shift buf left by that length.

Step 1 of the next lookup needs the result of step 4 of this one. However many instructions the processor could run at once, it can't start a lookup before the last one has finished its shift. So the time a lookup takes is the latency of this chain: the time each step waits for the one before it. Any step added to the chain adds its latency to every lookup.

items.title: 3. Where this sits in bzip2 and in mibz2
items.text:
The bit buffer is the first thing a bzip2 decoder touches, because Huffman coding is the last of bzip2's four compression steps, and a decoder undoes them in reverse. bzip2 splits its input into blocks of up to 900 kB and compresses each block on its own:

How bzip2 compresses a block, and how a decoder undoes it

Bytesthe block,≤ 900 kBRLE1long runs of abyte shortenedBWTbytes reordered,like by likeMTF + RLE2bytes become mostlysmall symbolsHuffmansymbols writtenas bit codescompressing: left to rightdecoding: right to left, Huffman firstthis post is about the first decoding step, reading the bit codes back The four steps of bzip2's compression of one block. Each is undone in the opposite order, so a decoder starts with the Huffman codes.

The first step shortens any run of four or more identical bytes to four bytes and a count: bzip2's first run-length coding, RLE1. The second, the Burrows–Wheeler transform (BWT), reorders the block's bytes so that bytes which occur in similar contexts end up next to one another. An earlier post works through it with the word banana. The reordered block is full of repeats, and the third step, move-to-front coding (MTF), turns repeats into small numbers. It keeps a list of byte values ordered by how recently each was seen, and replaces each byte by its position in that list: a byte that just appeared becomes 0, one seen a little earlier 1, and so on. Runs of zeros are then written compactly with two special symbols, RUNA and RUNB: the second run-length coding, RLE2.

What comes out is a sequence of symbols from a small alphabet: RUNA, RUNB, one symbol for each list position other than 0, and an end-of-block symbol. A block that uses 100 distinct byte values has an alphabet of 102 symbols. The block is mostly runs and small positions, so a few symbols are very common and most are rare. That imbalance is what the fourth step, Huffman coding, turns into fewer bits.

A bzip2 block uses not one code but several. The encoder builds between two and six code tables, each suited to a different mix of symbols. It switches between them every 50 symbols, picking for each group of 50 the table that codes it in the fewest bits. So the block begins with a header that tells the decoder how to follow along. It says which byte values occur in the block, which fixes the alphabet. It holds each code table, stored as the length of every symbol's code: the codes themselves follow from their lengths by a fixed rule, so the lengths are all that need storing. And it holds a selector for each group of 50 symbols, naming the table that group was coded with. bzip2's codes are at most 20 bits long.

A bzip2 block: the header, then its symbols in groups of 50

The headerByte values usedwhich of the 256 occurSelectorsa table number for each 50 symbolsCode tables, 2 to 6each as every symbol's code lengthThe symbols, as Huffman codes50 symbols · table 250 symbols · table 150 symbols · table 2…… end of blockThe selectors decide which table reads each group. The last group stops at the end-of-block symbol. Simplified: the header also holds the block's checksum and where the inverse BWT starts. The selectors are themselves compactly coded. The table numbers shown are an example.

So reading a block's symbols means reading its header, then, for each group of 50, taking the table its selector names and reading codes with it one after another, until the end-of-block symbol. mibz2 builds a lookup table like section 2's for each of the block's code tables. Within a group of 50, its fast loop runs while at least eight of the group's symbols remain, since four lookups can decode eight; the group's last few symbols go through a slower loop.

mibz2 splits a decode between two kinds of thread, as the post on block dispatch describes. One thread, the scanner, reads the stream from the start. For each block it reads the header and decodes all the block's symbols. This can only be one thread working in order: a block's end is found only by reading up to its end-of-block symbol, and the next block begins straight after it. The scanner then hands each block's symbols to a worker, and several workers run at once. A worker does the rest. It undoes the move-to-front coding and RLE2 together, inverts the Burrows–Wheeler transform in two parts (it builds a table, then walks it), then expands RLE1 and checks the block's CRC, a checksum stored in its header.

Where Huffman decoding sits in mibz2

Compressed streambzip2 blocks, each a header and its Huffman-coded symbolsThe scanner thread · every block, in orderBlock headerbytes used, code tablesHuffman decoding: this post1.19 c/B, about 10.5% of a one-thread decodeA worker · one block at a time, several workers at onceMTF + RLE2undo move-to-front1.79 c/BTable buildinverse BWT, part 11.66 c/BWalkinverse BWT, part 26.19 c/BRLE1 + CRCexpand runs, check0.44 c/BDecoded bytes, handed back in stream order Measured: the base build's one-thread stage costs on the Intel Xeon 8370C runner, in cycles per byte of output at the runner's reported clock, 11.28 c/B in all (the second benchmark run of section 9). At one thread the stages run one after another on one CPU; at four, the scanner's thread runs beside the workers.

At one thread every stage runs on the same CPU, one after another, so the scanner's share of the time is its share of the decode: on the Intel runner, 1.19 of 11.28 cycles per output byte, about 10.5%. At four threads the scanner runs alongside the workers. All four of the runner's CPUs are then busy, so the scanner's CPU time still costs wall time, at about a quarter of its own rate. These shares come from a census we took of what limits the decoder's speed on CI's runners, stage by stage. Its journal entry calls it the binding census, after the resource that binds each stage: the one whose limit it runs into first, whether that is the processor's instructions, memory, or waiting on another thread.
