items.title: 4. What the census found
items.text:
The census asked what limits today's decoder on CI's runners. One of its lines of inquiry took the stages that run in sequence, and read the scanner's machine code. In the four-lookup loop, each lookup ended by storing buf to memory, and the next began by loading it back.

A store followed by a load from the same address costs few instructions, and it doesn't wait for the cache: the processor hands the stored value straight to the load. That hand-over is called store-to-load forwarding. It still takes time, about 4–5 cycles on Intel's Ice Lake cores such as the 8370C's, and here it was part of the lookup chain. The census estimated a lookup at about 13–15 cycles with the reload, against about 8–9 with buf in a register. These figures are estimates, from the listing, the instruction counts and the measured cycles, not counts of events: CI's runners expose no hardware performance counters.

One lookup's chain, before and after

Before: buf kept in memoryreload bufa forward, ~4–5 cyclesshift rightthe top 10 bitstable loadthe entrymaskthe lengthshift left, storefor the next lookupabout 13–15 cycles a lookup on Ice LakeAfter: buf held in a registernothing to reloadshift rightthe top 10 bitstable loadthe entrymaskthe lengthshift leftstays in a registerabout 8–9 cycles a lookup Estimated, not measured: the census's reading of the listing for Ice Lake. The measured saving is in section 9.

Across the four runner models the census measured, the scanner took 6.9–10.3% of the four-thread wall time (7–10% in its summary) and 11–14% of the one-thread time. It estimated that removing the forward would recover 0.5–4.1% of the four-thread wall, and 1.7–5.6% at one thread, and called it "The cheapest and most certain mechanism on this front."
path: Huffman decoding: the bit buffer in a register

items.title: 5. Why the compiler kept the buffer in memory
items.text:
Nothing in the Rust asked for a store. The loop calls the reader's methods, which are small and marked #[inline(always)], so their bodies are compiled into the loop. Two calls are not inlined: the slow path for codes longer than ten bits, and the slow refill near the end of the input. Both are marked #[cold], and on master before the change both took the reader by reference, as &mut Bits (decode_entry_slow(e, br), refill_slow(&mut self)).

Passing a reference to a function that isn't inlined lets the reader's address escape. As far as the compiler (LLVM) can tell, that function might read or change the reader, so the reader's fields have to be in memory, at that address, whenever such a call can happen. The calls are rare, but one can happen at any lookup. A second constraint follows from the first. The loop writes each decoded symbol through a pointer into the output, out[n], and once the reader's address has escaped, LLVM must assume such a write might change it too. So it loads buf again after the writes (registration).

This is one of the four steps, from master before the change, as the archived listing gives it (the bench binary, rustc 1.99.0, in Intel syntax: destination first). r15 holds the reader's address:

ab240  mov    rsi,QWORD PTR [r15+0x18]                              bits.rs:74
ab244  mov    rax,rsi                                               bits.rs:74
ab247  shr    rax,0x36                                              bits.rs:74
ab24b  mov    edx,DWORD PTR [r9+rax*4]                              block.rs:326
ab24f  mov    eax,edx                                               block.rs:331
ab251  shr    eax,0xb                                               block.rs:331
ab254  and    eax,0x3                                               block.rs:331
ab257  je     ab450 <mibz2::block::read_item+0x12c0>                block.rs:331
ab25d  mov    ecx,edx                                               block.rs:332
ab25f  and    ecx,0x1f                                              block.rs:332
ab262  shl    rsi,cl                                                bits.rs:81
ab265  mov    QWORD PTR [r15+0x18],rsi                              bits.rs:81
ab269  sub    DWORD PTR [r15+0x20],ecx                              bits.rs:82
Instructions What they do mov rsi,QWORD PTR [r15+0x18] load buf back from the reader in memory: the forward mov, shr rax,0x36 its top ten bits (a shift right by 54), the index mov edx,DWORD PTR [r9+rax*4] load the table entry mov, shr, and, je the entry's symbol count: none means the slow path mov, and ecx,0x1f the bits to consume, the entry's low five bits shl rsi,cl consume them mov QWORD PTR [r15+0x18],rsi store buf back to the reader sub DWORD PTR [r15+0x20],ecx take them from live, in memory

Over a four-lookup iteration the registration counts five stores and three reloads of buf, and four read-modify-writes of live in memory: about one forward on the chain per lookup.
path: Huffman decoding: the bit buffer in a register

items.title: 6. The change: the state as a value
items.text:
The change, #204, moves the three fields into a small struct that can be copied, Reg, and has the loop hold one in a local variable (src/bits.rs):

pub struct Bits<'a> {
    data: &'a [u8],
    r: Reg,
}

#[derive(Clone, Copy)]
pub(crate) struct Reg {
    pos: usize,
    buf: u64,
    live: u32,
}
  • The logic moves unchanged. Refill, peek and skip become methods of Reg.
  • The cold paths take the state by value and return the state after: decode_entry_slow(&self, e: u32, r: Reg, data: &[u8]) -> (Result<u16, ErrorKind>, Reg), and refill_slow(mut self, data: &[u8]) -> Reg. No call receives the state's address, so the compiler can keep its fields in registers, and pass them into a cold call and back like any other arguments.
  • The loop works on a copy. read_item takes the state out of the reader before the symbol loop, with let (data, mut r) = br.parts();, and writes it back once, with br.set(r), on every way out of the loop.
  • The loop is rotated. The refill moves from the top of the four-lookup loop to its foot. With the refill at the top, the state was carried from one pass of the loop to the next in memory, which cost a store and a reload every refill. The refills happen at the same points as before:
if left >= 2 * STEPS {
    r.refill(data);
    loop {
        for _ in 0..STEPS {
            step!(true);
        }
        if left < 2 * STEPS {
            break;
        }
        r.refill(data);
    }
}

Bits's public methods keep their signatures, and the block header is parsed as before. This is the same step in the new build, from the same listing:

ab582  shr    rcx,0x36                                              bits.rs:71
ab586  mov    rdx,QWORD PTR [rsp+0x28]                              bits.rs:71
ab58b  mov    edx,DWORD PTR [rdx+rcx*4]                             block.rs:335
ab58e  mov    r9d,edx                                               block.rs:340
ab591  shr    r9d,0xb                                               block.rs:340
ab595  and    r9d,0x3                                               block.rs:340
ab599  je     ab853 <mibz2::block::read_item+0x1643>                block.rs:340
ab59f  mov    ecx,edx                                               block.rs:341
ab5a1  and    ecx,0x1f                                              block.rs:341
ab5a4  shl    rdi,cl                                                bits.rs:78

buf is in rdi, and the step ends at shl rdi,cl, with no store. The loop's only stores now are the symbol writes. It still loads values that don't change during the loop from the stack, such as the table's address ([rsp+0x28]). Nothing in the loop stores to them, so those loads wait on no forward, and their addresses don't depend on the chain.
path: Huffman decoding: the bit buffer in a register

items.title: 7. What was predicted, before any timing
items.text:
Before any CI timing, the change was registered: its mechanism, the measurements that need no timing, a prediction and a decision rule, committed before any CI timing of the branch (registration).

Instruction counts from callgrind, which counts every instruction a program executes, on the bench corpus:

Instructions Before After Change Per four-lookup iteration 153.8 144.8 −5.9% The whole scanner 746.2 million 727.4 million −2.5% Per byte of output 3.56 3.47 −2.5%

The forwards also leave the lookup chain: four in each iteration, about 0.94 a lookup on average. The registration then estimated the saving at about \(F\) cycles a lookup, where \(F\) is the store-to-load forwarding latency on the runner, plus the 2.5% of the scanner's instructions:

Figure Predicted Scanner stage, one thread, Intel Ice Lake (8370C), \(F\) about 4–5 15–25% faster Scanner stage, one thread, AMD and Intel Golden Cove (8573C) 0–25% faster Wikidata wall, one thread, Intel 1.5–3.5% faster Wikidata wall, four threads 0.5–2.5% faster MTF, table build, walk, RLE1, CRC unchanged: their code is untouched

The AMD range is wide because some cores can rename a store and a later load of the same address: they recognise the pair and hand the value over without the forward's latency. Whether CI's AMD runners do that for this code wasn't known.

The decision rule had four parts:

  • Correctness, required: CI green, and the same bytes on every corpus in every bench run.
  • Benefit, required: in at least one run, the Wikidata one-thread wall or CPU faster beyond noise, or the one-thread scanner stage faster beyond noise with the whole decoder's one-thread point estimate not slower; and the same figure not slower in the other run.
  • Refutation: a scanner cut under 10% on an Intel runner, or any other stage moving beyond noise, would refute the mechanism.
  • No harm, required: a wall figure flagged slower is settled by one more run on the same head. Flagged again, the rule fails. At most three runs, with each run's CPU named.

items.title: 8. Is it still the same decoder?
items.text:
The change has to give exactly the same symbols, and fail in exactly the same way on corrupt input. Before timing:

  • A differential ran master's bits.rs and block.rs against the new ones, outside the repository, on 52 files and 164,076 cases of intact and mutated blocks. It compared 9.15 billion symbols, every case was identical, and all 11 error kinds that can be reached were exercised.
  • A scanner-only driver gives the same 24,979,299 symbols, with the same hash.
  • New tests:
    • the reader's state stepped as the loop steps it, compared with the input's bits;
    • 4,000 fully written blocks, with real or corrupt codes up to 20 bits, bit flips and cuts. Each is compared with a reference that decodes one lookup at a time: the symbols, the error, the end bit and whether it read past the input;
    • 300 corrupted level-1 streams, compared with libbzip2.

In both benchmark runs, every corpus decoded to the same bytes with both builds, and CI passed.
path: Huffman decoding: the bit buffer in a register

items.title: 9. What the benchmark measured
items.text:
The CI benchmark decodes every corpus with the base build and the PR's build in alternating order, ten paired rounds a run. It runs on a GitHub-hosted runner with four virtual CPUs: two physical cores, each running two hardware threads (SMT siblings). The CPU model varies from run to run. It ran twice on #204's final head, 53cc38db: once on an AMD EPYC 9V74 (Zen 4) and once on an Intel Xeon 8370C (Ice Lake). Each change below is the PR's build over the base: the geometric mean of the rounds' paired ratios, with its 95% interval in percent beneath it. Negative is faster. "Wall" is the elapsed time to decode the Wikidata sample.

Figure Predicted Intel 8370C AMD 9V74 Scanner, one thread Intel: −15% to −25%AMD: 0 to −25% −12.9%(−13.9, −11.9) −5.0%(−6.3, −3.6) Scanner, cycles a byte 1.19 → 1.04 1.18 → 1.12 Wall, one thread Intel: −1.5% to −3.5% −2.7%(−4.3, −1.1) +1.0%(−0.7, +2.6) Wall, two threads none −2.5%(−4.6, −0.3) −1.3%(−4.0, +1.5) Wall, four threads −0.5% to −2.5% −1.3%(−5.6, +3.3) −0.3%(−3.2, +2.6) Other stages no change none moved none moved

On Intel, the stage cut missed its prediction. It was 12.9%, against 15–25%. That is above the 10% the rule set as the refutation, so a saving of the predicted kind was there, but smaller than the model estimated. By our arithmetic, which is derived rather than measured, the stage saved 0.15 cycles per output byte at the runner's reported clock. At the census's 0.0646 lookups per byte, that is about 2.3 cycles a lookup, against the 4–5 the model estimated. With no hardware counters on CI, the benchmark can't say which part of the model was wrong.

On AMD, the cut was smaller still, as the mechanism allowed. It was 5.0%, about 0.9 cycles a lookup by the same arithmetic, and inside the 0–25% registered for a core that may rename the forward. That fits renaming, but no counter shows it.

One-thread decoding got faster on Intel, and no change was detected on AMD. On Intel the whole one-thread decode was 2.7% faster, inside the predicted 1.5–3.5%. The scanner's own saving explains about half of that point estimate: 0.15 of 11.28 cycles per byte, 1.3%. The rest is within the noise of the other stages, none of which moved beyond noise. On AMD the one-thread decode was +1.0% (−0.7%, +2.6%), with no change detected either way.

One run's interval understates how much a figure moves between runs. Each interval above describes the spread between one run's ten rounds. A/A controls, benchmark runs on merges that left the decoder alone, show the one-thread figure also moving by about 0.7% from run to run. With that spread added, the Intel one-thread result is −2.7% (−4.8%, −0.6%): still faster.

At four threads, no change was detected on either runner. The prediction, 0.5–2.5%, is smaller than the benchmark can resolve at four threads, where the intervals here are 6–9 points wide. At four threads the scanner thread's CPU time fell from 0.15 to 0.12 seconds on Intel and from 0.09 to 0.08 on AMD, out of about 1.6 and 1.1 seconds in all. No figure was flagged slower in either run.

Under its rule, the change passed. Correctness held. The Intel run showed the benefit, with the one-thread wall and CPU both faster beyond noise, and the AMD run's same figure was not slower. The Intel stage cut was above the refutation threshold, no other stage moved, and nothing was flagged as a harm.

PR #204 met its registered decision rule and was merged on 5 November 2026, as 264ae5bb.
path: Huffman decoding: the bit buffer in a register

items.title: 10. What it shows
items.text:
The Huffman codes, the tables and the bits consumed are the same as before, and the scanner runs only 2.5% fewer instructions. What changed is the chain each lookup waits on. On Intel, 2.5% fewer instructions gave a 12.9% shorter stage, because what was removed, the forward, was part of that chain. Elsewhere in mibz2 the opposite has happened: in the post on memory-level parallelism, removing a third of the walk's instructions made no difference to four workers. An instruction count predicts time where the instructions sit on the critical path.

The pattern is easy to recreate. A loop carries a value from one iteration to the next, and also passes a reference to it to a function that isn't inlined, such as a cold path that takes &mut self. The value's address escapes, so it lives in memory, and every iteration costs a store and a reload. Passing the state by value and taking it back keeps it in registers. The census found two other store-to-load chains, in MTF's list and in the table build's byte cursors. Those are different: there the data lives in memory because the algorithm keeps it there. The bit buffer had no reason to be in memory, only a reference that let it escape.

A decode that takes more symbols a lookup is being prototyped separately, and would combine with this change. The census estimated that a wider table, now, would take at most about another 10% off the scanner, which is under 1% of the four-thread wall.

  • the change: #204, and its registration, committed before any CI timing;

  • the two benchmark runs: run 42057920798, attempts 1 (AMD EPYC 9V74) and 2 (Intel Xeon 8370C), reported on #204.

items.title: Pipelined teams in mibz2 0.2.6
items.text:
mibz2 · Research blog

mibz2, our bzip2 decoder written in Rust, decodes a file with small groups of threads that we call teams. A bzip2 file is a series of blocks that can be decoded independently, and each team decodes one block at a time. One thread in the team, the leader, does some of each block's work alone, and the team's other threads, its helpers, wait for it. That waiting is time the decoder could spend decoding. Our new release, 0.2.6, removes much of it.

In 0.2.6, a team works on three blocks at once. While its helpers do the expensive middle part of one block, the leader finishes the block before it and prepares the block after it. On the ten-core machine we test on, with ten threads, this is 7.2% faster than 0.2.5 (95% interval 5.4% to 8.9%), and 6.5–7.0% faster at 11 to 20 threads. It is not cheaper: it uses about 5% more processor time in total, and 7–8 MB more memory at its peak.

That it helps at all is not obvious. In 0.2.5 the leader takes part in the expensive middle part. Pipelining takes it out, so that part runs on one thread fewer and gets slower. The 7% is what is left after paying for that. The first version of the pipeline gained only 4%, for 9% more processor time. Two refinements made it worth shipping: the leader keeps the pipeline full after a small block, and threads that wait go to sleep instead of staying on the processor.

The previous post explained why 0.2.5 split ten threads into three teams of three, and proposed this pipeline as the next experiment. This post is its result. Section 1 shows what a team does with one block, and section 2 what pipelining changes and why it might not pay. Section 3 is the first pipeline's measurement, section 4 the two refinements, and section 5 the run that confirmed the release against 0.2.5. Section 6 covers the cost and where it applies.

items.title: Pipelined teams: how mibz2 0.2.6 decodes 7% faster on ten cores
items.text:
While a team's helpers invert one block, its leader finishes the last and prepares the next: 7% faster than 0.2.5 on ten cores, for 5% more processor time.

7 November 2026 · 13 min read · Research result

items.title: 1. What does a team do with one block?
items.text:
bzip2 compresses a file in blocks of up to 900 kB each, each compressed with no reference to the others, so each can be decoded on its own. One thread, the scanner, reads the file and undoes the outermost layer of every block, the Huffman coding. The rest of a block's work is done by a team, in three parts:

  1. MTF: undoing the move-to-front coding, which turns the scanner's symbols back into the block's bytes, though not yet in their original order.
  2. The inverse BWT: undoing the Burrows–Wheeler transform, which bzip2 used to reorder the block's bytes so that similar ones sit together. This puts them back in their original order.
  3. The finish: RLE1, which expands the runs of repeated bytes that bzip2 shortened first of all, and the CRC, which checks the result against the block's checksum. Then the block's output is handed on, in file order.

The inverse BWT is the expensive part, and the only part a team shares. It has two phases. The build fills a table with one 4-byte entry for each byte of the block, saying where the next byte of the original text is. For a full block this table, which we call the T-vector, is 3.6 MB. The walk then follows the table from entry to entry, writing out a byte at each step. Each step's address comes from the entry just read, so mibz2 starts many walks at known points through the block, and the team's threads share them. An earlier post works the transform through on a small example.

In 0.2.5, the leader does the block's MTF alone, then all three threads build and walk the table, then the leader puts the walk's pieces together and does the finish alone. The two helpers take part only in the build and the walk, and wait the rest of the time. In traces of four teams, the time outside the inverse BWT was 29–33% of a block's decode (the previous post, section 4). So for roughly a third of each block, a team's helpers had nothing to do.

The test machine is an Intel Core i9-10900K, with 10 cores (20 threads) and a 20 MiB last-level cache shared by all of them. On a machine of that shape, given ten or more threads, 0.2.5 runs three teams of three, nine decoding threads in all, plus the scanner. We write a plan as teams × threads per team, so this one is 3 × 3.

items.title: 2. What does pipelining change?
items.text:
The idea: have the leader do its lone work while the helpers do the shared part, instead of before and after it. In 0.2.6, while the two helpers build and walk block A, the leader finishes the block before it, Z, and runs MTF on the block after it, B. When it has done both, it joins the helpers in walking A. When A's walk ends, the helpers start building B, whose MTF is already done, and the leader finishes A. The figure shows the two layouts side by side.

A team of three, in 0.2.5 and in 0.2.6

0.2.5: the helpers wait while the leader works aloneLHHMTF Abuild Abuild Abuild Awalk Awalk Awalk Afinish AMTF Bbuild Bbuild Bbuild Bwalk Bwalk Bwalk BA takes the whole team from its MTF to its finish0.2.6: the leader finishes one block and prepares the nextLHHbuild Awalk Abuild Awalk Afinish ZMTF Bwalk Abuild Bwalk Bbuild Bwalk Bfinish AMTF Cwalk BB's MTF is done before its build starts; A is finished during B's build A sketch of the stages and who runs them, from the decoder's code; bar lengths are illustrative, not measured. L is the leader and H a helper. Blue is the leader's lone work, green the shared build and walk, grey a thread waiting. "Finish" is RLE1 and the CRC, and in 0.2.5 also putting the walk's pieces together; in 0.2.6 the last thread out of the walk does that.

We call this overlap: a block's MTF or finish runs at the same time as its team's build or walk of another block. It needs a second set of MTF buffers and a second buffer for an assembled block in each team, about 3 MB a team.

Why it might not pay. The build and the walk lose a thread. In 0.2.5 three threads build each table. In 0.2.6 two do, and the leader joins only the walk, and only once its own work is done. So the shared part gets slower, and the question is whether the time saved by overlap is larger than the time lost there. The previous post put that in a simple model, and found that if the shared part ran about 1.5 to 1.6 times slower without the leader, the gain would be zero (section 7). Nothing measured then said how much slower it would run.

items.title: 3. What did the first pipeline gain, and why so little?
items.text:
We tested the first version of the pipeline against the plain teams at the same plan, 3 × 3 on ten threads. The test was registered: its comparisons, its possible outcomes and what each would mean were fixed before the run. Each arm decoded a sample of the Wikidata dump, 11.85 MB of bzip2 that decodes to 209.7 MB, 20 times, the arms taking turns in each round. "Speed" here and below is the plain arm's elapsed time over the pipelined arm's, paired round by round, so above 1 means faster. Its 95% interval describes the spread across the 20 rounds of one run, on one machine and one corpus.

The pipeline was faster: 1.042 (1.016–1.068). But it used about 9% more processor time, the time all threads spent running added up (a paired ratio of 0.918, 0.895–0.942). In the model's terms, the result fits a shared part running about 1.4 to 1.55 times slower without the leader, depending on what the hand-offs between threads are assumed to cost. That is a fit, not a measurement, and it is close to the break-even point.

The traces showed why the gain was small. Only about a third of blocks overlapped: in 147 of the sample's 431 blocks, the leader's MTF ran during its own team's build or walk of another block. Two features of the first version kept the rest from overlapping.

Small blocks emptied the pipeline. A block of fewer than 262,144 bytes (256 KiB) is not worth sharing among three threads, so its team's leader decodes it whole, on one thread. 198 of the sample's 431 blocks are that small. In the first version, the leader took at most one new block while its helpers worked. If that block was small, it decoded it and prepared nothing else. The next block then had to be prepared with the helpers waiting, as in 0.2.5. Each small block cost about one block's overlap.

Waiting threads never slept. A thread waiting for the build to end (a helper that had finished its share, or the leader waiting to join the walk) checked a flag 4,096 times, then asked the operating system in a loop to run something else instead (a yield). When nothing else is waiting to run, a yield returns at once, so the waiting thread stays on its core and its wait counts as processor time.

items.title: 4. What did the two refinements change?
items.text:
Each refinement was tested on its own against the first pipeline, at 3 × 3 on ten threads and at 3 × 4 on twelve, with its question and outcomes fixed before the run. The figures below are the ten-thread ones; the twelve-thread results agree.

Small: the leader keeps the pipeline primed. After a small block, the leader now takes the next queued block too, and runs its MTF in the same stretch. It keeps going until it has prepared a block for its team, or finds none waiting. It never waits for a new block to arrive: a leader that held an unfinished block while waiting for the scanner could leave the two waiting on each other.

A small block in the pipeline, before and after the change

Before: nothing is prepared after a small blockLHbuild, walk Afinish Zsmall Sfinish AMTF Bwaitbuild, walk BMTF Cwalk BB invertedAfter: the leader takes the next queued block tooLHbuild, walk Afinish Zsmall SMTF Bbuild, walk Bfinish AMTF CwalkB inverted A sketch, not a measurement: bar lengths are illustrative. L is the leader, H the two helpers, and S a small block, which the leader decodes whole. After the change the helpers can wait a little at the end of a run, while the leader finishes B's MTF.

It worked as intended. Overlapped blocks rose from 144 to 236.5 of 431 in this run (medians over six traced rounds; the first run counted 147), and the pipeline got faster: 1.043 (1.020–1.066), with no change detected in processor time, 1.007 (0.987–1.028). It has a cost, which the figure shows: a leader busy with more blocks joins the walk later. Of the 233 blocks large enough for the team to invert together, those whose walk the leader joined late rose from 62 to 113. The registered outcomes had expected a later join to cancel the gain, and had no entry for a later join with a gain. Our reading, not a registered verdict, is that the later join is real and paid for, and that the extra overlap outweighs it, on this machine and corpus.

Park: waiting threads go to sleep. A waiting thread still checks its flag 4,096 times, then, instead of yielding, it adds itself to a list and parks: it sleeps until woken, using no processor time. The thread that ends the build wakes every thread on the list. Waking a parked thread takes a few microseconds, which a thread that never slept doesn't pay.

Parking left the elapsed time unchanged, 0.999 (0.981–1.017), and cut processor time by about 5% (a ratio of 1.055, 1.039–1.071). The saving could have come from spinning less before parking, rather than from parking. A control arm that only cut the checks from 4,096 to 2,000, still yielding, changed neither figure: 1.004 for speed and 1.006 for processor time, both intervals holding 1. So the saving is from parking.

Each change against the first pipeline, 3 × 3 on ten threads

Speed (above 1 is faster)0.961.001.041.08park0.999 (0.981–1.017)spin control1.004 (0.984–1.024)small1.043 (1.020–1.066)both1.038 (1.021–1.055)CPU saved (above 1 is less CPU)0.961.001.041.08park1.055 (1.039–1.071)spin control1.006 (0.986–1.027)small1.007 (0.987–1.028)both1.032 (1.018–1.046) Measured, the test machine, 20 paired rounds each, with 95% intervals. Both ratios are the first pipeline's figure over the changed one's, so above 1 is better: faster, or less processor time. Green dots are intervals wholly above 1. The spin control cuts the checks before a yield, and doesn't park.

Both together were about as fast as small alone, 1.038 (1.021–1.055), and saved less processor time than parking alone, 1.032 (1.018–1.046) against 1.055. A likely reason is that a busier leader leaves less waiting to sleep through, but that is not established.

Against the plain teams, in the same run, the pipeline with both changes was 1.072 (1.053–1.091) as fast as plain 3 × 3, for about 5% more processor time (a paired ratio of 0.951). Its peak memory was 75 MB, against 67 MB for the plain teams of 0.2.5's default. That is the version 0.2.6 ships.

One thing these runs can't do is split the gain into its causes. Some of it may come from the overlap, and some from the way the leader joins the walk as an extra thread once its own work is done. The runs measure the total.

items.title: 5. Did the new default hold up against 0.2.5?
items.text:
The 1.072 came from a comparison that was reported, not registered as a decision. So before release we fixed one more test, with its pass rule set before any run: the 0.2.6 build against the 0.2.5 release, each decoding as a caller gets it by default, at 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 16 and 20 threads, 20 paired rounds each. To pass, ten threads had to be at least 1.03 as fast, with its interval above 1. At 11 to 20 threads, each count's interval had to rule out being more than 2% slower. At 8 and 9 threads both builds run four teams of two, unchanged, so those two counts check that nothing else moved. The prediction was 1.07–1.08 at ten threads, about the same above, and no change at 8 and 9.

The run passed. The table gives each thread count's plan in 0.2.6 and its speed against 0.2.5. "CPU" is 0.2.6's processor time over 0.2.5's, and "memory" its peak memory over 0.2.5's, each from the medians of the 20 rounds. 0.2.5 ran the same plans, unpipelined:

0.2.6 against 0.2.5, by the threads asked for

speed against 0.2.50.981.001.021.041.061.081.108910111216201.0721.002, 1.0011.065–1.0704 × 2 both3 × 3, pipelined in 0.2.6threads asked for Measured, the test machine, 20 paired rounds a thread count, with 95% intervals. Speed is 0.2.5's elapsed time over 0.2.6's, so above 1 is faster. Green dots are intervals wholly above 1.

From the run's records, at ten threads the median decode of the sample took 0.144 s against 0.156 s, about 1,460 against 1,350 MB/s of output. Processor time rose from 0.98 s to 1.02 s, and peak memory from 69 to 76 MB. The outcome matched the prediction for speed and peak memory (1.10–1.13 against about 1.12), and came in a little under it for processor time (1.04–1.05 against 1.05–1.06). Above ten threads the plan is the same three teams, and the measured gain is about the same. A request for twenty threads still decodes on nine, plus the scanner.

items.title: 6. What does it cost, and where does it apply?
items.text:
The trade-off. 0.2.6 finishes sooner, but it doesn't do less work: it spends about 4–5% more processor time and 7–8 MB more peak memory than 0.2.5 on this workload. Elapsed time improves because work that used to run while two threads waited now runs beside them. The extra memory is each team's second set of MTF buffers and second assembled block.

Where it applies. Only the 3 × 3 plan is pipelined, and the decoder picks that plan only on a machine with 10 physical cores and a 20 MiB last-level cache, given 10 or more threads. Every other plan and every other machine shape decodes exactly as 0.2.5 did. The output is the same bytes in every case: the pipelined path is tested byte for byte against libbzip2, and on corrupt and truncated input, by forcing the plan on any machine. But its speed has been measured on one machine, the test machine, and one corpus, Wikidata. Another processor of the same shape gets the pipeline too, measured or not. The cloud machines that benchmark every change to mibz2 have 4 virtual CPUs on 2 physical cores, so they never take this path. They show only that nothing else moved. Thread counts of 13 to 15, 17 to 19 and above 20 were not measured, though they run the same plan.

The plain teams are still available. A caller that prefers lower processor time can ask for 0.2.5's three plain teams directly, with BzReader::parallel_planned and the plan Plan::Teams:

use mibz2::{parallel::Plan, BzReader, Kernels};

// three plain teams of three, as in 0.2.5
let reader = BzReader::parallel_planned(
    file,
    Plan::Teams { teams: 3, k: 3 },
    12, // blocks in flight: the default's window at this plan
    Kernels::detect(),
);

items.title: 7. Where do things stand?
items.text:
The argument runs like this. In 0.2.5, a team's two helpers waited through about a third of each block, while the leader did MTF and the finish alone. 0.2.6 has the leader do that work while the helpers build and walk another block. That takes the leader out of the build, which slows it, so the first version gained only 4%, for 9% more processor time. Two changes made it pay: preparing the next block after a small one raised overlap from about a third of blocks to about half, and putting waiting threads to sleep took back about half of the extra processor time. A registered run of the release against 0.2.5 confirmed 7.2% at ten threads, and 6.5–7.0% at 11 to 20.

0.2.5's three teams were 8.8–8.9% faster than 0.2.4's four teams of two at ten threads, and 0.2.6 is 7.2% faster than 0.2.5. Multiplied together, the two would put 0.2.6 about 17% ahead of 0.2.4 there. That is a projection from two separate runs, not a measurement: a direct comparison of the releases has not yet run.

What remains open is in two places. The previous post's question, why each extra block in progress slows the others, is unchanged by this release. And the pipeline still leaves the leader's serial work inside each team. The next question is whether moving that work onto threads of its own, outside the teams, would do better on the same number of cores (pull request 251). Nothing about it has been measured yet.

The general lesson: when part of a job can't be shared, it can still run beside the part that is. Whether that pays depends on what the shared part loses to make room, and here the answer was found only by measuring.

items.title: Why mibz2 stops scaling at eight threads
items.text:
mibz2 · Research blog

On a ten-core desktop processor, mibz2, our bzip2 decoder written in Rust, got faster as we gave it more threads, from one to eight. Past eight it stopped. Twelve, sixteen or twenty threads decoded no faster than eight. A decoder that can't use the cores it is given leaves time on the table for anyone decompressing large files, and the reason it stops says where the next gain has to come from.

The reason is not the number of threads. It is how many pieces of the file the decoder works on at the same time. A bzip2 file is a series of blocks that can be decoded independently, and mibz2 decodes several at once, each with a small group of threads. We measured two things. Every extra block in progress slows down every other block. And extra threads on the same block barely speed it up. Together they mean that fewer blocks, each with more threads, beat more blocks with fewer threads. Our latest release, 0.2.5, decodes three blocks at once with three threads each, where 0.2.4 decoded four with two each. In two runs at ten threads, it was 8.8% and 8.9% faster, used 11–12% less processor time and 18–19% less peak memory.

What we have not measured is why the blocks slow each other down. The leading explanation is that each block needs a large table, and the tables compete for the processor's shared cache. The evidence for that comes from a simpler test program, not from the decoder itself, and a careful review of an earlier draft of this analysis made us withdraw part of it. So this post keeps three things apart: what was measured, what is inferred, and what we will test next.

Section 1 explains how mibz2 splits a file among its threads. Section 2 gives the measurements behind the two findings, and sections 3 and 4 look at each one in turn. Section 5 is the release's own measurement, section 6 what the review changed, and section 7 the next experiments.

items.title: Why mibz2 stops scaling at eight threads, and why three teams help
items.text:
Each block decoded at once slows the others, and more threads per block barely help, so three teams of three beat four of two by 9%. Why blocks interfere is open.

7 November 2026 · 15 min read · Research in progress
path: Why mibz2 stops scaling at eight threads

items.title: 1. How does mibz2 decode with several threads?
items.text:
bzip2 compresses a file in blocks of up to 900 kB each (at its default level, 9). Each block is compressed on its own, with no reference to the others, so each can be decoded on its own too. That is what makes a parallel decoder possible: different threads can work on different blocks at the same time, and the decoder puts their outputs back in order at the end.

Decoding one block undoes bzip2's steps in reverse. One thread, which mibz2 calls the scanner, reads the compressed file and undoes its outermost layer, the Huffman coding, for every block (an earlier post covers that stage). The rest of a block's work happens on the threads that decode it, in three parts:

  1. MTF: undoing the move-to-front coding, which turns the scanner's symbols back into the block's bytes, though not yet in their original order.
  2. The inverse BWT: undoing the Burrows–Wheeler transform, which bzip2 used to reorder the bytes so that similar ones sit together. This puts them back in their original order.
  3. RLE1 and the CRC: expanding the runs of repeated bytes that bzip2 shortened first of all, and checking the result against the block's checksum.

The inverse BWT is the most expensive of the three. It works in two phases. The build makes a table with one 4-byte entry for each byte of the block, saying where the next byte of the original text is to be found. For a full block that table, which mibz2 calls the T-vector, is 3.6 MB. The walk then follows the table from entry to entry, writing out a byte at each step. Each step's address comes from the entry just read, so the steps form a chain through the table, jumping to an unpredictable place each time. A jump that finds its entry in a nearby cache is quick. One that has to go to main memory waits hundreds of cycles. Revisiting the space–time tradeoff in BWT inversion shows the transform and its table worked through on a small example.

A chain of dependent jumps can't be split between threads directly, since each step needs the one before. mibz2 gets around this by starting many chains at known points through the block, so several threads can share one block's build and walk. We call the threads that share a block a team. One of them, the leader, also does the block's MTF, RLE1 and CRC alone, and puts the walk's pieces together at the end (the assembly). The others are its helpers: they join in only for the build and the walk. A team decodes one block at a time, with one table, and then takes the next.

So a thread count is really two numbers: how many teams, which is the number of blocks and tables in progress at once, and how many threads each team has. We write a plan as teams × threads per team: 4 × 2 is four teams of two.

The machine these measurements come from is an Intel Core i9-10900K. It has 10 cores, each able to run two threads at once (20 in all), and a 20 MiB last-level cache, the L3, which all ten cores share. Until 0.2.5, mibz2's rule was teams of two, and as many teams as keep their tables within about 0.7 of the L3. On the test machine that is four teams. Asked for 8, 10, 12, 16 or 20 threads, the decoder ran the same four teams of two, plus the scanner. That is why it stopped at eight: past eight it declined the extra threads. Under that rule, 0.2.4 levelled off at about 1.27–1.31 GB/s of output from 8 threads up.

The two plans on the test machine's ten cores

items.title: 2. What happens when we change the number of blocks, and the threads on each?
items.text:
To see what four teams of two were missing, we ran a grid of plans that varied the two numbers separately: 2 to 8 teams, of 2, 3 or 4 threads each. Each plan decoded the same sample of the Wikidata dump, 11.85 MB of bzip2 that decodes to 209.7 MB, 20 times, in rotating order, with threads placed by the operating system as users run it. The figure below groups the plans by their number of teams. That is the most tables the plan can have in progress at once, not a measured count of how many were in progress at each moment.

Throughput by the number of teams, all thread counts per team together

Each team's rate, MB/s0200400600234568teams (blocks decoded at once)558–583461–466319–325110All teams together, MB/s04008001,2001,600234568teams (blocks decoded at once)1,382–1,3991,276–1,300882 Measured, the test machine, 20 rounds a plan (the team-size grid). A vertical bar spans the plans with that many teams but different threads per team. The rate is megabytes of decoded output a second.

Two things stand out. Each team gets slower as teams are added, and steeply: from 558–583 MB/s each with two teams, to 461–466 with three, about 320 with four and 110 with eight. Adding a fourth team adds a fourth block in progress, but makes every block slow enough that all four together are slower than three. Total throughput peaks at three teams, 1,382–1,399 MB/s.

And at a fixed number of teams, the threads per team hardly matter. With four teams, each team decoded 319, 325 and 320 MB/s with two, three and four threads. The extra threads cost processor time without buying speed. The table below gives the four-team plans against the old default, with the best three-team plans for comparison. "Against 4 × 2" is the ratio of throughputs, paired round by round, with its 95% interval across the 20 rounds; "CPU" is total processor time over 4 × 2's.

plan threads MB/s against 4 × 2 CPU peak memory, MB 4 × 2 (the old default) 8 1,276 1 1 82 4 × 3 12 1,300 1.017 (1.008–1.026) 1.26 82 4 × 4 16 1,279 1.003 (0.993–1.014) 1.52 82 3 × 3 9 1,382 1.075 (1.058–1.093) 0.89 67 3 × 4 12 1,399 1.097 (1.083–1.111) 1.04 68

The four-team rows were the experiment's registered tests: their pass rule, a gain of at least 3%, was fixed before any run. Neither passed. The three-team rows were exploratory: picked out after the fact, so they proved nothing on their own. They were then confirmed in runs registered for them, and the release's plan in two more (section 5). Peak memory, meanwhile, rose by about 15 MB with each team: 52 MB at two teams, 67 at three, 82 at four and 138 at eight.

That leaves two questions. Why does each extra block slow the others? And why doesn't a block go faster with more threads?

items.title: 3. Why would more blocks at once slow each block down?
items.text:
This part is inferred, not measured in the decoder. The leading explanation is about the shared cache. Each team's walk jumps unpredictably through its own 3.6 MB table, and is fast only while the entries it needs are in the L3. All teams share that one cache, so each extra table takes room the others were using. As an intuition: several people each searching their own large reference book, all spread out on one desk. With two books, most pages stay open. With eight, pages keep being put away to make room, and fetching them back is slow.

The evidence comes from a test program that runs only the inverse BWT, the build and the walk, with each block's thread fixed to a core of its own, and no teams. In October we ran it on the test machine with hardware counters, which count events inside the processor. One of them is the L3 hit share: of the memory requests that miss the cores' own small caches, the share the L3 answers rather than main memory. Plotted against the table bytes in use at once, it stays near 1 while the tables are small, then falls once they approach the cache's size.

L3 hit share against the table bytes in use at once (inversion only)

0.40.60.81.0010203040table bytes in use at once, MBshare of requests answered by the L3L3 size, 20 MiB4 tables: 0.9296 tables: 0.7948 tables: 0.64010 tables: 0.539blocks of a level-9 file, 3.6 MB a tableblocks of a level-3 file, 1.2 MB a table Measured, the test machine, in a program that runs only the build and walk, one block a core (footprint journal). bzip2's compression level sets its block size: at level 3 blocks are 300 kB, so their tables are a third the size of level 9's. Not a measurement of the decoder.

Four other observations from that program point the same way:

  • Requests wait longer. A request that misses the cores' own caches waited on average 67 cycles with four tables, 137 with six and 361 with eight.
  • Main memory saturates. From six tables on, traffic to main memory levels off at 28–29 GB/s.
  • A control isolates the table's size. A variant that changes the walk's code but keeps a 4-byte table got the same hit share as the standard one at six tables (0.814 against 0.793).
  • A smaller table moves the drop. A 3-byte table (2.7 MB a block) moved the program's best number of blocks from four to six, where it ran 1.100 (1.093–1.108) times as fast as the standard table's best.

That is good evidence that the size of the tables matters, in that program. It doesn't settle the question for the decoder, for three reasons.

First, the program isn't the decoder. It has no teams, no MTF, RLE1 or CRC, no scanner, and none of the decoder's other buffers. Second, table bytes don't explain everything even there. With the smaller level-3 blocks, ten tables kept a hit share of 0.940 and yet ran slower than eight, mostly in the build, with requests waiting longer at nearly the same hit share. So a limit on how many requests the cores can have outstanding, or on the number of cores loading the cache at once, is not ruled out. Third, the decoder's own counters were never read: the operating system's settings on the test machine didn't allow it during the team-size run.

There is also a simpler puzzle. Four full tables are 14.4 MB, below the cache's 20 MiB. Each team has other buffers besides its table, such as space for the walk's pieces and for the block's output: several megabytes of reserved capacity each. But capacity is not what is being read at any moment, and how much of those buffers sits in the cache at once is not measured. An earlier draft of this analysis added those capacities up to a 20 MiB "hot set" that filled the cache. The review showed that a sum of capacities and peaks can't establish that, and the claim was withdrawn (section 6).

Two other explanations also fit the measurements. The teams' waits for each other could be what makes blocks slow, rather than memory. And three teams of three use nine threads on ten cores, so one core is free, which changes how the operating system schedules everything else. No measurement of the decoder yet tells these apart.

items.title: 4. Why don't more threads on one block help?
items.text:
Measured: with four teams, a third thread per team bought 1.7% (0.8–2.6%) for 26% more processor time, and a fourth bought nothing detectable, 0.3% (−0.7% to 1.4%), for 52% more. A trace of each block's decode, which records when each block starts and finishes, shows the same thing from inside: with four teams, a block took on average 1.394, 1.380 and 1.403 ms with two, three and four threads.

Part of the reason is plain arithmetic: not all of a block's work is shared. Only the build and the walk are, and only inside the call that does the inverse BWT. The leader does the MTF before that call, and RLE1 and the CRC after it, alone.

One block's work in a team

MTFthe leader aloneSetupthe leader aloneBuild the tablethe whole teamWalk the tablethe whole teamAssemble the piecesthe leader aloneRLE1 and the CRCthe leader aloneoutside the calloutside the callinside theinversion call:67–71% of a blockOutside the call: 29–33% of a block's decode, in traces of four teams. The stages and who runs them, from the decoder's code. The shares are measured, in traces of four teams on the test machine: medians of six runs each at two, three and four threads a team. Inside the call the team also waits for its slowest member; those waits are not timed separately.

The traces give the time inside and outside the inversion call for each block:

plan a block's decode, ms inside the inversion call, ms outside it, ms outside share 4 × 2 1.394 0.993 0.400 28.75% 4 × 3 1.380 0.935 0.441 32.14% 4 × 4 1.404 0.946 0.462 32.64%

These are averages over the sample's 431 blocks, some of them small, so they are not the time for one full 900 kB block. On one of the cloud machines that benchmark every change to mibz2 (CI), with one thread, the stages cost, per output byte: 0.41 ns for MTF, 0.04 for assembly, 0.05 for RLE1 and 0.07 for the CRC, which the leader does alone, against 0.48 for the build and 1.09 for the walk, which a team shares.

So about 29–33% of a block's time is outside the shared part, and more threads can't shorten it. But that share is not the whole of the work that can't be shared. The inversion call also includes work the leader does alone (setting up, and assembling the pieces), and time the team spends waiting for its slowest member. The time outside the call also includes scheduling and the tracing itself. The traces can't separate these, so the true unshared share isn't known.

What the measurements don't separate is why the shared part itself doesn't speed up with a third or fourth thread. The candidates, each visible in the code, are:

  • the cost of waking helpers and of waiting for the last one to finish;
  • the setup and assembly the leader does alone, inside the call;
  • the build's checks that each thread writes only its own part of the table;
  • the number of pieces a block is split into, which grows with the threads per team;
  • two threads sharing one core, once there are more threads than cores;
  • memory, as in section 3.

Waiting isn't free either: a helper with nothing to do checks for work up to 2,000 times before it sleeps, which costs processor time.

One more measurement bears on core sharing. With four teams pinned to particular processors, giving the threads one core each ("spread") against pairing them on cores ("packed") made the biggest difference at two threads a team: packed was 23% slower (1,055 against 1,369 MB/s in the median round). With three threads a team it was 8% slower, and with four, 1%. But the packed arm also had fewer cores to use (4 against 8 for eight threads), so this compares how many cores were available, not which threads shared them.

items.title: 5. What did three teams of three gain?
items.text:
The grid's three-team plans were chosen after the fact, so before changing the decoder we registered a test of the change itself, with its pass rule fixed before any run: 0.2.5's plan against 0.2.4's, at 8 to 20 threads, 20 rounds each, and a second run to confirm it. Both runs passed. At ten threads:

run speed against 0.2.4 processor time peak memory first 1.089 (1.075–1.103) 0.88 0.82 confirmation 1.088 (1.076–1.101) 0.89 0.81

The intervals are 95% intervals across the 20 paired rounds of one run. Neither run detected harm at 11, 12, 16 or 20 threads, the registered check there. A separate comparison of the two releases found 0.2.4 taking 11.9% longer than 0.2.5 at ten threads, and 8.1–8.7% longer at 12 to 20.

At ten threads or more on a machine of this shape (ten cores, a 20 MiB L3), 0.2.5 runs three teams of three. A request for twenty threads still decodes on nine. The result covers this processor and this workload. It shows that three teams are faster. It doesn't show why, which is section 3's open question.

items.title: 6. What did the review change?
items.text:
The first version of this analysis was reviewed adversarially by another member of the project, who recomputed its numbers from the archived traces. All seven objections were accepted, and the version this post is based on takes them in. Four changes matter for the argument.

The first draft claimed that the decoder's buffers formed a 20 MiB working set that filled the cache. That was a sum of reserved capacities and peaks, not a measurement of what is read at the same time, and it was withdrawn. The first draft also read the flat block times in section 4 as memory saturation. The review pointed out that they can't separate memory from waiting, unshared work or core sharing, and that claim was withdrawn too. The outside share in section 4 was also recomputed: the first draft divided by the wrong total, and called the whole inversion call "build and walk", when it includes setup, assembly and waits. And the first draft's 1.10–1.30× estimate for the next experiment was replaced by the model in section 7, which shows that no such floor follows from the measurements.

items.title: 7. What will we try next?
items.text:
First: let the leader work on other blocks while its helpers build and walk. Today a team's helpers wait while the leader runs MTF before a block and RLE1 and the CRC after it. In the proposed pipeline, the leader runs the next block's MTF and the previous block's RLE1 and CRC while the other threads build and walk the current one. It needs one more buffer for the next block's bytes, about 1 MB a team. A prototype is being built.

A team's timeline, today and as proposed

Today: the helpers wait while the leader works aloneleaderhelpersMTF Abuild, walk Abuild, walk Afinish AMTF Bbuild, walk Bbuild, walk Bfinish BProposed: the leader finishes one block and starts the nextleaderhelpersMTF Bbuild, walk Afinish AMTF Cbuild, walk Bfinish BMTF Dbuild, walk C“finish” is the assembly, RLE1 and the CRC. Proposed, the helpers are one thread fewer. The proposal, not a measurement: bar lengths are illustrative. Whether it pays depends on how much slower the build and walk run with one thread fewer, and on what the hand-offs cost.

Whether it pays is not obvious, because the shared part loses a thread: in a team of three, the build and walk would run on two. A simple model, from the review, puts numbers on that. Let \(S\) be the leader's work outside the shared part, \(P_0\) the shared part today, \(\alpha\) how much slower the shared part runs with a thread fewer and more blocks in progress, and \(H\) the cost of hand-offs that can't overlap. Then the time a team spends per block, today and pipelined, and the speed-up, are

\[C_0 = S + P_0, \qquad C_1 = \max(S,\ \alpha P_0) + H,\] \[\text{speed-up} = C_0 / C_1.\]

For three teams of three, the grid's throughput gives \(C_0\) = 1.056 ms a block per team: three teams, 209.7 MB in 431 blocks, at 1,382 MB/s. That figure includes start-up and the end of the run, so it is an approximation, not a measured service time. Taking \(S\) = 0.40 ms, the time outside the inversion call in section 4, leaves \(P_0\) = 0.656 ms. The model's speed-up then depends almost entirely on \(\alpha\):

Modelled speed-up of the pipeline, against α

0.8×1.0×1.2×1.4×1.6×1.01.21.41.61.8α: how much slower the build and walk run, pipelinedbreak-even at 1.61break-even at 1.531.61×1.50×1.15×1.09×no hand-off cost0.05 ms a block Modelled, not measured. The break-even points are where the curves cross 1, at α of about 1.61 and 1.53. The measurements don't bound α.

If the shared part ran no slower, the pipeline would be 1.61× as fast, or 1.50× with 0.05 ms of hand-off cost per block. If it ran 40% slower, 1.15× or 1.09×. At 1.6× slower the gain is gone. If the shared part slowed to what it takes under four teams of two, 0.94–0.99 ms, the gain would be 1.07–1.12×, or 1.02–1.07× with the hand-off cost. Nothing measured so far says which \(\alpha\) to expect, so no gain and a loss are both possible outcomes, and will be registered as such.

The test will compare like with like. To isolate the pipeline, pipelined against not pipelined at the same plan and thread count: three teams of four against three teams of four, and three of three against three of three. Separately, pipelined three of four against today's default at ten threads, which is the comparison a user would care about. Each will report processor time and peak memory alongside the elapsed time. The prototype must also record when each thread starts and finishes each stage of each block, so that the trace shows blocks really overlapping. Without that, a result says nothing about the mechanism.

Second: placement, as a control. Pinned against unpinned threads, recording which thread ran on which processor, for today's plan and for three teams of four. It makes no prediction of its own. It is needed to read the pipeline's result, since that plan uses more threads than there are cores.

Third: a smaller table under teams. The inversion-only program's 3-byte table moved the fall in hit share to more blocks, so the table's size is a real factor. But that table's 1.10× gain was against the same program's standard table, not against the decoder: against the decoder's own team code (four teams of two), in the same tests, it ran at 0.687 (0.680–0.695) of the speed, on six cores against eight. A different compact table, which packs 30 entries into each 64-byte record, ran 4.8% and 7.7% slower than the standard one at four threads on CI. And no smaller table has been measured under teams. So it comes after the first two.

Last: shrinking the other buffers. There is no measurement of how much cache they take, so nothing yet says this would help.

items.title: 8. Where do things stand?
items.text:
The chain of the argument runs like this. A thread count is really two numbers, blocks in progress and threads per block. Each extra block slows every other block, enough that three blocks beat four. Extra threads on one block barely help, partly because about a third of a block's time is work its leader does alone. So three teams of three beat four teams of two, as two registered runs confirmed. Why extra blocks hurt is not settled: competition for the shared cache is the leading explanation, with good evidence from a simpler program and none yet from the decoder.

The pipeline prototype, its registration and the placement control are in progress. Nothing in this post changes the decoder.

The general lesson: more threads help only if the work they add runs alongside the slowest step. Here the slowest step has two parts, the blocks competing with each other, and each block's work that one thread does alone.

  • The release comparison, 0.2.4 against 0.2.5
  • The smaller-table test with counters and the footprint journal
  • The compact table under the staged walk
  • The CI run with the stage costs

items.title: Reading the BWT's runs off the MTF codes
items.text:
mibz2 · Research blog

bzip2's codes already say where the BWT's runs of repeated bytes are. Today mibz2 expands those codes into an array of every byte, then reads that array again to build the table it navigates the BWT with. It could instead keep the runs as it decodes the codes, and build a smaller navigation structure straight from them, without the big intermediate array.

Take the word banana. After the BWT its bytes are \(L=\texttt{nnbaaa}\), and bzip2's codes for them say, in effect: change to n, repeat it once; change to b; change to a, repeat it twice. That is already the three groups nn | b | aaa, as three run records: (n, 2), (b, 1) and (a, 3). The navigation structure can be built from those three records, and the six bytes never written out and scanned again.

What is proved, and what isn't. That the codes give the runs, and the bound on how many codes there are, are mathematical results (sections 2 and 4). The inversion still has to write every byte, so it is not faster in principle, and the one such structure mibz2 has tried navigated more slowly than today's table (section 5). Nothing here has been built or timed.

Some background, for what follows. Before a decoder can undo the Burrows–Wheeler transform (BWT), it rebuilds the transform's output: a column of bytes, \(L\), one for each of the block's \(n\) rows, up to 900,000 of them. bzip2 stores that column in coded form. Its move-to-front (MTF) stage writes each byte as a small number, its position in a list of recently used bytes, and it writes repeats of the last byte as a separate count. mibz2, our bzip2 decoder, turns those codes back into all \(n\) bytes of \(L\), then reads \(L\) again to build its table for the inverse BWT, the T-vector, at four bytes a row.

Why would a decoder want the runs? An earlier post showed that the inverse BWT's next-row map needs only one record per run of \(L\), rather than one entry per row. Published structures built from those records, move structures, step from row to row without a search. To build one, a decoder needs the runs.

This post's observation is that bzip2's codes list the runs of any block, as they do banana's. A code that names a byte other than the last one starts a run; a repeat count extends it. Apart from the block's first byte (section 2), nothing else starts or ends a run. So the runs, and from them a move structure, could be built from the codes directly, without writing the \(n\)-byte column and scanning it again. By our own accounting, building them would take time and memory that grow with the number of codes and runs rather than with \(n\), and the number of codes is itself bounded by the runs (section 4). It doesn't make the inversion that follows any shorter: that still takes time proportional to \(n\), as any inversion must, and that bound is already published.

That observation is not new to mibz2: it was recorded in issue #42 in October. The same issue then built and timed a move structure for mibz2's walk, and it lost by 90–108%, a loss that a run list handed over for free would not have changed (section 5). That experiment did not time a builder fused with MTF. What this post adds is the mechanism worked through, its edge cases, what it would cost in theory, and a search for prior work. It changes nothing in the decoder. The costs in section 4 are our own accounting, which an independent review has since checked (section 6).

Section 1 decodes the codes of banana by hand. Section 2 proves that the codes give every run, and section 3 turns the runs into a move structure. Section 4 gives the cost in theory and section 5 what mibz2 has measured. Section 6 says what is open.

items.title: Reading the BWT's runs off bzip2's move-to-front codes
items.text:
bzip2's move-to-front codes mark where each run of the BWT's last column starts, so the runs could be listed without writing the column. It is not built.

8 November 2026 · 15 min read · Open question
path: Reading the BWT's runs off the MTF codes

items.title: 1. How does bzip2 write banana?
items.text:
Suppose you compress the word banana with bzip2. The BWT sorts the word's six rotations and keeps their last letters, \(L=\texttt{nnbaaa}\), and the number of the row that holds the word itself (the earlier post works it through). The MTF stage then codes \(L\) one byte at a time.

It starts from the list of the bytes the block uses, in byte order: a b n. To write a byte, it takes the byte's position in the list, counting from 0, which we call its MTF index, and moves the byte to the front. The first byte, n, is at index 2, and the list becomes n a b. The next n is now at the front, index 0.

Index 0 means "the same byte again", and bzip2 never writes it as a number. It counts a stretch of zeros and writes the count in two symbols, RUNA and RUNB. They are digits worth 1 and 2 in the first place, 2 and 4 in the second, 4 and 8 in the third, and so on, added up: RUNA is one zero, RUNB two, RUNA RUNA three. The symbols for indices 1 and up we call literals, and they are stored one higher than their index, so that the symbol values 0 and 1 are free for RUNA and RUNB. Index 2 goes into the file as the symbol 3.

Coding \(L=\texttt{nnbaaa}\) this way gives five symbols, 3 RUNA 3 3 RUNB, then an end-of-block symbol. The table gives each step's MTF indices and the bzip2 symbols actually written for them:

Bytes List before MTF indices bzip2 symbols n a b n 2 3 n n a b 0 RUNA b n a b 2 3 aaa b n a 2 0 0 3 RUNB

The RUNA is one zero, one more n; the RUNB is two zeros, two more as.

The decoder does the same in reverse: a literal symbol \(s\) takes the byte at index \(s-1\) (mibz2's s - 1), writes it, and moves it to the front; a count of zeros writes that many copies of the front byte. mibz2's scalar loop is about forty lines long, and it writes every byte into \(L\) and counts each byte value as it goes.

From banana's symbols to its runs, and to the next-row map

bzip2 symbols3RUNA33RUNBLn0n1b2a3a4a5

1. Each green literal, symbol 3 for MTF index 2, writes a byte that differs from the one before, so it starts a run. RUNA and RUNB repeat the last byte: one copy and two.

items.title: 2. Why does every literal start a run?
items.text:
Because the front of the list is always the byte just written. A literal names an index of 1 or more, and every byte in the list is different, so a literal always writes a byte that differs from the one before it. A count of zeros always repeats it. So a run of \(L\) is exactly one literal followed by at most one count, and the run's length is one plus the count.

That makes the number of runs, \(r\), a count of the literals, with one exception, which comes from how the list starts. Before the first byte is written, the front of the list is the block's smallest byte, which hasn't been written yet. If \(L\) starts with that byte, bzip2 writes it as index 0, so the block's first run starts with a count, not a literal. The column of aaaa is aaaa, and bzip2 codes it as RUNB RUNA (two, plus two in the second place): one run, no literal at all. So

\[ r=(\text{number of literals})+[\,L\text{ starts with the block's smallest byte}\,]. \]

The other edge cases are smaller. A count is never zero: each RUNA or RUNB adds at least one, so a count that is present extends its run. The block's last run ends at the end-of-block symbol, so a decoder that lists runs must close the open run there; mibz2's loop already writes a pending count before it checks for the end. And a list of runs needn't be maximal to be correct. A decoder that cuts a run in two where it crosses a checkpoint, as mibz2's checkpointed MTF loop does, would give two records with the same byte, which still describe \(L\) exactly. It only costs a record.

We checked the argument with a short script that models bzip2's MTF and RUNA/RUNB rules (not mibz2's code). On 20,009 strings, random ones and periodic ones among them, it listed the runs from the symbols, compared them with the runs of the column computed directly, and undid the transform from the runs alone. Every case matched, the first-run exception included.

items.title: 3. How do the runs become a move structure?
items.text:
From each run, the decoder needs four numbers: its byte \(c\), its start \(p\) in \(L\), its length \(\ell\), and \(k\), the number of copies of \(c\) written before it: copies, not earlier runs, so an earlier run aa adds 2. The MTF decoder already counts each byte value as it writes, so \(k\) is that count at the run's start. In banana every run is its byte's first, so every \(k\) is 0; in aababa, below, two runs share a byte and \(k\) is not 0.

The inverse-BWT navigation post showed which rows a run takes over (its section 2). Write \(C(c)\) for the number of bytes in the block smaller than \(c\): the row where \(c\)'s rows begin in \(F\), the sorted first column. Then the run's rows begin at \(a=C(c)+k\), and the next-row map \(\Psi\) sends each of them to the matching position of the run:

\[ \Psi(a+t)=p+t,\qquad 0\le t<\ell. \]

One value has to wait. \(C(c)\) depends on the counts of every smaller byte, so it is known only at the end of the block. The records can be written while decoding, with \(k\), and given their rows once the counts are final. In banana the counts are a 3, b 1, n 2, so the a rows begin at 0, b at 3 and n at 4: the record (a, start 3, length 3, \(k\) 0) becomes rows 0–2 to positions 3–5, as in the last frame above.

\(k\) matters when a byte has more than one run. Take the word aababa. Its column is \(L=\texttt{babaaa}\), with the runs b, a, b and aaa, and its sorted first column is \(F=\texttt{aaaabb}\), so \(C(\texttt{a})=0\) and \(C(\texttt{b})=4\). The first a run, at \(p=1\), has \(k=0\): it takes row 0, so \(\Psi(0)=1\). The run aaa, at \(p=3\), comes after one a, so \(k=1\) and its rows begin at \(a=C(\texttt{a})+k=1\): \(\Psi(1)=3\), \(\Psi(2)=4\) and \(\Psi(3)=5\). The b runs do the same from row 4: the first takes row 4, and the second, with \(k=1\), takes row 5, so \(\Psi(5)=2\). The runs of one byte share out that byte's rows of \(F\), in the order they appear in \(L\), without overlapping, and \(k\) says where each run's share begins. Without it, both a runs would claim row 0.

Two runs of one byte share its rows in F

1. In aababa's column, a and b each have two runs. A byte's second run has k 1, so its rows start one past its first run's.

FL0ab01aa12ab23aa34ba45ba51 → 3

2. So the a rows of F are shared out in L order: row 0 to the first run, rows 1–3 to aaa. The two b runs take rows 4 and 5.

Conceptual, worked by hand and checked by a script. Green marks the two a runs; the band marks aaa, whose k of 1 sends its rows past the row the first a run takes.

Back in banana, a walk over the intervals needs one thing more. Each interval's record says where its rows go; its anchor names the interval that destination falls in. A walk that knows its current interval then finds the next one by stepping forward from the anchor, instead of searching all the interval starts (section 1.1 of the inverse-BWT navigation post). The records arrive in \(L\) order, so their destinations rise. Sorted by byte, a counting sort over the \(r\) records, their row starts rise too. One merge of the two lists finds every anchor. Brown and Langmead build a length-capped structure, which splits long intervals so that the walk's average step is bounded, from exactly such a run list in \(O(r)\) time and space (SEA 2026, Lemma 6).

items.title: 4. What would it cost, in theory?
items.text:
The saving is to handle the block's \(m\) symbols and keep \(r\) records, instead of writing and rereading \(n\) bytes. That pays only if \(m\) is much smaller than \(n\), and on long runs it is. A run of length \(\ell\) costs one literal and about \(\log_2\ell\) count digits, because the digits' place values double. So, as proved at the end of this section, \(m\le r(1+\log_2(n/r))+1\). At the \(n/r=13.85\) of the Wikidata corpus in section 5, that is at most about 4.8 symbols a run, or about 0.35 symbols a row: derived from the measured run count, not measured itself. Listing the runs is therefore sublinear in \(n\) only when \(r\) grows more slowly than \(n\). The inversion is not sublinear: it writes \(n\) bytes regardless. That sublinearity is not new: it follows from the input having coded the runs already.

In detail: while undoing MTF and the RUNA/RUNB counts, a decoder could keep one record per maximal run, merging a literal with the count after it (and any pieces of one run it was made to cut), together with a count per byte value. At the block's end it computes each \(C(c)\), gives each record its row start \(a=C(c)+k\), and builds a run-bounded move structure from the records. The \(n\)-byte column is never written or scanned. What follows is our own accounting of what that would cost. It is not a published result.

As above, \(m\) is the number of symbols in a block; write \(\sigma\) for the number of byte values it uses, at most 256. On a word RAM, the usual model in which one machine word is read or written in one step, with each symbol handled in constant time (and with blocks of any length: bzip2 caps a block at 900,000 bytes, so the asymptotics are about that generalised model):

  1. Building the records would take \(O(m+r+\sigma)\) time: one pass over the symbols, a counting sort of the \(r\) records by byte, and the counts. It would hold \(O(r+\sigma)\) words of working memory: the records and a count per byte value.
  2. Composed with a move structure built in \(O(r)\) time and space, and walked in \(O(n)\) time, the inverse BWT would take \(O(m+n+r+\sigma)\) time and \(O(r+\sigma)\) extra working memory. Brown and Langmead give such a route from a run-length BWT (SEA 2026, Lemma 6 and Theorem 9), for a text with an end marker; condition 3 below gives one for bzip2's BWT, which has none.

That memory figure leaves out the compressed input, the \(n\) output bytes, the block's Huffman tables and other metadata, and the decoder's other buffers. It is not a memory bound for a whole bzip2 decompressor, which also undoes bzip2's first stage, a run-length code applied before the BWT, and checks a CRC. And the time is still \(O(n)\), because \(n\) bytes must be written. Brown and Langmead already invert in \(O(n)\) time with \(O(r)\) extra space, so the composition is no new inversion bound. What it would change is the route: no \(n\)-byte column between MTF and the move structure.

Each of those statements has conditions:

  1. A fixed alphabet. Moving a byte to the front of the list costs up to \(\sigma\) steps. For bytes that is a constant, and mibz2 does most moves with a few vector shuffles; for a large alphabet it would not be.
  2. The symbols streamed. The bounds assume a stream of decoded symbols. mibz2 decodes a block's Huffman codes into an array of symbols first, which is \(O(m)\) memory, before MTF reads it (Symbols). The \(O(r+\sigma)\) figure needs Huffman decoding and MTF fused, or the array counted. Even fused, the block's Huffman selectors stay: one per group of 50 symbols, naming the table that group uses, all stored ahead of the symbols, so about \(m/50\) entries, which is \(O(m)\) state too. So an \(O(r)\) memory bound for the whole decompressor would have to account for them as well.
  3. No end marker. Brown and Langmead's text ends in a unique terminator, $. bzip2's BWT sorts rotations with no terminator and stores the start row instead. A periodic block's map then has several cycles (the appendix, section 6). Their Theorem 9 bounds the walk's steps on average over one traversal of a single cycle, so that proof does not transfer unchanged. A later paper gives a route that needs neither. Brown, Sanaullah, Zhang and Langmead (Optimal-Time Move Structure Construction, Theorem 3.9) build a balanced move structure, in which every step takes constant time in the worst case, for any permutation, in \(O(r)\) time and space. Its inputs are each interval's start, the start of its image, and the order of the images. For \(\Psi\) built from the records, these are the row starts in \(F\) order, the records' starts in \(L\), and each record's place in \(L\) order, all of which section 3's counting sort already gives. Nothing in that theorem assumes one cycle or a terminator. The inversion then starts at bzip2's stored start row, finds its interval in \(O(r)\) steps, and takes \(n\) steps of \(\Psi\), writing each row's byte. A periodic block's cycle is shorter than \(n\), so the walk goes round it more than once, which writes the period the right number of times. A script that models this walk reproduced every string of up to eight letters over three letters, the 135 periodic ones among them. Applying that theorem to bzip2's \(\Psi\) is our composition, not a result of the paper.

The number of symbols is bounded by the runs. This is an elementary lemma, not a new result, and its proof is short. Let the maximal runs of \(L\) have lengths \(\ell_1,\dots,\ell_r\), which add up to \(n\), and count \(m\) with the end-of-block symbol, as in section 1.

First, a stretch of \(q\ge1\) zeros takes exactly \(\lfloor\log_2(q+1)\rfloor\) count digits. With \(t\) digits, each worth 1 or 2 times its place value \(1,2,4,\dots\), the totals run from \(2^t-1\) (every digit RUNA) to \(2^{t+1}-2\) (every digit RUNB), and every count in between is reached. A run of length \(\ell\) that starts with a literal is that literal and \(\ell-1\) zeros, so it costs \(1+\lfloor\log_2\ell\rfloor\) symbols. The one exception of section 2, a first run of the block's smallest byte, has no literal and \(\ell_1\) zeros, so it costs \(\lfloor\log_2(\ell_1+1)\rfloor\). No other run starts with a count (section 2). Adding the end-of-block symbol,

\[ m = 1+\sum_{j=1}^{r}\bigl(1+\lfloor\log_2\ell_j\rfloor\bigr), \]

with the first run's term replaced by \(\lfloor\log_2(\ell_1+1)\rfloor\) in the exception. For banana's runs of 2, 1 and 3, that is \(1+2+1+2=6\), the six symbols of section 1. Since \(\log_2(\ell+1)\le1+\log_2\ell\), both cases give \(m\le1+r+\sum_j\log_2\ell_j\). The logarithm is concave, so by Jensen's inequality the sum is largest when every run has length \(n/r\):

\[ m\le r\left(1+\log_2\frac nr\right)+1. \]

Cutting a run at a checkpoint changes the records, not the symbols, so it doesn't change \(m\). A second script checked the exact count, not only the bound, on every word of up to twelve letters over two letters and up to eight over three, and on the columns of 3,000 random and periodic strings.
