items.title: 5. What has mibz2 measured?
items.text:
How small is \(r\)? It has been counted once. In October, an uncommitted scratch counter ran over the bench's Wikidata corpus, wikidata.bz2 (SHA-256 82f65ace…), and checked its map against the decoder's on every block. The 233 blocks of at least 65,536 rows hold 209.7 million rows, 99.996% of the corpus, and 15,148,086 runs: \(r/n=0.0722\), about 14 rows a run. Block by block, \(r/n\) ran from 0.053 to 0.200, with a median of 0.062. 71% of the rows lie in runs of 256 or more (the journal, issue #42). That was one local run, on one corpus. The inverse-BWT navigation post said \(r\) had not been counted. It had, on that corpus. Its upper bound, \(r/n\le0.28\), is on a different one, the primary Wikidata corpus wikidata-20261026.bz2 of 434 blocks, where \(r\) has still not been counted. That post now says so.

Would a move structure help mibz2? Issue #42 built one, length-capped as Brown and Langmead describe, and timed it, locally on a shared four-core virtual machine, at one thread, on those 233 blocks, over two runs (the write-up, the result). Walked as one chain, it took about 60% less time than the T-vector's chain. Walked as mibz2 walks, 32 chains interleaved so that their memory reads overlap, it lost. In cycles per decoded byte, locally:

Step Cycles a byte T-vector build + walk 12.0 Scan of \(L\) for runs 0.9 Build from runs 6.7–8.1 Move walk alone 13.5–17.1

Each figure covers both runs, and the ranges cover the three interval-length caps tried. The move walk alone, at 13.5–17.1 cycles a byte, cost more than the T-vector's whole build and walk, at 12.0, so skipping \(L\)'s reconstruction cannot make that walker win. Each of its steps ran about 41 instructions against the T-vector's 16. Built from a run list handed over for free, as if by MTF, the move structure's build and walk together cost 80–99% more than the T-vector's. Reading the runs off the codes would save the scan, under one cycle a byte, and the writes of \(L\), which nobody has timed separately.

The scratch runs were about twice CI's figures, so they are indicative only. The result is for that one structure and that walk, on one machine and one corpus. It timed a walker, not the construction of this post: no builder fused with MTF was timed, and other move structures were not tried.

items.title: 6. Where does this stand?
items.text:
Is any of it new? Not the observation, which mibz2 recorded in issue #42. The rules it rests on are bzip2's format, as Julian Seward designed it, and they are visible in any decoder: Go's or the Wuffs format notes, which describe RUNA and RUNB as repeating "the 0th element". We searched for work that builds a run-length BWT or a move structure from MTF- or run-coded input, and found none. That is not evidence that none exists. The nearest work builds a run-length BWT from other inputs: from the plain text in space bounded by \(r\) (Nishimoto, Kanda and Tabei, ICALP 2022), from an LZ77 parse (Kempa and Kociumaka, FOCS 2020), and a move structure for any permutation, from its intervals, in \(O(r)\) time (Brown, Sanaullah, Zhang and Langmead, 2026 preprint).

What is open is the speculative question: does bzip2's coded form give a stronger algorithm or bound than a generic run-length BWT does? One point bears on it. The symbols and the column determine each other exactly, so the symbols hold no information the runs lack. Any gain would have to come from what the decoder computes cheaply on the way: avoiding the expansion of \(L\), its scan and an \(n\)-byte temporary, which is a shortcut in computation, not extra information about the permutation. So the research question, beyond composing known results, is about the model of input: what bounds on one-pass move-structure construction, upper or lower, can be proved for a decoder that reads only the stream of MTF and RUNA/RUNB symbols, that don't already follow from known run-length BWT and move-structure results? It is open, and we have not established that an answer would be new.

How sure are we? Fairly sure of the run-listing argument, which section 2 proves and a script checked on a model of bzip2's rules, and of the bound on \(m\), which section 4 proves. Sure of the costs in section 4 under their conditions: a stream of decoded symbols, with the selectors and any stored symbols counted separately, and no claim for the whole decompressor. Not sure at all that any of it is new, beyond what the format already implies.

What did the review find? An independent review, in the method of the project's researcher role and relayed from the maintainer through ChatGPT, read the published post on 8 November (the review). It found the substance sound. It gave the proof of the bound on \(m\) that section 4 now carries, and the route without an end marker in condition 3, which we checked against the paper before adopting it. It asked that the memory model and the novelty question stay as narrow as they were. It was not a fresh-reader test: the reviewer knew the code and the papers. A test with a reader who knows neither is still to be done.

items.title: 7. The argument in brief
items.text:
bzip2's MTF codes write a literal exactly where a run of the BWT's last column starts, and a count of repeats for the rest of it, so the runs can be listed from the codes, with one exception at the block's start. Each run's byte, start, length and earlier count, with the block's byte counts, give its interval of the next-row map, and a merge gives the anchors a move structure needs. In our accounting, the records take \(O(m+r+\sigma)\) time and \(O(r+\sigma)\) words, without the \(n\)-byte column, and since \(m\) is at most \(r(1+\log_2(n/r))+1\), that time is sublinear in \(n\) on long runs. The inversion stays \(O(n)\), as Brown and Langmead already have it, and a balanced move structure gives it without an end marker. In the one setting mibz2 has measured, it would not have rescued the move structure tried there, whose interleaved walk alone cost more than the T-vector's whole build and walk.

The general point is that a stage's input is often already in the form a later stage wants, and the cheapest conversion is the one never done; whether it pays depends on what the later stage costs. The same runs could, for example, count compact30's pure-run groups without the column (the appendix, section 4).

Sources:

  • Issue #42: the run counts, the observation that MTF gives the runs, and the timed move structure.
  • The run-structures journal and the move-structure walk journal (27 October 2026).
  • The mathematical structure of inverse-BWT navigation and its technical appendix.
  • Nathaniel K. Brown and Ben Langmead, Bounding the Average Move Structure Query for Faster and Smaller RLBWT Permutations, SEA 2026, LIPIcs 371, paper 9 (arXiv:2602.11029).
  • Nathaniel K. Brown, Ahsan Sanaullah, Shaojie Zhang and Ben Langmead, Optimal-Time Move Structure Construction, arXiv:2603.22147 (2026; revised 22 October 2026), Theorem 3.9.
  • Takaaki Nishimoto, Shunsuke Kanda and Yasuo Tabei, An Optimal-Time RLBWT Construction in BWT-Runs Bounded Space, ICALP 2022, LIPIcs 229, 99:1–99:20.
  • Dominik Kempa and Tomasz Kociumaka, Resolution of the Burrows–Wheeler Transform Conjecture, FOCS 2020.
  • bzip2's MTF and RUNA/RUNB rules: Go's compress/bzip2, the Wuffs bzip2 notes and mibz2's mtf.rs.

items.title: Technical appendix
items.text: ← The mathematical structure of inverse-BWT navigation

items.title: Technical appendix: the mathematics of inverse-BWT navigation
items.text: This appendix holds the derivations and side results that the main post leaves out to keep its argument moving. It uses the main post's notation, defined in its section 2: the last column \(L\) of length \(n\), its \(\sigma\) distinct characters, their frequencies \(n_c\) and starting rows \(C(c)\), the first column \(F\), rank, select, the next-row map \(\Psi\), and the run count \(r\). Equations (1) to (8) are the main post's. This appendix numbers its own (A1) onwards. Its sections can be read in any order. Nothing here has been built or measured in mibz2.

items.title: 1. Navigation as a select problem
items.text:
Equation (1) of the main post gives a data-structure reduction:

\[ \boxed{\text{arbitrary }\Psi\text{-query}\longrightarrow\text{character-bucket identification}+\text{select query}.} \]

Given a row \(i\), determine the unique character \(c\) satisfying

\[ C(c)\le i<C(c)+n_c. \]

Then compute

\[ \Psi(i)=\operatorname{select}_c(L,i-C(c)). \]

This decomposes the problem into familiar operations on indexed sequences. It means mibz2 can, in principle, represent navigation without storing an explicit successor for every row.

items.title: 1.1 The output character is already known
items.text:
A T-vector entry conventionally combines the navigation destination and a character. But the character associated with row \(i\) is simply \(F[i]\), which is determined entirely by the histogram:

\[ \boxed{F[i]=c\quad\text{whenever}\quad C(c)\le i<C(c)+n_c.}\tag{A1} \]

For a byte alphabet, the character sequence in table order has at most 256 constant intervals and at most 255 changes.

This is an unconditional property of the inverse-BWT table, regardless of whether \(L\) is repetitive. Consequence for mibz2: the character field does not need to be independently stored in every navigation entry. It may be amortised over groups of rows, or recovered from a bucket directory. This is an important distinction from run-based compression: character sharing remains useful even for highly irregular BWT input.

items.title: 1.2 An exact bound on mixed-character records
items.text:
Suppose we divide table rows into fixed groups of \(g\) consecutive positions. Because \(F\) contains only \(\sigma\) character buckets, there are at most \(\sigma-1\) bucket boundaries. Every group containing more than one output character must contain at least one of those boundaries. Thus

\[ \boxed{N_{\mathrm{mixed}}\le \sigma-1.}\tag{A2} \]

For compact30, \(g=30\) and \(\sigma\le256\), so \(N_{\mathrm{mixed}}\le255\). At maximum block size,

\[ N_{\mathrm{groups}}=\frac{900{,}000}{30}=30{,}000. \]

Hence at most 255 groups can require exceptional handling solely because their output characters differ: at most 0.85% of groups, affecting at most 7,650 rows.

This does not limit the number of RAW groups caused by widely separated navigation destinations, but proves that character-bucket crossings are a small, alphabet-bounded issue. Practical gain: output-character sharing can be designed around a strict worst-case bound; it does not depend on how repetitive the source text is.

items.title: 2.1 The exact count of consecutive navigation entries
items.text:
Inside any character bucket, define

\[ \Delta(i)=\Psi(i+1)-\Psi(i). \]

Because the bucket represents increasing occurrence positions, \(\Delta(i)\ge1\). Moreover, \(\Delta(i)=1\) if and only if the two corresponding occurrences of that character are adjacent in \(L\). A run of length \(m\) contributes \(m-1\) such pairs, giving

\[ \boxed{\#\{i:\ i,i+1\text{ lie in the same character bucket},\ \Psi(i+1)=\Psi(i)+1\}=n-r.}\tag{A3} \]

This is an equality, not an average-case statement. There are \(n-\sigma\) adjacent pairs within buckets, so the exact fraction with consecutive destinations is

\[ \boxed{f_{\mathrm{consecutive}}=\frac{n-r}{n-\sigma}.}\tag{A4} \]

This gives the BWT run count a precise interpretation as a measure of local navigation irregularity.

Two concepts must not be conflated:

  • The number of descents of \(\Psi\) (positions where \(\Psi(i)>\Psi(i+1)\)) is at most \(\sigma-1\).
  • The number of failures of consecutive translation within buckets is exactly \(r-\sigma\).

The second quantity is relevant for run-based navigation compression.

items.title: 2.2 A sparse-correction representation
items.text:
Let the positions of character \(c\) in \(L\) be

\[ x_{c,0}<x_{c,1}<\cdots<x_{c,n_c-1}. \]

Define excess gaps

\[ g_{c,j}=x_{c,j}-x_{c,j-1}-1,\qquad j\ge1. \]

Then

\[ \boxed{\Psi(C(c)+k)=x_{c,0}+k+\sum_{j=1}^{k}g_{c,j}.}\tag{A5} \]

Within runs, excess gaps are zero. A positive excess gap occurs exactly when consecutive occurrences of \(c\) belong to different runs. The number of positive gaps is

\[ \boxed{\sum_c\#\{j:g_{c,j}>0\}=r-\sigma.}\tag{A6} \]

Thus the navigation map can be described by one starting destination per character, the positions of \(r-\sigma\) nonzero corrections, their magnitudes, and bucket boundaries.

The query becomes predecessor or prefix-sum over sparse corrections. This is mathematically equivalent to the interval representation, but suggests sparse bitvectors, indexed delta streams, or two-level directories.

What we have gained: an exact structural complexity parameter for the map. The important variable is principally \(r\), the number of BWT runs, rather than \(n\), descents, or Coxeter length (the inversion count, section 7).

items.title: 3.1 Entropy of the stable-sort permutation
items.text:
Fix the histogram \((n_1,\ldots,n_\sigma)\). The number of possible last-column sequences is

\[ M=\frac{n!}{\prod_c n_c!}. \]

There is a bijection between those sequences and permutations increasing within corresponding character buckets. An arbitrary member of the family requires at least

\[ \boxed{B_{\min}=\left\lceil\log_2\frac{n!}{\prod_c n_c!}\right\rceil}\tag{A7} \]

bits in a fixed-length representation. Stirling's approximation gives the leading term

\[ \log_2 M\approx nH_0(L), \qquad H_0(L)=-\sum_c\frac{n_c}{n}\log_2\frac{n_c}{n}. \]

For a byte alphabet \(H_0(L)\le8\). Thus the stable-sort permutation with fixed histogram contains at most approximately eight bits per row, generally less.

This bounds representation information, not access latency. A four-byte T-vector stores redundancy deliberately for cheap successor retrieval.

items.title: 3.2 Elias–Fano gives a constructive representation
items.text:
Every character bucket contains a strictly increasing sequence of positions. Elias–Fano encoding is designed for such sequences.

For character \(c\), a standard Elias–Fano representation uses approximately

\[ n_c\left\lceil\log_2\frac{n}{n_c}\right\rceil+2n_c \]

bits before indexing overhead. Summed over all characters,

\[ \boxed{B_{\mathrm{EF}}\lesssim2n+\sum_c n_c\left\lceil\log_2\frac{n}{n_c}\right\rceil.}\tag{A8} \]

For an approximately uniform byte distribution this is about \(10n\) bits, or approximately 1.125 MB for a 900,000-byte block, versus 3.6 MB for the T-vector.

Elias–Fano supports indexed access to elements without decoding all predecessors; theoretical constant-time access depends on suitable select indexing. It provides a formal alternative even when \(r\) is large. It does not exploit long runs as aggressively as a run-based representation, since its general bound depends on symbol frequencies.

items.title: 3.3 A separate information bound from run count
items.text:
Count length-\(n\) words over an alphabet of size \(\sigma\) with exactly \(r\) runs. Choose positive run lengths in \(\binom{n-1}{r-1}\) ways, the first character in \(\sigma\) ways, and each subsequent character in \(\sigma-1\) ways:

\[ \boxed{N(n,r,\sigma)=\sigma(\sigma-1)^{r-1}\binom{n-1}{r-1}.}\tag{A9} \]

The bits required to enumerate this broader family are

\[ \boxed{B_{\mathrm{run}}= \left\lceil\log_2\sigma+(r-1)\log_2(\sigma-1)+\log_2\binom{n-1}{r-1}\right\rceil.}\tag{A10} \]

For \(r\ll n\), this is \(O(r\log(n/r)+r\log\sigma)\).

This counts all words with specified run count, not only valid BWT images or fixed-histogram words. It is an achievable representation-size benchmark for the larger family, not a tight bound for bzip2 blocks.

items.title: 3.4 Two independent measures of compressibility
items.text:
The two measures

\[ \boxed{H_0(L)}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\boxed{r} \]

answer different questions. Low entropy means concentrated character frequency; low \(r\) means few constant BWT runs. A block can have low entropy and many short runs, or high entropy and few long runs.

Property Mathematical implication Relevant structure Low \(H_0(L)\) Fewer stable-sort arrangements Entropy-based sequence encodings Low \(r\) Few translated navigation intervals Run descriptors and move structures Small gaps between occurrences Narrow destination spans Base-plus-offset records Small \(\sigma\) Few output-byte bucket boundaries Shared-character headers

There need not be one universally optimal compact representation.

items.title: 4. What the intervals say about compact30
items.text: mibz2's compact30 research (Building a smaller bzip2 decoding table) stores thirty rows per 64-byte record, hence the name, with exceptional RAW records that hold full entries, and attempts to reduce the working set without sacrificing memory-level parallelism.

items.title: 4.1 The ordinary-record condition
items.text:
compact30 groups thirty consecutive rows into 64-byte records and uses a label transform

\[ \varphi(i)=32\left\lfloor\frac i{30}\right\rfloor+(i\bmod30) \]

or

\[ \boxed{\varphi(i)=i+2\left\lfloor\frac i{30}\right\rfloor.}\tag{A11} \]

Two unused labels per group correspond to the record header. For a complete group \(G=[a,a+30)\), ordinary-record conditions are a shared output character and labelled successor offsets fitting in 16 bits. Since \(\Psi\) and \(\varphi\) increase within a bucket, the endpoints suffice.

Ignoring special padding and sentinel cases:

\[ \boxed{F[a]=F[a+29]} \]

and

\[ \boxed{\varphi(\Psi(a+29))-\varphi(\Psi(a))\le65{,}533.}\tag{A12} \]

This bounds encoded successor-label span, not necessarily raw row-index difference. It captures monotonicity used by the existing builder.

items.title: 4.2 Gap-based interpretation
items.text:
Suppose the group lies entirely in bucket \(c\), with first destination \(x\) and last destination \(y\). Between the thirty occurrences,

\[ y-x=29+\#\{j:x<j<y,\ L[j]\neq c\}. \]

Therefore

\[ \boxed{\Psi(a+29)-\Psi(a)=29+h,}\tag{A13} \]

where \(h\) is the count of intervening non-\(c\) characters. The labelled span is

\[ \begin{aligned} W={}&29+h\\ &+2\left(\left\lfloor\frac y{30}\right\rfloor-\left\lfloor\frac x{30}\right\rfloor\right). \end{aligned}\tag{A14} \]

Apart from bucket crossings, compact30 RAW groups arise from too many intervening characters among thirty occurrences. It is occurrence-gap arrangement, not absolute destination position, that matters.

items.title: 4.3 Guaranteed ordinary groups
items.text:
If a complete 30-row group lies inside one translation interval,

\[ \Psi(a+t)=p+t,\qquad0\le t<30. \]

The raw span is exactly 29, and the labelled span at most 31. The group is guaranteed to fit an ordinary compact30 record. Its offsets form a precomputable pattern, precisely the bulk-emission case in the existing constructor, where the builder writes a whole record from a precomputed pattern because one run of \(L\) fills the group.

items.title: 4.4 Exact formula for pure groups
items.text:
Let translation intervals be \(I_t=[a_t,b_t)\). For group width \(g\), the number of complete aligned groups contained in interval \(I_t\) is

\[ G_t=\max\left(0,\left\lfloor\frac{b_t}{g}\right\rfloor-\left\lceil\frac{a_t}{g}\right\rceil\right). \]

Therefore

\[ \boxed{G_{\mathrm{pure}}=\sum_{t=1}^{r}G_t.}\tag{A15} \]

For compact30,

\[ \boxed{R_{\mathrm{pure}}=30G_{\mathrm{pure}}.}\tag{A16} \]

This is computable from BWT run boundaries and character ranks without building the entire navigation table.

Every complete group not inside one translation interval crosses a boundary. There are at most \(r-1\) such boundaries, each inside at most one aligned group:

\[ \boxed{N_{\mathrm{nonpure}}\le r-1.}\tag{A17} \]

The bound may be loose and non-pure groups can still be ordinary records. But when \(r\ll n/g\), almost all complete groups are guaranteed pure.

items.title: 4.5 Consequence for construction
items.text:
BWT runs determine destination intervals. Record boundaries can be enumerated in row order, with endpoint spans found by sequential sweeps through run descriptors. Once runs are known, group classification can take

\[ \boxed{O\left(r+\frac ng+\sigma\right)} \]

time without materialising every successor. A scan of \(L\) can then scatter final entries into classified records. This gives an \(O(n+r+n/g)\)-time construction strategy with appropriate run, record and cursor storage.

It does not prove lower instruction count or fewer writes than the fused builder. It proves that record classification need not be interleaved with every per-row scatter: structure permits classification at the interval and group level.

So compact30's exceptions can be bounded and predicted. Character crossings are bounded by 255 groups; pure-run groups can be counted from (A15); ordinary eligibility is expressed by (A12). This enables interval/group-level classification and verification rather than opaque per-row heuristics.

items.title: 5.1 Powers of the navigation permutation
items.text:
Conventional traversal visits \(i,\Psi(i),\Psi^2(i),\ldots\). A multi-step transition computes \(\Psi^k(i)\) while emitting the \(k\) intermediate characters:

\[ W_k(i)=F[i]F[\Psi(i)]\cdots F[\Psi^{k-1}(i)]. \]

The desired operation is

\[ \boxed{i\longmapsto\left(W_k(i),\Psi^k(i)\right).}\tag{A18} \]

For a general permutation this could need \(n\) stored entries; an interval-exchange permutation gives a better bound.

items.title: 5.2 Bound on pieces of \(\Psi^k\)
items.text:
Start with a partition \(P\) into \(r\) translated intervals, each with constant output byte; there are \(r-1\) boundaries. Refine it so that two successive steps follow fixed source intervals. Splits occur at preimages of original boundaries. Since \(\Psi\) is bijective and translates each existing piece, images of the pieces are disjoint intervals partitioning the destination domain. Each original boundary introduces at most one new split across the whole refined partition. Each further step adds at most \(r-1\) boundaries. Thus

\[ \boxed{N_k\le\min\{n,\ 1+k(r-1)\}.}\tag{A19} \]

On every refined interval, \(\Psi^k\) is a translation and \(W_k\) is constant.

For two and four steps respectively:

\[ \boxed{N_2\le2r-1,\qquad N_4\le4r-3.} \]

This bound becomes uninformative when \(k(r-1)\) approaches \(n\).

items.title: 5.3 Multi-character transition table
items.text:
Each interval stores its starting row, displacement to \(\Psi^k(i)\), and the emitted \(k\)-character word. With interval identifier, output retrieval and destination computation are straightforward. An explicit representation uses

\[ \boxed{O\left(kr(\log n+k\log\sigma)\right)}\tag{A20} \]

bits when \(k(r-1)\ll n\). For fixed small \(k\), that is \(O(kr\log n)\).

This proves a compact representation for the function, not constant-latency arbitrary interval lookup. Multi-character navigation need not inherently require an \(n\)-entry jump table.

items.title: 5.4 Implication for mibz2
items.text:
Kärkkäinen, Kempa and Puglisi's 2012 work studied reducing cache misses through multi-character BWT navigation, including two characters per lookup. mibz2 cites it as prior art. mibz2 has also built such a table: the pair walk of PR #34, whose entries hold the row two steps on, was measured and dropped, because each step cost about twice as much and the table took about three times as long to build (Why 32 couriers beat one). The interval view suggests representing \(k\)-step transitions by run-sensitive translated intervals instead of a complete super-alphabet table.

The number of intervals increases at most linearly with \(kr\). For repetitive blocks it can be substantially below \(n\), though it may become large for run-rich blocks. Interval identification, segment boundaries and output ordering remain essential. A mathematical \(k\)-step operation does not imply one cache miss or CPU instruction.

So the pair \((\Psi^k,W_k)\) has at most \(1+k(r-1)\) translated, constant-output intervals. This establishes a compact theoretical representation of multi-character decoding transitions when \(kr\ll n\), without guaranteeing CPU speedup.

items.title: 6.1 Cycle count
items.text:
Let \(\operatorname{cycles}(\Psi_L)\) be the number of permutation cycles, and \(m_1,\ldots,m_r\) the maximal run lengths in \(L\). A characterisation due to Likhomanov and Shur, reported in a survey of the bijective BWT, states

\[ \boxed{L\text{ is a valid cyclic BWT image}\iff\operatorname{cycles}(\Psi_L)=\gcd(m_1,\ldots,m_r).}\tag{A21} \]

For primitive input, the permutation is one cycle. Periodic inputs may have several. We must not assume every bzip2 traversal visits all distinct rows in one cycle.

items.title: 6.2 Necklaces and exact enumeration
items.text:
The BWT identifies cyclic rotations, so its images correspond naturally to necklaces. With counts \(n_1,\ldots,n_\sigma\) and \(g=\gcd(n_1,\ldots,n_\sigma)\), Burnside's lemma gives

\[ \boxed{N_{\mathrm{BWT}}=\frac1n\sum_{d\mid g}\phi(d)\frac{(n/d)!}{\prod_c(n_c/d)!}.}\tag{A22} \]

The number of primitive necklaces is

\[ \boxed{N_{\mathrm{primitive}}=\frac1n\sum_{d\mid g}\mu(d)\frac{(n/d)!}{\prod_c(n_c/d)!}.}\tag{A23} \]

Here \(\phi\) is Euler's totient and \(\mu\) the Möbius function.

items.title: 6.3 Coprime-frequency simplification
items.text:
When \(g=1\), all source strings with that histogram are primitive:

\[ \boxed{N_{\mathrm{BWT}}=\frac1n\frac{n!}{\prod_c n_c!}.}\tag{A24} \]

The BWT restriction reduces the stable-sort family by a factor of exactly \(n\); the information saving is

\[ \boxed{\log_2n\text{ bits}.}\tag{A25} \]

At \(n=900{,}000\), this is approximately 19.78 bits for the entire block. Identifying the original rotation requires a primary index with roughly the same amount of information.

Cycle structure is useful for validity checks, periodicity, testing and traversal assumptions, but it is not a promising independent source of major storage savings. The stable-sort restriction accounts for most of the representational reduction.

items.title: 7. What does the permutree thesis contribute?
items.text:
Tamayo Jiménez studies weak-order lattices, permutree congruences, pattern-avoiding permutations, and related geometry. The inverse-BWT permutation belongs to a classical parabolic quotient of the symmetric group.

Let

\[ J=\{s_i:\ i,i+1\text{ lie in the same character bucket}\}. \]

Then

\[ \boxed{\Psi\in W^J}, \]

where \(W^J\) consists of permutations with no right descents at positions in \(J\).

items.title: 7.1 Weak-order inversion statistic
items.text:
The Coxeter length is

\[ \ell(\Psi)=\#\{(i,j):i<j,\ \Psi(i)>\Psi(j)\}. \]

Stable sorting implies

\[ \boxed{\ell(\Psi)=\#\{(i,j):i<j,\ L[i]>L[j]\}.}\tag{A26} \]

This gives an exact algebraic rank, but it should not be confused with BWT run count.

items.title: 7.2 Large inversion count can coexist with easy navigation
items.text:
For \(L=b^ma^m\), \(a<b\),

\[ \Psi(i)=\begin{cases}i+m,&0\le i<m,\\i-m,&m\le i<2m.\end{cases} \]

There are just \(r=2\) runs but

\[ \boxed{\ell(\Psi)=m^2}. \]

Thus quadratic Coxeter length coexists with two translated intervals. This is a valid cyclic BWT image of an alternating periodic word.

Weak-order geometry measures distance from identity under adjacent transpositions; it does not measure cost of successor queries.

items.title: 7.3 Meets and joins
items.text:
The parabolic-quotient family has weak-order meets and joins, but mibz2 evaluates one fixed permutation rather than optimising over permutations. Meets and joins need not preserve valid BWT images. The permutree thesis does not directly imply a faster decoder; its relevance is the algebraic setting, while useful data structures come from stable sorting, succinct sequences and run-bounded interval permutations.

So weak-order geometry provides context, not the central optimisation. Parabolic quotients explain increasing buckets and inversion structure, but the objects the decoder actually evaluates are

\[ \boxed{\operatorname{select}_c(L,k),\quad\text{translated intervals},\quad\text{move queries},\quad\Psi^k.} \]

These admit operational data structures and meaningful complexity bounds.

items.title: 8. Correctness checks and oracles
items.text:
The mathematical properties support independent invariants:

Invariant Exact property What it checks Permutation \(\Psi\) bijective on \([0,n)\) No missing or duplicated destinations Stable-sort identity Equation (1) of the main post Correct correspondence with \(L\) Bucket monotonicity \(\Psi(i+1)>\Psi(i)\) within buckets Counting-sort ordering Run structure Exactly \(n-r\) within-bucket adjacent pairs advance by one Correct run correspondence Interval translation Equation (2) of the main post, on every run Correct interval descriptors compact30 classification Equation (A12) Ordinary/RAW representation decisions BWT cycle validity Equation (A21) Valid cyclic-BWT structure Multi-step navigation Equation (A18) Correct jump destinations and emitted words

These diagnose internal errors more precisely than end-to-end decoded-output comparison.

items.title: 8.1 Independent oracle
items.text:
Given \(L\) and its histogram, construct the reference mapping through equation (1) of the main post. For every row \(i\) verify

\[ \Psi_{\mathrm{candidate}}(i)=\operatorname{select}_{F[i]}(L,i-C(F[i])). \]

This is a complete equivalence check, stronger than traversal from the primary index alone (which need not visit all distinct rows for periodic blocks). For \(k\)-step representations verify

\[ \Psi_{\mathrm{candidate}}^{(k)}(i)=\Psi^k(i) \]

and

\[ W_{k,\mathrm{candidate}}(i)=W_k(i). \]

These are development oracles, not obligatory checks in production decoding.

items.title: 9. The design space and the results
items.text:
Section 6 of the main post keeps three resources apart: navigation storage, construction work and critical-path memory dependencies. mibz2's compact30 work reduced footprint and benefited concurrent traversal, but direct construction remained expensive; the 4 November post says bulk emission covered 74.3% of rows on the main Wikidata corpus. The 7 November pipelining work overlaps a block's construction and traversal with other stages of neighbouring blocks: a team's leader runs the next block's MTF and finishes the previous block while its helpers build and walk the current one.

So mibz2 need not choose only between the complete T-vector and packed per-row T-vectors. Move structures store interval transitions and support repeated navigation. When \(r\) is small they offer a theoretical reduction in live navigation storage, with established constructions and query guarantees. The representations the theory offers, with what each costs:

Representation Space for navigation Access complexity Main consideration Conventional T-vector \(32n\) bits One direct lookup High footprint Packed destinations About \(20n\) bits, plus symbols/metadata Direct addressing Bit extraction Per-character Elias–Fano About \(nH_0(L)+O(n)\) bits Indexed select More dependencies Simple run descriptors \(O(r\log n)\) bits \(O(\log r)\) predecessor Repeated searches Balanced move structure \(O(r)\) words \(O(1)\) with interval state Interval transitions Length-capped move structure \(O(r)\) words Amortised \(O(1)\) over distinct full-cycle visits Coverage assumptions \(k\)-step intervals \(O(kr(\log n+k\log\sigma))\) bits Interval-dependent Multi-character operation

The results, in one table:

Gain Established mathematical result Value to mibz2 Stable-sort representation \(\Psi\) is a collection of character-select sequences Succinct sequence structures Run-bounded representation \(\Psi\) has at most \(r\) translated intervals Space scaling with \(r\) Move structures \(O(1)\) stateful moves in \(O(r)\) words Alternative to full T-vector Linear-time inversion \(O(n)\) time and \(O(r)\) additional RLBWT working space under assumptions End-to-end theoretical feasibility Fixed-record identities Exact character crossings, spans and pure-group bounds Formal compact30 analysis Multi-step interval bound At most \(1+k(r-1)\) pieces for \(k\)-step navigation Compact multi-character transitions

Sources: as listed in the main post.

items.title: One shift per run
items.text:
mibz2 · Research blog

To undo the Burrows–Wheeler transform (BWT), a bzip2 decoder follows a chain through each block: from one row of the transform's sorted matrix to the next, emitting one byte at each step. mibz2, our bzip2 decoder, stores that chain as a table with one navigation entry per row, which we call the T-vector. Each entry is four bytes, holding the next row and the byte to emit. At the maximum bzip2 block size of 900,000 bytes, the T-vector occupies 3.6 MB. The inverse BWT is the expensive part of decoding a block, because each step's address comes from the entry just read; mibz2 walks many such chains at once so that their memory reads overlap. An earlier post works the transform through on a small example.

The entries of that table are not independent. When the transformed word banana is decoded, rows 0, 1 and 2, the three that emit a, have next rows 3, 4 and 5. One descriptor covers all three: the first row, the first next row and the length. Every run of equal bytes in the BWT's output works the same way, so the whole table can be described by one shift per run, \(r\) of them, instead of one entry per row, \(n\) of them. A walk can follow those shifts without searching for the right one at each step, by remembering which run it is in. Data structures that do this, move structures, are published, with proofs: Nishimoto and Tabei (2021) gave constant-time steps in \(O(r)\) machine words, and Brown and Langmead (2026) inverted a whole BWT in \(O(n)\) time with \(O(r)\) additional working space, starting from a run-length BWT representation.

What is not proved is that any of them beats mibz2's 32-lane, four-byte-per-row implementation in elapsed CPU cycles. Everything in this post is mathematics and published theory: nothing in it has been built or measured in mibz2, and it changes nothing in the decoder. \(r\) has been counted on one corpus, in a scratch run; section 3 gives that count, and an upper bound on another.

Section 1 shows both ideas on banana, and section 2 proves the first in general. Section 3 shows when it saves nothing. Sections 4 and 5 give the published theory, and section 6 what it would cost mibz2 and what would settle it. Secondary results are in a technical appendix.

items.title: The mathematical structure of inverse-BWT navigation
items.text:
The inverse BWT's next-row map is one shift per run of equal bytes, so it can be stored per run rather than per row. Whether that beats mibz2's table is unproven.

8 November 2026 · 14 min read · Open question

items.title: 1. What does the next-row map look like for banana?
items.text:
Suppose you want to compress the word banana with bzip2. The BWT writes down each of its six rotations, sorts them, and keeps two things: the last column of the sorted list, \(L\), and the number of the row holding the original word, here 3. The first column, \(F\), is the same bytes in sorted order. The last column of the table, the next row, is explained below it.

Row Rotation Next row 0 abanan 3 1 anaban 4 2 ananab 5 3 banana 2 4 nabana 0 5 nanaba 1

Reading down the rotations' last letters gives \(L=\texttt{nnbaaa}\), and their first letters give \(F=\texttt{aaabnn}\). The next row of row \(i\), written \(\Psi(i)\), is the row whose rotation is row \(i\)'s rotation with its first byte moved to the end. Row 3, banana, becomes ananab, which is row 2. To decode, start at row 3, emit \(F[3]\), move to \(\Psi(3)\), and repeat. The rows visited are

\[ 3\to2\to5\to1\to4\to0, \]

and the bytes emitted are banana. mibz2's T-vector stores exactly this: for each row, \(F[i]\) and \(\Psi(i)\).

Moving a rotation's first byte to its end puts that byte last, so \(\Psi(i)\) is always a row whose \(L\) byte is \(F[i]\); position \(j\) of \(L\) is the last byte of row \(j\), so a position is also a row. Which a goes to which follows from the sort. Rows 0–2 start with a and are sorted by the five letters after it. With the a moved to the end, rows 3–5 sort by the same five letters, so they come in the same order. The argument holds for every byte of every block.

The kth a of F goes to the kth a of L

FLa1n00a2n11a3b22ba133na244na355

1. Row 0 holds the 1st a of F, so its next row is the 1st a of L: position 3.

FLa1n00a2n11a3b22ba133na244na355

2. The 2nd a goes to the 2nd: row 1 to 4.

FLa1n00a2n11a3b22ba133na244na355

3. The 3rd goes to the 3rd, row 2 to 5: three curves of the same shape.

Conceptual, worked by hand from the table above. Green marks the run aaa of L and the rows it receives, in all three figures.

Three curves, one record

FLa1n00a2n11a3b22ba133na244na355+3

1. L's three as sit side by side, one run, so the three curves are one ribbon that moves every row by +3.

three entries0 → 31 → 42 → 5one recordsource0destination3length3bytea

2. One record replaces the three entries: row 0 + t goes to 3 + t for each t below the length, 3.

The b at position 2 receives row 3, a shift of −1, and the run nn receives rows 4–5, a shift of −4. We call the three source intervals A, B and N, after their bytes: in \(F\) they come in byte order, in \(L\) in position order. Written out, the whole map is

\[ \Psi(i)=\begin{cases}i+3,&0\le i<3,\\i-1,&i=3,\\i-4,&4\le i<6.\end{cases} \]

Three row entries become one descriptor, and six table entries become three. That counts entries, not bytes: a descriptor holds more than a T-vector entry (section 2.1). Had the copies of a in \(L\) been split into two runs, the a rows would split into two descriptors. The three pieces are the three runs of \(L\), nn, b and aaa, and that is the first result of this post. The next-row map is a set of shifted intervals, one for each run of the last column.

items.title: 1.1 Walking the intervals without a search
items.text:
To find the next row of row \(i\) from intervals, a decoder would first have to find which interval holds \(i\): a search among the \(r\) starting rows. A walk doesn't need it, because it carries the interval's name along with the row. Each descriptor also records its anchor: the interval its destinations begin in. Interval A's destinations begin at row 3, in interval B.

One step of the walk, from row 1 in interval A

Fa0a1a2b3n4n5ABNstate(1, A)3 + (1 − 0) = 4

1. The walk holds row 1 and its interval, A, so it reads A's record directly: offset 1 − 0, destination 3 + 1 = 4.

Fa0a1a2b3n4n5ABNanchor of AB4 is past B’s end

2. A's record names its anchor, B, the interval its destinations start in, so the walk compares 4 with B's end only: 4 lies past it.

Fa0a1a2b3n4n5ABNnew state(4, N)

3. One step on, N holds 4, so the state is now (4, N): one addition and two boundary checks, no search, where a T-vector step is one read.

Repeated from row 3, the same actions visit row 3 in B, then 2 in A, 5 in N, 1 in A, 4 in N and 0 in A, and emit banana. In a large block one interval's destinations can cross many intervals; section 4 shows how splitting intervals bounds the forward steps by a constant, and a constant number of steps is still not one memory read. Carrying the interval as traversal state turns each step into arithmetic and a short forward step, with no search. This is the idea behind move structures (section 4).

The difference is between random row access, where any row can be asked for at any time, and stateful successor navigation, where each question follows from the last answer. mibz2 needs mostly the second. Every lane of its walk follows a path and keeps state, which is why move structures are relevant to it.

items.title: 2. Why does every run give one shift?
items.text:
The banana table follows from two facts: \(\Psi(i)\) lands on a copy of \(F[i]\) in \(L\), and equal bytes keep their order. Let

\[ L=L[0]L[1]\cdots L[n-1] \]

be the BWT last column of a block, and let

\[ \Sigma=\{c_1<c_2<\cdots<c_\sigma\} \]

be its distinct characters, ordered by byte value. Write \(n_c\) for the frequency of character \(c\), and define \(C(c)=\sum_{d<c}n_d\), the number of bytes smaller than \(c\): the row where \(c\)'s block of rows in \(F\) begins. The first column is

\[ F=c_1^{n_{c_1}}c_2^{n_{c_2}}\cdots c_\sigma^{n_{c_\sigma}}. \]

Define zero-based rank and select by

\[ \operatorname{rank}_c(L,j)=|\{i<j:L[i]=c\}| \]

and

\[ \operatorname{select}_c(L,k)=\text{position of the }(k+1)\text{st occurrence of }c. \]

The usual backward LF mapping is

\[ \operatorname{LF}(j)=C(L[j])+\operatorname{rank}_{L[j]}(L,j). \]

mibz2 uses the inverse direction, which we shall consistently call \(\Psi\):

\[ \boxed{\Psi=\operatorname{LF}^{-1}} \]

and therefore

\[ \boxed{\Psi(C(c)+k)=\operatorname{select}_c(L,k).}\tag{1} \]

In words: the \((k+1)\)st \(c\) of \(F\) goes to the \((k+1)\)st \(c\) of \(L\). That is the stable-sort identity the banana table showed. For each row \(i\), mibz2 needs to recover the next row \(\Psi(i)\) and emit the byte \(F[i]\), while preserving the bookkeeping required by its segmented traversal: mibz2 cuts each block's walk into segments that start at known rows, walks them in parallel and joins them. That is the mathematical operation being optimised. The byte \(F[i]\) needs no storage per row, since the histogram fixes it (appendix section 1).

Now let \(r\) be the number of maximal equal-character runs in \(L\), and \(r_c\) the number of runs containing character \(c\), so that \(r=\sum_{c\in\Sigma}r_c\). Consider a run of character \(c\) beginning at position \(p\), with length \(m\):

\[ L[p:p+m]=c^m. \]

Let \(k=\operatorname{rank}_c(L,p)\) be the number of earlier occurrences of \(c\). The run corresponds to the interval of rows in \(F\) starting at \(a=C(c)+k\). By equation (1), for every \(0\le t<m\), \(\Psi(a+t)=p+t\). Therefore

\[ \boxed{\Psi(i)=i+(p-a),\qquad a\le i<a+m.}\tag{2} \]

The entire run is represented by one constant displacement. Every character occurrence belongs to exactly one run. Their corresponding intervals partition the domain of \(\Psi\):

\[ \boxed{\begin{gathered}\Psi\text{ admits a partition into }r\text{ intervals,}\\\text{on each of which it is a translation.}\end{gathered}}\tag{3} \]

In banana, the run aaa starts at \(p=3\), and the a rows start at \(a=0\): the shift is \(+3\), as the figure showed. In combinatorics, such a map is a discrete interval-exchange permutation. This identification is more operationally useful than membership in a weak-order lattice, because it tells us exactly how to evaluate the permutation.

The \(r\) pieces are an upper bound, not always the fewest. For the valid cyclic BWT of abc, \(L=\texttt{cab}\), \(F=\texttt{abc}\) and \(r=3\), but \(\Psi=(1,2,0)\) has just two maximal translated intervals: rows \([0,2)\) have displacement \(+1\), and row \([2,3)\) has displacement \(-2\). The partition of equation (3) is the one the runs induce. Adjacent pieces can share a shift.

items.title: 2.1 What the intervals cost to store
items.text:
For each interval \(t\), store its starting position \(a_t\) and first destination \(p_t\). Order the intervals by their starting positions, \(0=a_0<a_1<\cdots<a_r=n\). Then

\[ \boxed{\Psi(i)=p_t+(i-a_t)\quad\text{for}\quad a_t\le i<a_{t+1}.}\tag{4} \]

No per-row destination array is required. For \(n\le900{,}000\), each position fits in 20 bits, so the basic representation uses approximately \(B_{\mathrm{interval}}\approx40r\) bits, two 20-bit values per interval, plus indexing and metadata. The T-vector uses \(B_{\mathrm{T}}=32n\) bits. Ignoring indexing overhead, the interval representation is smaller whenever \(40r<32n\), or

\[ \boxed{\frac rn<0.8.} \]

This is only a storage comparison for basic descriptors, not a complete performance or working-memory bound. A practical move structure needs additional information to locate the next interval. Nevertheless, it proves there is a potentially much smaller, exact representation whenever the BWT contains sufficiently long runs.

items.title: 3. When do the shifts save nothing?
items.text:
When the runs are short. The valid cyclic BWT of abba is \(L=\texttt{baba}\): four rows and four runs, \(r=n=4\). Its descriptors take \(40r=160\) bits, more than the T-vector's \(32n=128\) bits, before any index is added. For banana, three runs in six rows, they take \(40r=120\) bits against \(32n=192\).

So run-based storage is not guaranteed to be smaller. The comparison is of descriptors alone. A practical move structure also stores anchors and an index, so its break-even point lies below \(r/n=0.8\), by an amount nobody has measured for mibz2.

Nor does a block that compresses well necessarily have few runs. The two simplest measures, the zero-order entropy \(H_0(L)\) of the byte frequencies and \(r\), answer different questions: a block can have low entropy and many short runs, or high entropy and few long runs (appendix section 3). The run count itself has a precise meaning: exactly \(n-r\) pairs of adjacent rows within a character's block have consecutive next rows (appendix section 2).

How small is \(r\) on mibz2's blocks? It has been counted once, in October, by an uncommitted scratch counter on the bench's Wikidata corpus, wikidata.bz2. Over its 233 blocks of at least 65,536 rows, 99.996% of its rows, \(r/n=0.0722\), and block by block it ran from 0.053 to 0.200, with a median of 0.062 (the journal, issue #42). That was one local run on one corpus. On the main Wikidata corpus, which the rest of this section uses, \(r\) has not been counted, but an earlier figure bounds it. On that corpus, 207,006,515 rows in 434 blocks, the builder of compact30, our research table that packs thirty rows into each 64-byte record, wrote 74.3% of rows through its bulk emitter, as 5,127,300 complete 30-row records, each covered by one run of \(L\) (the 4 November post, section 6). Each of those runs holds at least one such record, so there are at most 5,127,300 of them. The remaining 53.2 million rows can lie in at most 53.2 million further runs. So, across the corpus, \(r\le58.3\) million and \(r/n\le0.28\). This is derived, not measured, and it is an aggregate: it says nothing about the spread from block to block, and the true \(r\) may be much smaller.

items.title: 4. How does a walk move between intervals in constant time?
items.text:
The interval-exchange permutation of section 2 is precisely the sort of permutation handled by move structures, introduced by Nishimoto and Tabei. Their 2021 result establishes \(O(1)\)-time move queries with \(O(r)\) words of space after balancing represented intervals.

An ordinary query is \(i\mapsto\Psi(i)\). An interval representation must locate the interval containing \(i\), potentially requiring an expensive predecessor search: finding the last interval start at or before \(i\). Instead retain the pair \((i,t)\), where \(t\) identifies the interval. The next row follows directly:

\[ j=p_t+(i-a_t). \]

We then need the interval \(t'\) containing \(j\). A move structure stores, for each interval, the interval its destinations begin in (its anchor, in section 1.1), and advances through descriptors to locate \(j\), as the banana walk stepped from B to N. Unbalanced intervals may require multiple advances. The crucial theorem is that intervals can be split into \(O(r)\) balanced pieces, guaranteeing a constant number of advances:

\[ \boxed{(i,t)\xrightarrow{O(1)}(\Psi(i),t')}\tag{5} \]

using \(O(r)\) words in the word-RAM model, the standard model in which reading one machine word is one step. Carrying \(t\) is essential. This is not one-memory-access arbitrary-row lookup. The theorem shows that compact representation does not imply logarithmic lookup time. That removes a theoretical objection, not the hardware concern about several serial descriptor loads: an \(O(1)\) bound in the RAM model is not a claim of one load, or of fewer cycles.

mibz2 already maintains per-lane state. It walks 32 interleaved lanes, each following one segment, so that 32 independent memory reads can be in flight at once (32 lanes, 8.6 chains), and it supports parallel work across blocks. A move structure adds a run/interval identifier to each lane, giving state

\[ (\text{row},\text{interval},\text{segment state}). \]

A fresh segment start may require predecessor search once. For \(P\) segment starts initialised with binary search, seeding costs \(O(P\log r)\); later transitions maintain interval state. The structure therefore removes general predecessor queries from the hot path. It does not remove memory dependencies: a move query may load several descriptors. It does change the algorithmic problem from repeated searches to constant-time state transitions.

items.title: 5. Can a whole block be inverted this way?
items.text:
Brown and Langmead's Bounding the Average Move Structure Query for Faster and Smaller RLBWT Permutations (SEA 2026) studies length capping. (RLBWT is the run-length BWT: the last column \(L\) stored as its \(r\) runs, each a character and a length.) Set the average interval length to \(n/r\); for constant \(c\), split until every interval is of length at most

\[ \boxed{L_{\max}=c\frac nr.}\tag{6} \]

The number of additional intervals is approximately at most \(r/c\), so \(r'\le r+r/c\), up to rounding. Their Theorem 2 bounds aggregate work over all \(n\) distinct positions, not strict worst-case cost per query. The number of interval advances is bounded by a constant multiple of \(n\):

\[ \boxed{T_{\mathrm{all\ moves}}=O(n).}\tag{7} \]

For a single-cycle permutation, full traversal visits every position once. The mathematical argument can be set-based, not necessarily requiring one serial traversal order. They also show \(O(r)\)-time/space construction of a capped structure for LF or its inverse from RLBWT. Their Theorem 9 establishes

\[ \boxed{\begin{gathered}\text{BWT inversion time}=O(n),\\\text{additional working space}=O(r).\end{gathered}}\tag{8} \]

This is a complexity theorem for inversion, not merely compressibility.

How directly does it apply to bzip2? The theorem starts from run-length BWT. mibz2 reconstructs the byte sequence \(L\) after MTF (undoing bzip2's move-to-front coding, the stage before the inverse BWT), so discovering the runs involves examining \(n\) bytes. bzip2's MTF codes already mark where each run starts, so the runs could instead be listed while decoding (a follow-up post). Given \(L\) and its counts, the runs can be enumerated in \(O(n)\) time, and the capped structure built from them in \(O(r)\), giving an \(O(n+r)=O(n)\) path with \(O(r)\) navigation storage, when the input sequence and output buffer are accounted for separately. This does not make the entire decompressor \(O(r)\) total memory. Linear asymptotic construction does not mean lower constant cost than mibz2's fused counting-sort builder.

The single-cycle amortisation argument applies directly to primitive strings, those that are not a repetition of a shorter string. Periodic cyclic BWTs may have several cycles (appendix section 6); mibz2's segmented traversal needs to preserve applicable assumptions. The balanced 2021 structure gives a per-move guarantee independent of single-cycle amortisation, at additional construction complexity. Brown and Langmead's Orbit library implements move-structure variants, but is not a verified drop-in replacement for mibz2's Rust T-vector.

So there exists a mathematically established family of navigation structures whose storage scales with BWT runs rather than rows, and that supports efficient repeated successor traversal without a fresh general predecessor search on each step.

items.title: 6. What would it cost mibz2, and what would settle it?
items.text:
A smaller table helps mibz2 only through a chain of costs. Fewer bytes mean less of the cache taken by each block's walk. But each step then reads one or more descriptors instead of one entry, and the builder must find the runs and write the descriptors before the walk begins. What the 32 lanes need is many independent reads in flight at once, and a step that reads two descriptors in turn can have two waits on its path, not one. Three resources stay separate:

\[ \boxed{\begin{gathered}\text{navigation storage},\\\text{construction work},\\\text{critical-path memory dependencies}.\end{gathered}} \]

A representation may improve one and worsen another. The mathematical space/time bounds do not equate them. The representations the theory offers, and what each costs, are compared in appendix section 9.

The same intervals bear on mibz2's other work. In compact30, every 30-row group lying inside one interval is guaranteed an ordinary record, and these groups can be counted from the runs without building the table (appendix section 4). Taking \(k\) steps at once needs at most \(1+k(r-1)\) intervals (appendix section 5).

The central research question changes from how much can we compress the existing navigation table? to:

What is the least expensive stateful navigation representation for a BWT interval-exchange permutation, while preserving high memory-level parallelism across simultaneous traversals?

Two measurements would settle whether it is worth building. The first is the run count of each block on mibz2's corpora, and so the size of the descriptors, block by block, against the T-vector's. The second, only if those are small, is a 32-lane walk over a move structure, timed against the T-vector walk with the cost of building each counted. Both have been done once, locally. The run count is the one in section 3. And in issue #42, a length-capped move structure's build and 32-lane walk cost 90–108% more than the T-vector's, at one thread, because each interleaved step took more instructions (the write-up). The issue is closed, with a condition for reopening it: a setting bound by memory rather than instructions, such as several workers sharing the cache. The most consequential result to investigate further is the move structure, especially Brown and Langmead's 2026 length-capping construction. It is the closest existing theoretical answer to the problem mibz2 solves.

items.title: 7. The argument in brief
items.text:
The next-row map sends the \(k\)th copy of each byte in \(F\) to its \(k\)th copy in \(L\), so each run of \(L\) is one shifted interval, and the map is at most \(r\) of them. A walk that carries its interval needs no search to take its next step, and move structures make that step take constant time in \(O(r)\) words. Brown and Langmead turn this into a linear-time inversion with run-bounded working space.

What is proved: the inverse-BWT navigation problem supports representations and algorithms with run-bounded space, efficient repeated traversal, and (in the RLBWT model) asymptotically optimal inversion time.

What is not proved for mibz2: that these beat its 32-lane, four-byte-per-row implementation in elapsed CPU cycles once table construction, segmented starts, emitted characters and shared-cache behaviour are counted. The permutree thesis identifies a legitimate algebraic neighbourhood, but the directly applicable algorithmic theorems come from succinct data structures and run-length BWT (appendix section 7).

The general lesson is that a table walked in order can often be replaced by less data plus state carried by the walker, since each step already knows where the last one was.

Sources:

  • Technical appendix: the secondary derivations, bounds and checks, with their equations.
  • Daniel Tamayo Jiménez, Combinatorics of Permutreehedra and Geometry of s-Permutahedra, PhD thesis (2023): weak order and parabolic quotients.
  • Takaaki Nishimoto and Yasuo Tabei, Optimal-Time Queries on BWT-runs Compressed Indexes, ICALP 2021, LIPIcs 198, 101:1–101:15: constant-time move structures.
  • Nathaniel K. Brown and Ben Langmead, Bounding the Average Move Structure Query for Faster and Smaller RLBWT Permutations, SEA 2026, LIPIcs 371, paper 9: length capping, and inversion in \(O(n)\) time and \(O(r)\) space.
  • Hideo Bannai, Dominik Köppl and Zsuzsanna Lipták, A Survey of the Bijective Burrows–Wheeler Transform (2025), in the Festschrift for Giovanni Manzini, OASIcs 131: cyclic BWT and necklace enumeration.
  • Juha Kärkkäinen, Dominik Kempa and Simon J. Puglisi, Slashing the Time for BWT Inversion, DCC 2012, pp. 99–108: multi-chain and multi-character inversion.
  • Building a smaller bzip2 decoding table: from 49 instructions to 12 (4 November 2026): compact30 architecture and builder evidence.

items.title: mibz2 gets a pit crew
items.text:
mibz2 · Research blog

mibz2, our bzip2 decoder written in Rust, decodes the blocks of a file in parallel, each block on a team of threads. Most of a block's work can be shared among a team's threads, but two steps can't: the move-to-front step before the shared part, and the finish after it. In release 0.2.6, as the last post showed, each team's leader runs those steps itself while its two helpers work on the shared part. This post is about the next step: taking that one-thread work out of the teams altogether. Two threads of their own, which we call service threads, do it for every block, and the teams only do the shared part. They are the teams' pit crew, so the teams never have to leave the track.

Threads asked for, and threads that decode. A caller gives mibz2 a thread setting, and the setting is the budget of the decoding plan. It counts the decoding threads, the team members and any service threads, and nothing else. The support threads come on top of it: the scanner, which reads the file, and a few others that pass blocks along. At a setting of ten, 0.2.6 uses nine decoding threads, three teams of three, since teams of three can't use the tenth. The service layout uses eight: two teams of three plus the two service threads. So it inverts two blocks at a time instead of three.

What we found. On the ten-core machine we test on, the service layout decoded our test file 4.5% faster than 0.2.6's default and spent 12.7% less processor time. That comes from a registered run, one whose comparisons and decision rules were fixed before it ran. The simplest reading is that freeing every team member for the shared work more than pays for having one team fewer, as long as the pit crew keeps up. Two service threads did. One, tried only beside three teams, did not.

Three limits come with it. The layout is a prototype on a research branch, not mibz2's default. It was measured on one processor, an Intel Core i9-10900K, and principally on one file, a sample of the Wikidata dump. And the gain belongs to the layout as a package. Two teams without service threads were slower, so the service threads matter. But the runs changed several things at once, and which of them earns the gain is not yet separated.

The results in brief:

  • The registered gain: 4.5% faster than the default, with 12.7% less processor time and 10 MB less peak memory. A later run, which didn't judge the comparison, measured 7.3%.
  • Two teams alone lose: without service threads, two teams were slower than the default, so the gain doesn't come simply from running fewer teams.
  • One service thread was too few for three teams: with one, three teams of three were 20% slower than the default, because that thread couldn't keep up. A second service thread beside the same three teams fixed that, but bought speed with more processor time: a trade, not a win. No run tried one service thread with two teams.
  • Preparing further ahead didn't detectably help: letting the service threads prepare three or four blocks ahead, instead of two, was inconclusive. The teams still wait about a sixth of the time, and what they wait for isn't yet identified.
  • Not yet a default: a safety review cleared the two research versions that were measured, not a production version. A default needs its own measurements and its own review.

The figure sets the comparisons with the default side by side. Each dot is a speed ratio, the default's elapsed time over the layout's, so above 1 is faster.

The service layout against the 0.2.6 default

Against the 0.2.6 default0.800.901.001.10speed against the default (above 1 is faster)One service thread, 3 × 3 + 1 (pull request 251)0.799 (0.786–0.812)Two pipelined teams, no service threads (258)0.866 (0.851–0.881)Service layout, first run (251)1.045 (1.023–1.068)Service layout, registered run (258)1.045 (1.017–1.073)Service layout, later run (271)1.073 (1.041–1.106)registered, judgedreported, never judged Measured, the test machine, a thread setting of ten, 20 paired rounds each. Each dot is the geometric mean of a run's paired ratios, and its line the 95% interval of that estimate, within that run; it is not the range of individual rounds. Green dots are comparisons registered as decisions before their run; amber dots were reported beside them and never judged. The numbers in brackets are the pull requests of the runs.

Section 1 shows what a service thread does, and section 2 why that might pay and why it might not. Sections 3 to 5 are the three runs: one service thread failing, two beating the default with the controls beside them, and the result seen again. Section 6 is about what still holds the teams back, and section 7 about the costs, the scope and what a default would need.

items.title: mibz2 gets a pit crew
items.text:
Handing each block's serial steps to two dedicated threads gives mibz2 a rare double win, decoding 4.5% faster on ten cores with 13% less CPU.

9 November 2026 · 16 min read · Research in progress

items.title: 1. What does a service thread do?
items.text:
A bzip2 file is a series of blocks of up to 900 kB, each compressed with no reference to the others, so each can be decoded on its own. One thread, the scanner, reads the file and undoes the outermost layer of every block, the Huffman coding. The rest of a block's work is in three parts:

  1. MTF: undoing the move-to-front coding, which turns the scanner's symbols back into the block's bytes, though not yet in their original order.
  2. The inverse BWT: undoing the Burrows–Wheeler transform, which puts the bytes back in their original order. It has two phases. The build fills a table with one 4-byte entry for each byte of the block, 3.6 MB for a full block. The walk follows the table from entry to entry. Both can be split among several threads.
  3. The finish: putting the walk's pieces together, RLE1 (expanding runs of repeated bytes), and the CRC (checking the result against the block's checksum). Then the block is handed to the reader, in file order.

MTF and the finish run on one thread each. The inverse BWT is the expensive part, and the only part a team shares. In 0.2.6, at a setting of ten or more on a machine of the test machine's shape, the decoder runs three teams of three. Each team has a leader and two helpers. While the helpers build and walk one block, the leader finishes the block before it and runs MTF on the block after it, then joins the walk.

The service layout takes MTF and the finish away from the teams. Two service threads do them for every block, serving both teams. Each team's three threads only build and walk. The figure shows the two layouts at a setting of ten.

Who does what, at a thread setting of ten

0.2.6: three pipelined teams of three9 decoding threads, 3 blocks inverted at onceLHHLHHLHHService layout: 2 teams of 3, 2 service threads8 decoding threads, 2 blocks inverted at onceHHHHHHSSL: a leader. It runs MTF and the finish, thenjoins the walk.H: a thread that only builds and walks a table.S: a service thread: MTF and the finish, forboth teams. A sketch of the layouts, from the decoder's code; it shows which thread does which stage, not timing. Each green outline is a team. Both layouts also run the scanner and a few bookkeeping threads, not drawn; the service layout adds one more of these, a feeder that passes the scanner's blocks to the service threads.

Work moves between the two kinds of thread through two queues. A service thread takes a block from the scanner, runs its MTF, and puts it on the prepared queue. A team takes the next prepared block, builds and walks its table, and puts the result on the finishing queue. A service thread then takes it from there, finishes it, and hands it on. The buffers each stage needs are a fixed set, reused from block to block, so the queues can't grow without bound.

A block's path through the service layout

1The gridScannerHuffman decode2Pit crewService threadprepare: MTF3Pit bayPrepared queuewaits for a team4On trackA team of threebuild and walk5Pit bayFinishing queuewalked blocks6Pit crewService threadfinish: RLE1, CRC7Finish lineReaderoutput in orderEither service thread does either job: one crew for both pit stops. A sketch of the stages and queues, not timing: the car is one block, and its drive shows the order of its stops, not how long each takes. Coral is work on a service thread (the pit crew), blue work on a team (on the track), green the scanner, the queues and the reader. A service thread that becomes free finishes a walked block first, unless the prepared queue is empty, in which case it prepares one.

A free service thread has to choose between preparing and finishing. Each time it picks its next job, it finishes first, because finishing frees buffers and gets output to the reader. The exception is an empty prepared queue: then it prepares, because an idle team wastes three threads. The rule acts only at that choice. A thread already in the middle of a finish isn't interrupted, so an empty queue isn't always refilled at once.

A service thread also won't start preparing while a set number of blocks already wait in the prepared queue. That keeps preparing from running ahead and holding buffers that finishing needs. The number is the admission threshold, and it is two, one per team. Section 6 comes back to it.

items.title: 2. Why might it pay, and why might it not?
items.text:
Why it might pay. In 0.2.5's plain teams, a team's two helpers had nothing to do for roughly a third of each block, while the leader ran MTF and the finish alone. 0.2.6 fills that time by overlapping, at a price: the leader leaves the build, so the shared part of each block runs on one thread fewer. The figure shows the difference over time.

A team's time, before and after the pit crew

0.2.6: the leader makes its own pit stopsLeaderfinish n−1MTF n+1walk nHelperbuild nwalk nHelperbuild nwalk nBlock n’s build runs on two threads while the leader is in the pits.Service layout: a pit crew makes the stopsTeambuild nwalk nbuild n+2Teambuild nwalk nbuild n+2Teambuild nwalk nbuild n+2Service 1finishMTFfinishService 2MTFfinishMTFTeam threads only build and walk; the crew serves both teams.time (schematic, not to scale)on track: build and walkin the pits: MTF and finish Schematic, from the decoder's code, not measured: the widths are not durations. Coral is the one-thread work (in the pits), blue the shared build and walk (on the track). n is the block the team is inverting. In the service layout the service threads' jobs come from both teams' blocks.

In the service layout no team member leaves the build and walk to run MTF or the finish. The teams can still wait for those stages, for a prepared block or for free buffers, as section 6 shows.

Why it might not. There are three costs. First, at a setting of ten the layout makes two teams, not three, so only two blocks are inverted at once. Second, all the one-thread work of every block goes through the service threads. If they can't keep up, both teams wait for them. Third, every block now crosses between threads twice, from a service thread to a team and back, and each hand-off takes some time.

Before the first run, a model built from earlier single-thread measurements put the one-thread work at about 0.57 nanoseconds per byte of output. At the rate the decoder then reached on this machine, that came to about 0.8 of one core. On paper, then, one service thread looked nearly enough. The model said itself that its inputs came from another machine and another layout.

items.title: 3. Why isn't one service thread enough?
items.text:
The first run (pull request 251) was registered. Its first attempt failed its noise check, which runs two copies of the same decoder under different names, and was discarded. An unchanged rerun was registered before it ran, and passed that check at 1.003. The test file is the Wikidata sample: 11.85 MB of bzip2 that decodes to 209.7 MB. Each arm decoded it 20 times, the arms taking turns in each round.

Speed here and below is the reference's elapsed time over the arm's, so above 1 means the arm is faster. CPU is the reference's processor time over the arm's, all threads added up, so above 1 means the arm spends less. Both are paired round by round. Each ratio is the geometric mean of the 20 rounds' ratios, and its 95% interval is the uncertainty of that estimate within one run. It is not the range of the individual rounds.

With one service thread beside three teams of three, at a setting of ten, the decoder was much slower than the default, on ten decoding threads to its nine. The trace showed why. The service thread was marked busy 96% of the time, finished blocks backed up behind it, and the teams waited for it. Moving the one-thread work onto one thread had made that thread the bottleneck. The model had put the work at 0.8 of a core, but in practice one thread couldn't keep up with three teams. No run tried one service thread with two teams. Two teams would change how much work reaches it, so that case is open.

The run's judged comparisons with the default, each arm written as teams × team size + service threads:

arm, at its setting speed (95%) CPU (95%) 3 × 3 + 1, at ten 0.799 (0.786–0.812) 1.099 (1.079–1.118) 3 × 3 + 2, at twelve 1.058 (1.035–1.081) 0.901 (0.888–0.914)

The second row is two service threads beside three teams of three, at a setting of twelve. It was 5.8% faster than the default, but spent 11% more processor time and 8 MB more peak memory, on eleven decoding threads to the default's nine. A gain bought with more threads and more processor time is no reason to change a default, so we didn't pursue it.

The run also measured the layout this post is about, two teams of three plus two service threads, at a setting of ten. It was 4.5% faster than the default, with 12% less processor time and 10 MB less peak memory. But that comparison was reported, not registered as a decision. And the run had no plain two-team arm, so it couldn't say whether the gain came from the service threads or simply from running two teams. The next run was designed to answer both.

items.title: 4. Did two service threads beat the default?
items.text:
The second run (pull request 258) judged three comparisons, each against an arm chosen to answer one question:

  • Against the default: is the service layout faster than 0.2.6 at a setting of ten?
  • Against plain two teams: two teams of three without service threads, each leader doing its own MTF and finish, at the same setting. Do the service threads make the difference?
  • Two pipelined teams against the default: 0.2.6's own pipelined teams, but two of them. Does today's decoder gain just from running two teams?

The run passed every validity check, including its noise check at 0.997. The judged comparisons:

comparison (decoding threads) speed (95%) CPU (95%) service vs default (8 vs 9) 1.045 (1.017–1.073) 1.146 (1.123–1.170) service vs plain two teams (8 vs 6) 1.402 (1.368–1.437) 0.941 (0.924–0.959) two pipelined teams vs default (6 vs 9) 0.866 (0.851–0.881) 1.214 (1.196–1.233)

The service layout beat the default, by the margin the first run had reported. Its CPU ratio of 1.146 means it spent 0.873 of the default's processor time. That is 12.7% less, or between about 11% and 14.5% less over the interval. By the rule fixed before the run, a speed gain without a processor-time cost, together with a gain over plain two teams, was the outcome "for the service layout".

The controls rule out the simplest explanation. Two teams alone did not reproduce the gain. Plain two teams were far slower than the service layout, and 0.2.6's pipelined teams, cut to two, reached only 0.866 of the default's speed. So the win doesn't come from having two teams instead of three. The figure puts the four arms' costs side by side, from the run's medians.

Time, processor time and memory, at a thread setting of ten

Elapsed, s (lower is faster)0.2.6 default0.144Service layout0.137Two pipelined teams0.166Plain two teams0.193Processor time, s0.2.6 default1.026Service layout0.895Two pipelined teams0.850Plain two teams0.847Peak memory, MB0.2.6 default74Service layout64Two pipelined teams57Plain two teams52Bars start at zero. Measured, the test machine, medians of 20 rounds of the registered run (pull request 258). The service layout (green) is the only arm both faster and cheaper than the default (blue); the two two-team arms without service threads are cheaper but slower.

Every two-team arm spent less processor time than the default. The service threads cost some of that back, since the service layout spent about 6% more than plain two teams, but it alone is faster than the default as well. The medians agree with the paired ratios without replacing them, because the ratios are computed round by round.

What the controls don't separate. The comparison with plain two teams measures everything the layout changes at once: two more threads, the one-thread work moved onto them, the feeder, the queues and the hand-offs. They were not varied separately. The run is evidence for the layout as a package, not for any one of its parts.

The model made before the run had predicted each control. Each came out on the predicted side, and each a little beyond it:
